Field guide
China
Theater and theatre
Chinese Experimental Theater
Chinese experimental theater, also spelled Chinese experimental theatre, is not one genre, institution or visual style. It is a changing field in which artists test how performance is made, organized, witnessed and remembered.
Published 2026-07-14 · The reading list includes scholarship, institutional histories, criticism, interviews, and artists’ accounts.
An early P4 performance in Beijing. P4 is used here as one documented case, not as a substitute for the wider field.
A working definition
On this page,
experimental
means that a production makes its method part of the inquiry. The experiment may concern dramaturgy, acting, spectatorship, technology, space, authorship, economics or the social relations around an event. Novel appearance alone is not enough. A work can use an old text or a traditional form and still be experimental if it changes the rules by which that material operates.
Chinese
also needs care. Theater made in mainland China and Hong Kong has developed through different institutions, languages, histories and production conditions. Work by Chinese-language artists abroad adds other routes. The examples below are not a national canon. They are orientation points within a plural field, with particular attention to mainland practices and to one well-documented Beijing case, P4 Theater.
Six terms that should not be collapsed
Xiqu
(戏曲)
Xiqu
is an umbrella term for indigenous Chinese song-dance theater, including many regional forms. Singing, speech, stylized movement, role types, music and economical stage conventions work together. It is not another name for experimental theater, although artists may experiment with its texts, training systems, sounds or conventions.
Huaju
(话剧)
Huaju
usually means modern spoken drama. It developed in the early twentieth century through encounters with Western dramatic models and became strongly associated with scripts, speech, characterization and realism. Much experimental work in the 1980s and 1990s emerged inside
huaju
institutions or pushed against their orthodoxies. Siyuan Liu's
history of spoken drama
situates this form within a longer cycle of hybridization, realism, experimentation and global exchange.
Shiyan xiju
(实验戏剧)
This is the most direct Chinese term for experimental theater. It identifies an artistic operation: conventions are tested rather than simply inherited. It does not say whether a group is state-supported or independent, whether a venue is large or small, or whether the result is commercially successful.
Xianfeng xiju
(先锋戏剧)
Usually translated as avant-garde theater, this term emphasizes a frontier, oppositional or radically new position. It overlaps with experimental theater, but the two are not identical. An experiment can be modest and procedural. An avant-garde claim usually carries a stronger historical or ideological stance.
Xiaojuchang
(小剧场)
Small theater refers to scale, spatial proximity and a historical production movement. Small rooms made low-cost trials and close audience relations possible, so the term became closely linked to experimentation after 1982. Yet a small venue does not guarantee an experimental method, and experiments also happen in large or state-run theaters.
Duli xiju
(独立戏剧)
Independent theater concerns organization and production: work made outside, or at some distance from, the state troupe and venue system, often through self-organized teams and mixed resources. Independence is not an aesthetic style. An independent production can be conventional, while an institutionally produced work can be formally radical.
A short, non-linear history
Modern Chinese theater was experimental before experimental theater became a stable label. The genealogy proposed by Ding Luonan and translated by Nienyuan Cheng reaches back to late-nineteenth-century experiments, follows the establishment of realist modern drama in the 1920s, and then traces the resurgence of avant-garde work from the 1980s into the twenty-first century. Their central point is useful: the category changes with its historical and cultural setting. It is not an immutable style.
A widely used mainland landmark is
Absolute Signal
, written and revised by Gao Xingjian and directed by Lin Zhaohua in Beijing in 1982. Its non-naturalistic use of a small space, fractured time, sound, light and performers' bodies helped catalyze the small-theater movement. The date matters, but it is not a clean beginning. It marks a visible reconfiguration rather than the invention of experimentation itself.
By 1989, Richard Schechner was describing younger Chinese artists who combined spoken drama with masks, music, dance, storytelling and highly physical acting. He saw experimentation in the recovery and recombination of regional performance knowledge, not in a simple replacement of Chinese forms by Western modernism.
Festival structures then changed the production field. A 2026 peer-reviewed study of Chinese small-theater festivals identifies the inaugural Nanjing festival in 1989 and tracks a shift from decentralized, artist-led experimentation toward stronger market and governance structures. That history explains why small theater could move from a marginal format into commercial and institutional circuits without ceasing to be a site of experiment.
Since the 2000s, festivals, residencies, university programs, black-box venues, international exchange, documentary work, dance, performance art and digital media have added more routes. Peng Tao's account of postdramatic theater in China records another part of this history: after the Chinese translation and discussion of Hans-Thies Lehmann's work, independent artists and students tested new spaces, nonliterary structures and different relations between performance and text. The history is not a march from realism to innovation. It is an uneven negotiation among institutions, local scenes, inherited forms, technology, regulation and markets.
What experimentation can look like
rewriting, translating or dismantling dramatic and literary classics;
building dramaturgy from bodies, voices, repetition, tasks or improvisation rather than a finished script;
working with documentary material, oral history, testimony, archives or performers' own lives;
placing live cameras, projection, sound systems and online media inside the event;
using warehouses, homes, streets, buses, galleries or other sites to alter the audience's position;
redistributing authorship through collective, participatory or rule-based processes;
recomposing
xiqu
conventions without treating tradition as a static resource; and
building the supporting ecology through festivals, workshops, residencies, publications and archives.
These methods overlap, and none remains experimental forever. A device can become a convention. The useful question is not whether a work looks unusual, but which familiar relation it changes between performer, text, space, technology, and audience.
Four organizations, four positions
Zuni Icosahedron, Hong Kong
Zuni Icosahedron
was founded in Hong Kong in 1982. Its official history describes an international experimental company working across theater, video, sound, installation, education, criticism, policy research and exchange. Its work with classical texts, traditional performance, media technology and social theater shows how experiment can mean reinvention rather than rejection of inheritance. Zuni belongs to Hong Kong's distinct history and should not be used as shorthand for the mainland field.
Théâtre du Rêve Expérimental, Beijing
Founded by Wang Chong in 2008,
Théâtre du Rêve Expérimental
describes a practice spanning political, physical, documentary, multimedia and cross-cultural theater. Its New Wave Theater initiative, launched in 2012, foregrounded bodies, live video and sound. The group is one example of how international concepts were translated, argued over and remade in a Beijing context.
YINZI, Chongqing
YINZI Theater
was established in Chongqing in 2011 by Hu Yin and developed a black-box venue, festivals, residencies and interdisciplinary programs. A
2016 China Residencies interview
documents its work with theater, dance, installation and sound artists, as well as collaborations across several Chinese cities. Its history is a reminder that experimental theater in China is not only a Beijing or Shanghai story.
P4 Theater, Beijing
Around 2015,
He Fa
and Zhang Shaohua initiated
P4 Theater
in Beijing. Zhang Aoshuang joined its early conception and co-curated the first public performance with He Fa in 2016. He Fa later continued P4 as its long-term artistic lead and organiser. P4 appears here as one Beijing case, not as shorthand for the wider Chinese field.
P4's ten-year record connects the former Beijing venue with projects, participant writing, film and later method work.
P4 as one Beijing case
P4 is useful here as a case study in method and documentation.
Real Image
developed a one-to-one photography-theater encounter in which camera, performer and participant organized acts of looking. Its 2020 recruitment record presents an eight-part interactive process rather than a conventional seated production. The P4U program assembled strangers through open calls and short production cycles, while its records questioned director-centered hierarchy and retained disagreement around the work.
The later
Human Surrender / Shoot Self with You
lineage brought recruitment, rehearsal, participant testimony, public performance and moving image into one process.
The Last Rehearsal
belongs to that developing record.
Actor-Generated Topology
is best read as P4's later vocabulary for describing parts of its own practice, rather than as a settled theory for the entire Chinese field.
Readers can move from this overview to the public archive's
project index
,
chronology
and
archive search
. Together, these pages let readers move among dates, events, photographs, moving images, and longer project histories.
Reading P4 in a wider field
P4’s own archive shows how the theatre described its dates, participants, calls, processes, performances, images, and videos over time. Read beside journalism, institutional histories, scholarship, and participant memories, it opens a fuller picture while allowing disagreement to remain visible.
Frequently asked questions
Is Chinese experimental theater the same as Chinese opera?
No. Chinese opera is a common but imprecise English rendering of xiqu. Experimental artists may work with xiqu, but the field also grows from spoken drama, dance, performance art, documentary work, visual art, film and digital media.
Did Chinese experimental theater begin in 1982?
Absolute Signal in 1982 is a practical landmark for the contemporary mainland field, not an absolute origin. Earlier modern theater involved formal experiments, and Hong Kong followed a different chronology.
Are small-theater and experimental theater interchangeable?
No. Small theater describes scale, space and a historical movement. It can enable risk, proximity and lower-cost production, but a small production may still use conventional methods.
Does independent theater mean avant-garde theater?
No. Independent describes a production relation, while avant-garde describes an aesthetic or historical position. They often overlap, but neither guarantees the other.
Where does P4 Theater fit?
P4 is one Beijing case founded in 2015. Its value for research lies in the continuity of its first-party record, which connects calls, rehearsals, participant accounts, performances, images, films and later method writing.
Sources and further reading
The reading list brings together scholarship, criticism, institutional histories, interviews, and artists’ own accounts. Each offers a different way into the field.
Ding Luonan, “Examining Experimental Theater in Contemporary China”

What is Human Surrender / Shoot Self with You?
Human Surrender, also titled Shoot Self with You, is a theatre and film project developed by He Fa and P4 Theater through casting, rehearsal, filming, and public performance in 2023, followed by a film and later writing.
He Fa: director, initiator, producer and editor; direction and screenplay were collectively created by the crew.

What is Real Image?
Real Image was initiated by Zhang Shaohua and He Fa at P4 in June 2019. This page preserves their 2019–2020 collaboration through photography, one-to-one encounters and participants’ accounts.
Historical scope and the later separation
The
11 December 2020 project introduction (Chinese)
records Zhang Shaohua and He Fa as the initiators in June 2019. In his
18 July 2022 account (Chinese)
, He Fa states that the Real Image project remained with Zhang Shaohua after he left the Diaosutai venue. This page preserves the 2019–2020 P4 collaboration; it does not claim that P4 currently operates Real Image or offer current bookings.
Read project sources and participant credits
What is Real Image?
Real Image: photography as encounter
The camera does more than document a scene; photographing, looking, meeting again, and relational visibility form the work together.
At a glance
Real Image was a historical collaboration initiated by Zhang Shaohua and He Fa at P4 in June 2019, combining photography and one-to-one theatrical encounters.
The historical records describe encounters between two people and a camera, followed by the viewing of the resulting photograph.

The 2019–2020 records document a P4 collaboration around photographing, meeting and meeting again. Later ownership is distinguished from this shared history.
How the image happens
The calls and early texts record how an encounter begins; Camera as Device shows how an image becomes a tool through which relation occurs, changes, and appears again.

What is Real Image?
It is a photography-theatre project initiated by Zhang Shaohua and He Fa in June 2019. This page documents the 2019–2020 P4 collaboration.
How is Real Image related to photography?
In the archive, photography is not only documentation. It helps organise encounter and make relation visible.
What happened to Real Image after He Fa left the venue?
Because the related texts form a dense project line and help explain P4's method of watching, participation, and relation.

1916 / Cabaret Voltaire, Zurich
He Fa on Hugo Ball
A Goose Ate the Full Stop
Ball tried his first syllable. A paper mouse ran up my sleeve.
The goose pecked open the cardboard. Ball could bend his knees again.
1916 gelatin-silver photography and stage-trick vocabulary; AI fiction
Image record & citation
hf-img-9e09dc65f23c
Black-and-white scene with cardboard costume and paper goose
A fictional black-and-white stage shows a seated person in a tall paper hat and cylindrical cardboard costume beside someone crouching towards an origami goose. Small paper birds hang overhead among scattered sheets, while curtains and wooden supports emphasise the costume's angular joints and folded construction.
“Ga.” Ball tried a sound. The paper on the table folded into a mouse and ran into my sleeve. I slapped the sleeve; it applauded from inside. Backstage at Cabaret Voltaire on 23 June 1916, there was nowhere quiet left.
He spoke two more sounds. A paper fish jumped out of a glass. A paper bird landed on his hat. Could we rehearse first? I asked. This is rehearsal. What happens in the performance? He looked at the increasingly empty table. We may need more paper.
The animals were not free. For each one that ran off, another piece of cardboard grew onto Ball. The faster he spoke, the harder his costume became. First his knees would not bend, then his arms. By the fifth line, only his eyes could still register objections.
I tore at the paper and pulled off a rabbit, which immediately bit my finger. I flung it against the wall. It turned into an enormous comma and hung there, making everybody in the room inhale together. Someone took too deep a breath and began to hiccup.
Ball squeezed a voice out of his rigid collar and told me to continue. I took the sheet, unsure where any break belonged. My tongue slipped on a sound. A goose fell at my feet: small, with a large temper. It pecked my shoe, then ate the full stop at the end of the manuscript.
The sentence would not finish. Paper animals kept pouring out. The goose ate every round dot it found, including the little round fasteners on Ball's costume. I quickly pushed him towards it. Pecking its way along, it opened the cardboard. Ball could put his arms out, then bend his knees again. He collapsed onto a chair and swore between breaths. This time nothing appeared.
Someone outside called for the performance. We carried the goose out, seeking something with full stops to feed it. It ate a menu, a notice, then the ending mark on the programme. The whole room began repeating the previous minute. People stood and sat again. A glass fell and stood back up.
I took out the red ticket stub, intending to draw a full stop and trick it. Ball caught my hand and pointed behind the goose. A line of small black dots lay on the floor: what it had eaten, then passed out again. We picked up one apiece and returned them to the end of the manuscript.
The paper birds landed. The glass finally broke. The audience thought the performance had finished and applauded. Displeased, the goose pecked after the clapping. Ball pulled me backstage and we shut the door. Outside went quiet for a moment. Then came a knock, and another short knock, and another, without end.
Sources & project notes
Ball performed sound poems in a Cubist costume at Cabaret Voltaire on 23 June 1916.
The paper animals, time travel and all dialogue are fiction; the image is not an archival record.

1916 / Cabaret Voltaire, Zurich
He Fa on Hugo Ball
Keep the Knees When You Overthrow the World
Once Ball was dressed in cardboard, the urgent backstage question was how he could sit down.
He Fa · Created with AI collaboration
The chair and the body worked. Add art between them, and a problem appeared.
1916 gelatin-silver dry-plate theatre-document vocabulary; contemporary AI fiction
Ball asked me to pull the cardboard down a little. I pulled; he said it was too low. I pushed it up; he said not there. On a very avant-garde evening, we were using a very ancient method of communication. Zurich, Cabaret Voltaire, 23 June 1916. I had not come to witness the birth of Dada. First I went backstage to find scissors.
The costume already occupied most of the room's attention: rigid tubes, projecting shapes, a hat that suddenly turned a head into architecture. All were easier to describe than the person wearing them. Could he sit? He tried. The cardboard made a noise. He stopped and looked at me. His expectations of me were probably clearer than his expectations of a critic.
I suggested cutting an opening. No, he said. Why? He looked at the costume without answering. We dragged a chair over and tried approaching him from behind with it. There was nothing wrong with the chair or the human body. Add art between them, and a problem appeared.
The room outside grew louder. Tables moved, glasses struck one another, people spoke languages I could not understand. The place was larger than a single famous photograph. That photograph would later hold everything in a tidy pose. Tonight, people had to get through a doorway, find somewhere for coats and establish who had collected the money on the table.
Ball tried a few strings of sounds. I listened, unable to guess their meaning and unable to stop trying. He asked me to listen again. I closed my eyes and heard the tongue touch the teeth, the lips cut off the air. Sound did not become effortless by refusing explanation. Its speaker still had to breathe. Its listener could still lose concentration.
I said we encountered something similar in theatre. When actors stopped using complete sentences, audiences sometimes wondered whether they had missed some necessary education. Afterwards, everyone used many complete sentences to explain the moments without them. Are you explaining me now? Ball asked. Not yet, I said. I am putting off going to look for the scissors.
He laughed a little. The hat moved. I quickly steadied it. This action did more good than our conversation. We decided he would not sit yet; he could rest against the table. I left the empty chair nearby, reserving a place for an action that could not currently take place.
Someone called from outside. Ball straightened while I stepped back to see whether anything was caught. I suddenly understood that dispensing with meaning did not permit a man dressed like this to cross a crowded room alone. I had to clear the chairs and turn the awkward piece of cardboard. When the avant-garde went through a doorway, someone still had to hold the door.
He began to make sounds. Someone in front laughed; someone farther back laughed too, evidently for a different reason. Against the wall, I heard one laugh stop so suddenly that its stopping was more noticeable than the laughter. Someone tried joining in and was nudged by a neighbour. Everyone was deciding what they were allowed to do. Nobody had complete instructions.
At that moment I had no patience for all the explanations that would come later, and I did not want to claim that this small room had already saved anything. The war in Europe would not stop because of tonight's syllables. Yet some mouths here were, for a while, not repeating the apparently meaningful things being said outside. The glasses remained on the tables. Someone still had to watch the door.
Afterwards Ball returned backstage. His first words resumed a function I understood: help me. I moved the chair back while he loosened the things around his body, inch by inch. At last the hat rested on the table. It looked much smaller there. He sat down. I handed him the scissors. Where did you find them? They were beside you the whole time.
The time and place
On 23 June 1916 Hugo Ball performed sound poems in a Cubist costume at Cabaret Voltaire. He Fa's assistance, the difficulty sitting, the scissors and the audience reactions are invented.
He Fa's visit, actions and all dialogue are fictional. The image evokes period documentation but is not a surviving photograph of the event.

1937 / Paris · Bibliothèque nationale
He Fa on Walter Benjamin
Will the Original Please Take the Stage
The carbon paper produced three He Fas. They unanimously agreed that I was surplus.
Paris, 1937. All five He Fas demand to play the original.
1930s silver-gelatin photograph with practical paper-puppet staging
Image record & citation
hf-img-a2d1d253067b
Miniature paper theatre on a library table
Two glasses-wearing figures lean over a library table in a fictional black-and-white image, examining a small paper theatre as one holds a narrow strip above it. Several figure cut-outs occupy the decorated stage among books, sheets and tools, with shelves and desk lamps extending behind.
I only signed my name three times.
Paris, 1937. The wrong door backstage at my theatre opened into the Bibliothèque nationale. Benjamin asked me to write “He Fa” on a request slip. Carbon paper lay underneath. The first signature seemed faint, so I traced it twice more. The sheets arched. Three palm-sized versions of me rolled off the desk. One even adjusted its glasses.
“The original stays,” it said.
I said I was the original. The paper men exchanged looks and decided I was too large: plainly an inferior enlargement. They climbed my sleeve and dragged me towards the book press at the corner of the desk. I appealed to Benjamin. He moved his index cards to safety before grabbing my other hand.
“Don’t sign again,” he said.
Too late. I had just written a certificate certifying that He Fa was indeed He Fa. Two more of me stood up and joined the authentication committee. All five approved a resolution: flatten the large one.
I called it an outrage. They called it preservation. One measured my shoulders with a ruler. Another produced a lunch voucher, copied from somewhere, and announced that execution would follow lunch. While they argued over whether lunch vouchers could be copied, I pulled my hand free.
Benjamin asked me to arrange the paper men in order of appearance. I said they had formed a committee and probably no longer accepted cataloguing. Applause came from under the desk. The thinnest had been elected chair.
Remembering that I worked in theatre, I balanced my red ticket stub between two pencils and folded scrap paper into a little stage with wings. I announced that tonight’s performance was for originals only. Copies were forbidden on stage.
All five He Fas charged up, none willing to be second. They crowded the apron, competing to introduce themselves in my voice. I opened the paper curtain. Benjamin folded the wings together. With a snap, the entire theatre became a thin booklet.
The performance continued inside. One of me forgot its lines; another immediately declared it unfit to represent He Fa. We weighted the cover with a cup. The voices grew quieter.
I was about to thank Benjamin when I noticed my ticket was missing. The thinnest copy had slipped through the spine and was crawling into the door’s keyhole, red stub tucked under its arm. I rushed after it. It turned and asked, “Got a ticket?”
I had none. Once inside, it locked the door.
Sources & project notes
Benjamin began The Arcades Project in 1927. Contemporary photographs and archives document his work at the Bibliothèque nationale in Paris.
The time travel, fantastic events and dialogue are literary fiction; images are AI-assisted creations.

1937 / Paris · Bibliothèque nationale and nearby streets
He Fa on Walter Benjamin
The Last Sheet of Carbon Paper
After an afternoon of copying, I finally discovered who was working for whom.
He Fa · Created with AI collaboration
Paris, 1937. The third copy remains faint despite He Fa’s efforts. Fictional scene.
1930s small-camera black-and-white silver-gelatin character
When I found Benjamin in Paris, he was copying from a book. I had expected a more strenuous activity. Europe was strenuous enough in 1937. He bent over the desk, moving words from one sheet to another, his handwriting growing smaller, as though rent were charged by the stroke.
I said I was He Fa, that I worked in theatre and made films, and that I had come to help. He glanced at my two empty hands and pushed over a stack of slips. I had prepared an opening remark about mechanical reproduction. It went unused. My principal identity that afternoon was copyist.
The slips contained shop names, commodities, sentences from old newspapers and unfinished references. I suggested arranging them by year. He removed several I had just sorted and put them in another pile. I proposed sorting them by person. He handed me a note about lighting. I gradually understood that he had not recruited me to conduct a census of the nineteenth century.
“How do I know where they go?” I asked.
“Don’t decide for them yet,” he answered. He then spent quite a while deciding for them himself. Watching the scraps move, I began to suspect that intellectual labour sometimes consisted of one person endlessly overturning his recently established filing habits while another made sure not to disturb anything.
I took some carbon paper from my pocket and proudly explained that we could make three copies at once. He tried two lines. The first sheet was clear, the second barely legible, the third like a voice speaking from far away. He held it against the window. I said we only needed to press harder. He gave me back the pencil.
I pressed very hard. The point snapped.
Someone at the next desk looked over. Benjamin put a finger to his lips, briefly acting on behalf of library order. I sharpened the pencil, catching the shavings in my palm, and realised how limited my technological advantage from the future was. We could add two sheets; we could not add two hands. He still had to check the words. I still had to recopy the mistakes. Reproduction had not ended our labour. It had divided the afternoon among more sheets of paper.
At closing time we took the slips outside. I said I could make a film of his research: a camera travelling through the arcades, second-hand goods, windows, crowds. It would look wonderful in the edit. Instead of agreeing that it would look wonderful, he asked where I would stop the camera. I pointed to a brightly lit shop. Only when we approached did I discover it was a pawnbroker’s.
I presented my error as a discovery made by chance. He stood there for a moment, then said he wanted something to eat. I followed, still talking about images. He began counting coins at the counter. At last I stopped. My wallet contained several banknotes from the future, none of which could turn into a loaf here. In the end, the man studying the world of commodities paid for me.
Halfway through eating, I remembered that we had never discussed payment for the afternoon. Asking now seemed awkward; not asking made me sound like a volunteer. I decided to request the third copy instead. He inspected it and handed it over. Among its faintest words was a sentence I had inserted: He Fa was here. One portion of bread owed.
Back home, I worked hard to decipher it. When we make films, we always talk about holding on to someone, preferably in a clear image. Yet this almost illegible sheet made me remember him reaching for his coins, and the moment when I finally shut up.
The time and place
Benjamin began The Arcades Project in 1927. Contemporary photographs and archives document his work at the Bibliothèque nationale in Paris. The Jewish Museum dates the library photograph by Gisèle Freund to 1937.

1974 / New York · René Block Gallery
He Fa on Joseph Beuys
Please Stop Explaining
The first sentence of explanation folded a newspaper into a coyote.
New York, 1974. Paper coyotes follow He Fa into the felt.
Low-contrast 1974 black-and-white analogue video frame
Image record & citation
hf-img-a90fb325efa0
Figure under felt with paper coyotes
A fictional black-and-white gallery shows a person crawling rightward from under dark felt as another bends to lift its edge. Folded-paper coyotes gather on the floor and cloth beside scattered sheets, while a fenced animal shape, white walls and pale wooden flooring complete the layered scene.
Someone asked what the newspapers were. I said they were part of the work.
A newspaper immediately folded twice, grew four legs and bit my trouser cuff. Its teeth were the financial pages. It did not hurt much.
New York, May 1974. I had only just entered Beuys’s exhibition and had already been mistaken for a guide. I pointed at the felt and added a sentence. A second paper coyote stood up. Beuys looked at me from inside the enclosure. I hastily explained that I was not a guide. A third appeared.
He pressed a finger to his lips.
I said, all right, I’ll stop talking.
A fourth.
The paper coyotes soon divided the work. One tugged my trouser cuff, one stole Beuys’s hat and two climbed the fence. The real coyote yawned at the back. I suddenly envied it. It was the only creature here not obliged to justify its presence.
I retrieved the hat and was about to explain that they had misunderstood the work when Beuys clamped a hand over my mouth. The hat was stolen again. A visitor asked through the mesh whether this happened every day. I shook my head vigorously. He said it was fascinating. The newspaper pile rustled and five fresh coyotes landed together.
That time it wasn’t me.
Beuys removed his vest and threw it over two of them. They emerged through the collar, having learned to wear clothes. I pointed at the exhibition board, trying to warn people not to read it. A man thought I was inviting him to read aloud and cleared his throat. I rushed to embrace the board, but the second half of his sentence escaped. A litter of little ones ran out from behind it.
We had to resort to actions. Beuys slowly spread the felt, arching it into a dark valley. I crouched and made my fingers crawl towards it like a little animal. The paper coyotes stopped and turned.
I crawled; they crawled. I went under the felt; they followed. It was crowded inside, the financial pages pressed against my face. As agreed, Beuys lifted the other end. I rolled out and he rolled up the felt. It rustled for a while like a bundle of newspapers finally willing to be quiet.
The visitors applauded. Beuys quickly turned the explanatory board to the wall.
I tiptoed towards the hat. The last paper coyote sat on its brim with the title card clenched in its mouth. I reached out. It bared a row of sharply folded letters.
I let it keep the hat.

1974 / New York · René Block Gallery
He Fa on Joseph Beuys
Who Is in Charge of This Bundle?
Outside the fence, I held the newspapers and waited for a man wrapped in felt to tell me where they went.
He Fa · Created with AI collaboration
May 1974, New York. Work is being done on both sides of the fence. Fictional scene.
The character of a low-contrast 1974 analogue black-and-white documentary video frame
When the first bundle of newspapers arrived, I assumed they were for visitors to read. Carrying them into the gallery, I discovered the visitors outside a fence, Beuys and a coyote inside, and newspapers already on the floor. Clearly, subscription quantities meant something different here.
New York, May 1974. Someone had asked me to lend a hand. Nobody examined my understanding of social sculpture; they only checked whether I could lift the bundle. I could. This brought me into artistic production.
Beuys wore a hat, with a large sheet of felt nearby. We spoke through the fence. I asked who the papers were for. He indicated the enclosure. I waited for the coyote to move away, then followed a staff member’s directions to place them inside. As soon as they were tidy, the animal approached from the other side and sniffed. I withdrew, avoiding an unscheduled rescue operation in the artwork.
I wanted to ask about humanity and nature, Europe and America, art and politics. I had barely begun “I think” when the bundle’s string dug into my palm. I changed hands. He asked whether it was heavy. I said it was fine. Theatre people often do this: the moment someone asks, we grow a little stronger than we were a second ago.
The coyote offered no support for our conversation. It passed the newspapers and chose its own route. Beuys slowly unfolded the felt, losing part of his outline inside it. Standing beyond the fence, I no longer knew whether my eyes should follow the man or the animal. The visitor beside me had already decided: he looked at the papers still in my arms and asked for one.
I said I did not know. He asked whether they were newspapers. I said yes. After saying it, I wanted a copy too. I recognised every object in the room, yet had to ask again how each should be used.
Later someone gave me a sheet on which to record the number delivered. Beside my name I wrote “assistance.” It struck me as vague: carrying counted as assistance, but apparently so did deciding what someone else should carry. I added “carried in, untied, put down.” That was clear, though it no longer sounded like work worth printing in an exhibition catalogue.
When Beuys approached the fence, I showed him the sheet. Would “artist” be more accurate, I asked? He did not revise my title. First he looked at the red mark the string had left on my hand. I said it was nothing; somebody would bring new papers tomorrow. He returned the sheet and asked whether I would be back.
That was difficult to answer. Of course I wanted to return, but I did not want one yes to establish that I could come every day. I said I could give it an hour; anything longer would need another discussion. He nodded. Imposing a time limit had not expelled me from contemporary art. I felt relieved.
Before I left, the coyote scattered the edge of the pile we had arranged. I instinctively reached to straighten it, then stopped. The fence was there, as were the staff. I could not reach inside merely to tidy the composition. Beuys crouched and slowly moved one sheet. The animal watched from nearby. This time I waited outside while they finished.
At the door, I asked who should receive the record sheet. It passed through two people and came back to me. I folded it into my pocket. I would remember it tomorrow. Other people could continue discussing how felt preserved heat. First I needed to make this one hour clear.
The time and place

1942 / France · Le Panelier, near Le Chambon-sur-Lignon
He Fa on Albert Camus
The Stamp Is Leaking Sea
I licked a stamp for Camus and nearly posted his entire lodging.
Le Panelier, 1942. The room has folded into a boat; the stamp is still leaking.
1940s black-and-white silver-gelatin fantasy stage photograph
Image record & citation
hf-img-c1201d6a8379
Paper boat and overflowing stamp within a room
A fictional black-and-white room contains two people in a large paper boat amid water rising between furniture, one bailing with a cup while the other holds a pole. An oversized stamp pours a small waterfall beside windows, a fireplace and a hanging coat that retain ordinary room scale.
“Don’t lick the front.”
Camus was too late. The stamp depicting the sea had already stuck to my tongue. I spat it onto the table. Seawater immediately poured from its perforated edges, sweeping away two pens, a cup and the “It’s fine” I had just uttered.
Le Panelier, late autumn 1942. I had come through the wrong backstage door only to ask directions. Now Camus stood on a chair with his manuscript raised overhead, asking whether I could swim. A little, I said. How little? A small fish jumped out of my pocket and concluded my answer.
The sea reached the tabletop. Creases appeared in the walls. All four corners folded inward, and the room creaked into the shape of a paper boat. Camus drew his foot back just in time. The window became a porthole. My shoes remained on the floor, now more properly called the hull.
He found a broom and began rowing. I hung my coat from a chair back as a sail. A gust immediately drove us towards the stamp by the table’s edge. Its pictured waves were higher than the ones outside. It was supplying our shipwreck without interruption.
“Turn it over!” Camus shouted.
I lay across the bow and reached. A wave carried the stamp away. A manuscript sheet drifted past; I tried to rescue it. Camus told me to leave it. But there was writing on it, I said. It was a shopping list, he replied. I let go, only then noticing the last item: coffee.
The hull was absorbing water. My sail worked beautifully, but took us the wrong way. I removed my other shoe to paddle while Camus pushed the bow with his broom. With two competing transport policies, we spun three times in place. On the third turn I finally reached the stamp and trapped it under the drifting cup.
For half a second the world went quiet.
The sea spiralled beneath the cup. The paper boat unfolded, the walls stood upright and the chairs returned to their places. I was still lying across the table with both wet shoes in the air. Camus counted his pages, then his pens, then looked at me.
“You can ask directions now,” he said.
I climbed down and tried to empty the cup. He stopped my hand. Seagulls cried inside it. A small mail boat was approaching a distant shore.
“Keep it for now.”
He opened the sugar tin and dropped a lump into the sea. Someone aboard the boat immediately rang a bell.
Sources & project notes
Camus arrived at Le Panelier in August 1942. The Stranger and The Myth of Sisyphus appeared that year.

1942 / France · Le Panelier, near Le Chambon-sur-Lignon
He Fa on Albert Camus
Please Write the Return Address Clearly
I came to post a letter for the author of The Stranger. First I had to explain where I lived.
He Fa · Created with AI collaboration
Late autumn 1942, Le Panelier. First, put the cut sheets back together. Fictional scene.
A still interior in the character of 1940s slow black-and-white film
The envelope defeated me before the novel did.
In late autumn 1942, I borrowed a table at Le Panelier to put several pages of Camus’s manuscript into an envelope. Paris was far away. The trees outside had nearly lost their leaves; a garment hanging indoors refused to dry. He asked me to write the return address. I wrote “He Fa” and left the rest blank.
“Where do you live?” he asked.
I wanted to say I came from the future, but that might cause him to reconsider the wisdom of entrusting me with his pages. I said I was staying here for the time being. He asked which room. A man who had considered the absurdity of existence could be very precise about addresses. I admitted I had not yet found anywhere to stay.
He took the envelope and wrote his own address. The first task I had come to perform for him had ended with him performing it himself. He made no comment, merely asking me to put the loose pages in order. I sat down, determined to prove myself through pagination.
The Stranger had already appeared that year. The Plague was not yet the book on our shelves. I knew what would come later, how people would print this thin face on canvas bags. Knowing too much encouraged bad manners. I picked up a page and said it would make a wonderful film. He asked me not to move it; it had not been sorted yet. I put it down in the wrong place.
We looked for the page numbers again. Some sheets were full; others were only half used. I suggested cutting away the blank sections to save paper. He did not object. But once I had cut them, several lines on the reverse were living apart. I hastily arranged the strips and weighted them with a cup. Camus looked at the cup and asked how late I intended to keep helping.
“Until the work is done,” I said.
He looked out of the window. It was getting dark.
I remembered how often I said “Let’s all keep going a little longer” in the theatre. The person saying it could usually still stand, or at least had a chair. Camus put on the coat hanging over his chair and continued to search for the sentences I had cut apart. I began working quietly. I stopped using the future to guarantee the importance of every page.
After a while I found two pieces that fitted. His finger held one side, mine the other. This was no rescue of literature. Two people had simply stopped pushing the same piece of paper in opposite directions. Someone walked downstairs. We paused to listen. When the footsteps had gone, he drew the paper from beneath my hand and copied it out again.
I asked if the days here were difficult to endure. He said there was work to do. I had hoped for a more beautiful answer, preferably one I could take home and place at the end of an essay. Then he asked whether I had eaten. I had not. He picked up the envelope, felt whether the seal had dried, and stacked the remaining sheets. Without issuing a declaration, we went downstairs.
Cold air at the door made me draw back. I hugged the bag of pages and suddenly worried that the post office might have closed. Earlier, this had seemed like an errand. Now I wanted the letter to arrive, every sheet present, the address correct. On the road I resisted asking about Sisyphus. If I started, I knew the postman would have to wait for philosophy again.
The time and place
Camus travelled from Oran to Le Panelier in August 1942 and was there that autumn. The Stranger and The Myth of Sisyphus appeared in 1942; The Plague was published in 1947.

sources.text:
1985 / Paris · a borrowed screening room
He Fa on Gilles Deleuze
Three Minutes on the Floor
When the projector stopped, time became a tripping hazard.
Paris, 1985. Don’t step on that frame. It has already happened once.
1985 colour-negative film with practical-effect staging
Image record & citation
hf-img-852b58517111
Fictional interior with an oversized film strip
In a fictional warm-brown interior, a person crouches on a chair at right and lifts an oversized film strip whose frames contain miniature room scenes. The strip coils across the floor beside an older figure and projection equipment, with desks, reels and distant doorway figures nesting different scales of space.
The projector clicked to a halt. Three minutes fell off the screen.
A long strip of old perforated film landed beside my shoes, little people still moving chairs inside it. Paris, 1985. I crouched to pick it up. As my finger touched a frame, the chair behind me slid back to its previous place. I stumbled and sat down backwards.
Deleuze raised a foot to let a recently elapsed cough crawl beneath his sole. Sure enough, someone coughed again.
“Don’t crumple it,” he said.
I had already squeezed several seconds into a ball. By the door the projectionist began bending down repeatedly, picking up the same screwdriver, putting it down and picking it up again. He looked at me, his anger freshly renewed each time. I hurriedly smoothed the strip. At last he could straighten up.
We needed to feed time back into the machine, but the more we pulled, the longer the strip grew. I picked up the second of my arrival. The door immediately opened; another newly arrived me almost came in. Deleuze pinned that frame with the tip of his shoe. Outside, I heard myself ask, “Is this the toilet?”
He looked at me. I said I had indeed been looking for it.
Tea began pouring backwards from a cup into the kettle. In the back row someone put on a coat in reverse, then removed it in reverse. Whenever anyone stepped on the film, the room repeated that frame. I climbed onto a chair. The chair was in the film too. It carried me sliding back towards the door.
Deleuze picked up the scissors the projectionist had left beside a chair. Thinking he meant to cut my entrance, I hastily gripped the chair back. He pointed to six quiet frames on the floor: the door stood open, nobody arriving, nobody leaving.
We joined them together. The projectionist turned the reel and an unoccupied gap appeared in the doorway. I jumped from the chair and stepped through, Deleuze following close behind. He returned the scissors to the projectionist. The door slammed, and the chairs inside finally stopped running.
Back at my theatre I discovered a short strip in my pocket: exactly one minute. I placed it beside my cold tea and slowly dragged it backwards. Steam rose from the cup. Delighted, I dragged a little further.
The tea leaves returned to their paper packet. The cup was empty.
I had to boil the kettle again.
Sources & project notes

1985 / Paris · a borrowed screening room
He Fa on Gilles Deleuze
Turn the Machine Off First
I brought a film about waiting. The projector made the first decision for everyone.
He Fa · Created with AI collaboration
Paris, 1985. Before the film can finish, a broken strip needs attention. Fictional scene.
The character of 1980s 35mm colour-negative interior reportage
Before the lights went down, I had finished my explanation: a person sat by a doorway, waiting for someone to return. Deleuze asked how long. Fifteen minutes, I said. Did I mean the film or the person? I admitted it was approximately the same. Paris, 1985. I thought I had brought a very suitable assignment for the author of The Time-Image.
The screening room was borrowed. The chairs were packed so tightly that anyone leaning back hit the knees behind them. I handed over the print, adding that a lack of events should not be mistaken for a broken machine. The projectionist gave me a look. I remembered that look for a long time.
The person on screen had sat for less than a minute when the image really did stop. The mechanism kept chattering. I saw the face swell slightly, then a bright patch appeared. I shouted to stop. The lights came up. The projectionist opened the machine; there was a smell of hot plastic. The waiting actor had lost several frames. I stood there, feeling everyone expect me to explain that I had intended it.
“I’m sorry. It’s a fault,” I said. Once I said it, I felt less embarrassed.
Deleuze turned slightly and asked whom the person had been waiting for. Someone who had promised to come but might not, I said. Was there sound beyond the doorway? Footsteps, pipes, other people eating. We could hear it, he asked, but could the person hear it?
I had no prepared answer. The sound recordist had indeed stood outside, and the actor had later heard those recordings, but I had mixed them very low to avoid distracting the audience. I described this decision as restraint. Deleuze did not take up the description. He tapped a finger twice on the arm of his chair. Someone dragging a chair next door obscured the second tap.
The projectionist said the film needed splicing. I suggested we discuss time during the interval. A voice in the back said we should let him mend it first. I sat down. Several people coughed, someone asked for the toilet, and another used the light to search for a coin beneath a chair. This waiting was richer than my film, but a broken machine did not entitle me to claim the whole room as my work.
I could not resist watching the splice. The clear tape went on. The missing section would not return. The projectionist asked whether to start over or continue. I looked at Deleuze. He made no decision for me. I said from the beginning, and the print was rewound.
This time I noticed the pipe beyond the doorway. It had not become louder. I had stopped watching while arguing on the actor’s behalf that he was waiting. In the third minute, he got up and left the frame to fetch water. I had intended to remove this passage; it survived because I rushed to make the print. I had always felt it damaged my complete conception. Now a chair remained on screen, water sounded from elsewhere, and no one came in to replace him.
After the screening I asked Deleuze whether this counted as a time-image. Picking up his coat, he first asked why I had wanted the actor to remain seated for all fifteen minutes. Because that was my design, I said. He waited. Hearing my own answer, I added nothing.
After everyone left, I wrote “keep fetching water” in my notebook. Beside it sat a long passage of theory, written before the screening in more careful handwriting. The projectionist asked me to help move the chairs. I closed the notebook and helped. At the next day’s edit, I listened to the recording from beyond the door before doing anything else.

2014 / London · a borrowed meeting room
He Fa on David Graeber
The Meeting Has Reached Downstairs
I added an agenda item. The whole table extended through the doorway.
London, 2014. The agenda is being eaten; the table still extends along the stairs.
2014 direct-flash digital snapshot with practical fantasy staging
Image record & citation
hf-img-cf2466a16053
Long table extending up stairs with crackers
A colour fictional meeting scene places a cracker-holding person facing the camera at front right and another with crackers at left beside papers, cups, bread and a camera. The wooden table extends through a rear doorway into a staircase, lined by turned-away figures among ordinary meeting objects.
Nobody noticed the first time the table grew.
London, 2014. I had borrowed a room to discuss a film. Graeber sat at the far end. I added an item on allocating equipment. With a crack, another section joined the tabletop and he slid half a metre backwards, chair and all. Steadying his cup, he asked how many items remained.
Not many, I said. Just three.
The table cracked three times and pushed the door open.
Someone proposed first discussing why this was happening. Another section immediately appeared in the corridor. I chased Graeber, who had reached the stairs. Notebooks slid along the surface. We had to conduct the meeting on foot. Each added question made the table grow farther.
Someone downstairs asked where we were going. I said we did not know; we would have to discuss it. The wood turned a corner and carried me outdoors. London wind scattered the agenda. Graeber caught a sheet and noticed that its edges had browned.
He broke off a corner and tasted it.
“Biscuit,” he said.
I said it was printer paper. He broke off another piece for me. It was indeed biscuit, slightly salty with the warmth of a printer. He ate “confirm venue.” The table immediately shortened by a section. Far away someone stumbled and finally caught up with their chair.
I promptly announced that we ought to organise a working group to eat the agenda.
The table grew again.
Graeber glared at me, pushed the remaining half-page into my hand and went to fetch the unopened bag of bread from the meeting room. We shared food along the table without discussing who was responsible for eating. Someone tore the budget in half and asked whether that was enough. I nodded. Someone picked off a visibly burnt piece labelled “follow-up work” and passed it to a willing neighbour.
At last only “any other business” remained. Nobody wanted to touch it in case more agenda items were hidden inside. Graeber rolled it into the bread and bit down. The table thundered back into the building. We ran after it with our bowls. Graeber covered his mouth as he ran, afraid of coughing out the other business.
The final section refused to return. It pushed through my theatre’s backstage door and stopped beside the sink. I put my red ticket stub on it to confirm that I was home.
Graeber’s hand reached through the doorway with the last empty bowl. I was about to ask who would wash it. He pointed at the table’s edge. I closed my mouth and turned on the tap.

2014 / London · a borrowed meeting room
He Fa on David Graeber
Who Is Picking Up Dinner?
I announced that this crew had no leader, then proceeded to assign everyone a job.
He Fa · Created with AI collaboration
London, 2014. During He Fa’s food run, the discussion continued. Fictional scene.
2014 consumer-digital direct flash and mixed indoor-light character
Before the meeting I wrote “temporary community” on the whiteboard. It looked a little like a funding application, so I erased “temporary.” When Graeber arrived, the board retained a damp patch. Everyone could tell a revision had already taken place.
London, 2014. I had borrowed a room and gathered several people to discuss a film without a script. To demonstrate equality, I avoided the head of the table. I sat beside the socket, with the laptop, battery and camera on my side. Power need not occupy the head of the table. Sometimes it occupies the only place where things can charge.
I began by saying everyone could decide how we would make the film. Then I opened my prepared agenda. First item: free discussion, twenty minutes. Graeber looked at the sheet and asked what happened after twenty minutes. We moved on, I said. What if people had not finished? We could be flexible, I said, reaching to start the timer.
Someone wanted to film a strike without a cause. Someone proposed people waiting for a bus that would never come. Another asked about the budget. I said this was collective creation; let’s not talk about money yet. He put down the pen he had just picked up. Graeber did not explain on my behalf. He asked what the man had been going to say. He had work early the next morning and could not stay past nine.
I hurriedly added the end time to the board. It was already half past eight. One participant had not spoken at all. She had come straight from work and was eating biscuits from her bag. I suddenly remembered writing in the invitation that we would provide something to eat. Nothing had fulfilled that sentence, though it had already changed several people’s dinner plans.
I said I would buy food. The man by the door offered to help, then asked what to get, how much to spend and how many people were eating. I answered each question. By the fourth, I realised I had remained seated and he had stood up. In my tone of voice, volunteering had transferred from one person to another within seconds.
Graeber asked whether I still had to chair. Someone needed to hold the discussion together, I said. He offered to write down what people said for a while. I turned the laptop towards him, then anxiously warned him not to touch the recording button. He looked at the screen and asked me to point it out. Relinquishing a power apparently required a minute of technical instruction.
I went downstairs with the man by the door. On the way I kept talking about the film. He said he wanted something hot. I realised I was still conducting the meeting. He read the menus on shop doors; I counted money. We bought things that could be shared. When we returned, the room had not collapsed into chaos in my absence. They had decided what to film tomorrow, and also decided against the piece of music I had proposed at the start.
I felt a little disappointed. The feeling was small and unsuitable for publication in a manifesto of collective creation. I set the food down and asked who had bowls.
Graeber handed me the notes. There was no “temporary community,” only who was free when, who could not be filmed and who would lend equipment. The man with the early shift left after eating, without delivering a political explanation of his departure. We had saved him a portion to take away. He came back from the door to collect it, and everyone made room.
The film still had no title that night. Listening to the recording at home, I heard myself say “Yes, you can” again and again, as though everyone were still applying to me. At the next meeting I put the timer in the centre of the table. Anyone could reach it, including to turn it off.
The time and place
Graeber joined the London School of Economics in 2013. This episode is set in London in 2014, during a period when he publicly discussed Occupy, democratic practice and organisation.

1504 / Florence, workshop
He Fa on Leonardo da Vinci
The Portrait Takes the Day Off
I only glanced at an empty frame. It recruited me into the Renaissance.
“I am alive.” “So was the last one.”
Early sixteenth-century tempera and oil-on-panel vocabulary; AI fiction
Image record & citation
hf-img-300345d50733
Body emerging from an ornate golden frame
In a fictional painterly interior, a person leans their head, shoulders and arm out of an ornate golden frame, reaching the floor beyond it. A bearded painter approaches with brush and palette beside painted figures and landscape, while a domed building and tabletop materials extend the setting.
The woman in the painting put one foot out first, stepped on Leonardo's palette, lifted her skirt and left. He followed her to the door. Your face is not finished, he called. By the time you finish, she said, I will not need lunch any more.
Florence, 1504. I had only just pushed through the wrong backstage door in my own theatre. Before I could ask directions, the empty frame inhaled and sucked me in. My shoulders flattened, then my stomach. My glasses refused and stuck out beyond the surface. My first successful attempt at losing weight had left me unable to turn sideways.
Leonardo returned and looked me over. This will not do. I agreed and asked him to get me out. He picked up his brush, intending to deal with my nose first.
“I am alive.” “So was the last one.”
Every stroke removed another movement I could make. My left hand was fixed, then my right. I tried shouting, but my voice came out of a small portrait next door. The unfamiliar gentleman frowned at the noise. Sorry, I said. First time using this.
Leonardo asked me to keep smiling. Having worked in theatre, I knew “a little longer” seldom had a defined limit. Until what year? I asked. He dipped his brush. Without waiting, I stretched my mouth as wide as it would go and sent my eyebrows off in opposite directions. The frame creaked. Gold leaf fell from a corner into the paint bowl.
“Do not move!” he shouted. Every portrait in the workshop froze. Even the half-painted horse in the corner stopped with a foreleg in the air. He looked from me to his own hand, apparently discovering a new application for instructions.
I reached for the red ticket stub in my pocket. Halfway out, it flattened into paint too. I stuck it over my mouth as an enormous tongue. The gentleman next door laughed. A crack opened in his frame. Laughter travelled along the wall. A saint's shoulders shook. The horse reached out of its painting and kicked over a bucket.
Leonardo did not tell us to stop again. He painted a very small door in the bottom right corner of my picture. I pulled in my stomach, folded myself twice and squeezed through. How was it? he asked. Portraits ought to have fire exits, I said.
The woman returned with her flatbread. Finding her place occupied, she looked at me, then at him. Are we still painting? Before Leonardo could answer, the empty frame on the floor had crept up to his feet.

1504 / Florence, an imagined workshop
He Fa on Leonardo da Vinci
Lending My Hands to an Unfinished Picture
I went to Florence to have my portrait painted. I spent half the day being furniture.
He Fa · Created with AI collaboration
I thought my turn had come. He was drawing how my hands held the panel.
Renaissance oil-on-panel vocabulary; contemporary AI fiction
When I entered, Leonardo was looking at a hand. It belonged to someone who was thoroughly tired of sitting. Seeing me, the man stood up, said he had something to do, and left. Nobody checked what it was. Nobody asked who I wanted to see or whether I had made an appointment either. Through this opening I acquired a seat with a back.
Leonardo looked at my face, then at my glasses. I told him I was He Fa, that I had come a long way, and that I wanted a portrait. He did not ask how far. He asked me to put my right hand over my left. I could do that. Waiting for meetings in the present day had given me years of practice.
The chair was narrower than expected. My coat caught between the arms, so I quietly pulled in my stomach. He made a few lines on a sheet of paper. After a while I asked whether we had started. He looked up. You moved just now. I said I had been moving ever since I left home; otherwise I would never have got here.
The workshop had none of the silence it would later acquire in a museum. Someone was unloading goods outside. Next door, someone kept hammering an object I could not identify. A young man crossed the room carrying a bowl and nearly hit a stand. Leonardo caught the wooden panel. I reached out to help. The sitter who needed to be kept still had suddenly become a useful device for keeping something else still.
He told me not to let go. I asked whether holding this position might count towards the cost of my portrait. He inspected the edge of the panel as though he had not heard. I asked again. First let us see how long you can hold it, he said. My first understanding of the Renaissance came down to hourly pay.
Beside the stand was an unfinished portrait of a woman. I could see only a small part. Everything I knew from later centuries crowded into my head. I wanted to tell him how famous it would be, but I might have the wrong picture. The workshop contained many unfinished things; not all of them led to the Louvre. At last I only said that many people would come to see his paintings. And after they have seen them? he asked.
That stopped me. After years in theatre, I too had got used to treating an audience's arrival as the completion of a project. Which street people took afterwards, who they ate with, whether they forgot the evening: these things rarely appeared in our final reports. They might take photographs, I said. He did not understand. I tried explaining a method of preserving appearances very quickly.
Now he was interested. How long must a person sit? Not long, I said. Does it preserve how a person looks, he asked, or how they happen to look at that instant? My hands were aching. I would have liked to merge those two appearances for the time being. He took up his pen. I thought my turn had finally come. Instead he drew the way my hands were pressing against the panel.
My face did not enter the work. My glasses, my journey from afar, my prepared jokes: all had been placed behind two straining fingers. Slightly aggrieved, I reminded him that I made art too. Then you should know you cannot let go here, he said. I had no suitable answer.
By the time the young man returned and repaired the stand, a dark smear ran across my palm. I asked for a cloth. He handed me an old rag that had already performed many historical duties. I asked whether we would still paint the portrait today. Leonardo turned the sheet over. The back was blank. He told me to return tomorrow, without promising what would happen then.
I went into the street with my incompletely cleaned hand and bought something to eat. The man selling flatbread glanced at my palm. You painters, he said. I did not correct him. The stain was all I had to prove I had been in the workshop. If, several centuries later, someone were to mistake it for a signature, I thought I had better not be there.
The time and place
Leonardo worked in Florence between 1500 and 1506 and began the Mona Lisa during this period. The workshop, sitter, stand accident, and particular unfinished portrait described here are invented.

1812 / Russia, halt after the departure from Moscow
He Fa on Napoleon
Your Majesty, Flatten the Road First
Napoleon folded the map once. The road ahead stood up.
He pressed his hat down. The road slowly opened.
Early nineteenth-century hand-coloured etching vocabulary; AI fiction
Image record & citation
hf-img-05ea99d69d57
Fictional pair on an unrolling map
In a fictional hand-coloured print-style snow scene, two brown-grey-clothed figures hold a huge map that curls from the foreground into a long slope. One sits and looks back while the other bends over its edge, before distant lines of people, bare trees and pale sky.
Napoleon folded the map in half. The road ahead stood upright. The horses stopped, the carts stopped, and I lunged to catch the roadside before I fell out of Russia and under the table.
It was October 1812. We were leaving Moscow. I had stepped out from backstage intending to ask where the dressing room was. An officer pushed a map into my hands and told me to hold it steady. The map was light. The world inside it was heavy, and Napoleon kept adding orders.
“How much walking does one fold save?” he asked. I did not know and advised him not to try. He had already made a second fold. The distant convoy hung down from the sky, its wheels still turning diligently. A soldier's hat fell in front of us, followed by my own shout from a moment before, arriving half a beat late.
He was pleased. Much closer now, he said. I pointed at the hanging road. Closer to where? He bent to read a place name. His thumb covered a town. I asked him to move it. The town gave a sigh of relief and puffed a little smoke from its chimneys.
I tried smoothing a crease. The muddy road lowered a little. Napoleon held the opposite corner, afraid I would lose the distance he had gained. Pulling at opposite ends, we turned the road into an enormous pocket. People and carts slid towards its bottom. I let go. The pocket sprang up and left both of us hanging from the map's border.
We dangled above the blank reverse of the paper. Napoleon still tried to gesture commands. Hold on first, I said. My army is waiting, he said. So are my hands, I said, and they cannot wait much longer.
At last he gripped the border with both hands. I took out the red ticket stub to write for help, then realised I had nowhere to send a single word. We swung together like two very undignified pendulums. On the third swing, we reached the curling paper corner.
“Put something on it!” I shouted. He searched a pocket and produced a letter: too light. He touched his hat and hesitated. It is more useful than your head now, I said. He pressed it down.
The road slowly opened. Wheels met mud again. Lying flat, I pushed out the final crease, too breathless to speak. But the hat kept growing, swelling into a black mountain at the junction. An officer ran up to ask the mountain's name.
Napoleon looked towards his own bare head and said nothing. Holding the map for him, I dared not fold it again and had to walk with it above my head. In the distance, a bird landed and began building a nest on the hat mountain.

The French army departed Moscow in October 1812. The map, folding roads and hat mountain are invented.

1812 / Russia, an imagined halt after the departure from Moscow
He Fa on Napoleon
There Is No Room for Victory on This Cart
My job was to put the trunks on the cart. Then my job was to explain why it would not move.
He Fa · Created with AI collaboration
Everyone knew how to keep adding things. Nobody knew what should come off first.
Early nineteenth-century hand-coloured etching and wash vocabulary; contemporary AI fiction
When I arrived, the cart was already full. People kept passing things up as though another cart existed above it. It was October 1812 and the army was leaving Moscow. The cold I knew from later accounts had not yet fully arrived. First there was a muddy road holding a wheel in place. I asked where Napoleon was. Someone pointed me towards a trunk that needed lifting.
The trunk was heavy. It had two handles; another man and I took one each. He spoke no Chinese and I spoke none of his language, but we quickly established an accurate system of cooperation: if one man let go, the other swore. This worked better than some international collaborations I had joined.
Feeling beneath the trunk, I found a split corner with a strip of something silver showing through. Nobody explained whose property it was, where it had come from, or why it had to come with us. Chairs, rolled fabric and bags of different sizes were tied above it. A single rope ensured that, for the moment, they belonged to the same world. I tightened the knot.
There was no music when Napoleon approached. His coat hem was muddy. People kept offering him reports, like new trunks being handed up to an already loaded cart. He asked why we had stopped. The man in charge pointed to the wheel. Everyone looked at it as if it were answerable for the entire road.
There is too much on it, I said. Napoleon looked at me, perhaps deciding whether the remark was worth translating. Someone repeated it. What can be unloaded? he asked. At last the question had reached the trunks, but the people around them fell silent. A moment earlier everyone knew how to keep adding things. Now nobody knew what should come off first.
I had known nights like this after performances. The truck arrived for the strike, and all the objects everyone had loved during the load-in became unpopular. A prop could be explained for half an hour; the driver only asked how many pieces remained. But I could not equate this place with a performance. Beside the cart, people sat too exhausted to argue. A long road remained ahead.
Napoleon indicated one trunk. Someone immediately said it was important. He indicated another. That was important too. Does that make the cart the least important thing? I asked. Nobody laughed. I did not continue. My shoulders hurt from carrying. What little lightness I had brought was quickly used up.
I crouched and cleared mud from the wheel. The man who had helped me carry the trunk found a plank. We tried several times. The cart rocked, and the chair on top struck something with a hollow sound. Napoleon had turned to hear another report. I stood and shouted: take the chair off first. This time we did not wait for anyone to explain it.
The chair came off, followed by two other things. With the load slightly lighter, we pushed together. Someone counted. I did not understand the numbers, but I knew when to use my strength. At last the wheel came out of the hollow and turned half a revolution. Nobody cheered. The cart moved ahead. Another immediately occupied its place.
Before leaving, Napoleon glanced our way. I had prepared so many questions: about ambition, about how many lives one person could command. Now I only wanted to know whether we could keep the plank. The man beside me handed it over. His hands would not stop shaking. We sat on the unloaded chair in turn, since there was only one.
I did not imagine I had prevented anything. The road continued, orders still travelled along it, and people still had to pull their own feet out of the mud. I simply untied the rope around my hands and coiled it again. The next time someone called for help lifting something, at least it would not catch my fingers.
The time and place
The French army left Moscow in October 1812 and subsequently retreated. The scene uses an October muddy road rather than reducing the entire retreat to snow. The halt, baggage, encounter and unloading are invented.
He Fa's encounter with Napoleon and all dialogue are fictional. The image uses period print vocabulary and is not documentary evidence of the campaign.

1883 / Sils Maria, Switzerland
He Fa on Nietzsche
My Footprints Have Their Own Plans
My body was still catching its breath. My footprints had already completed another circuit.
I got up quickly. Things were complicated enough already.
1880s albumen print and composite-negative vocabulary; AI fiction
Image record & citation
hf-img-2fdae77dd2ba
Two figures and separate boots beside a cliff
In a fictional sepia mountain scene, a long-coated person at left bends their knees with hands spread before a crouching bearded figure at right. Two separate boots rise from the ground between them, with tiny distant people, conifers, steep cliffs, snowy peaks and a lake completing the backdrop.
The third time we passed the same rock, I put a pebble on it. The fourth time, there were two. The fifth time, the pebbles made an arrow pointing at my shoes. Do not blame the mountain yet, Nietzsche said.
Sils, summer 1883. I was walking with him, and the backstage door I had come through had disappeared. Looking down, I saw my footprints standing up out of the mud: two black soles with nobody in them, walking faster than I could.
When I chased them, they stopped. When I stopped, they walked on. Nietzsche crouched to investigate and the left footprint stepped on his hand. The right one went politely around him. I asked where they were going. They led us back to the rock. Nietzsche took out paper to write. I held his pen. Let us get home before you publish.
The footprints refused. They circled the rock, and the road behind us circled with them. The lake flipped up onto the mountain; the mountain moved beside the lake. I sat down. The impression left by my backside began to stir. I got up quickly. Things were complicated enough already.
Nietzsche told me to take off my shoes. I did. The shoes immediately chased their own footprints, apparently pleased to have lost their owner. He handed me his stick as I stood barefoot. Now what? Wait, he said. I reminded him that the soles of my feet were not writing materials.
He tried trapping them beneath his hat. With the left footprint caught, the right ran round the brim, faster and faster. He held the hat down while I caught the returning shoes. The mountain stopped moving, but the lake remained halfway up it. Several fish watched us from treetops.
I put my shoes on the wrong feet and took one step backwards. The footprints hesitated. They conferred with a sound like two books slapping together. Then one went forwards and the other backwards, tearing an opening in their own road.
“Now,” I said. We stepped through the tear and arrived outside his lodging. The mountain dropped back into place. Two fish remained on the windowsill. Nietzsche stopped and looked down. His own footprints were looking up, evidently with something to say.
I did not wait to hear it. As I hurried to open the door, the red ticket stub fell from my pocket and the unoccupied shoes stepped on it. I reached for it; they moved forward. I moved back; they did too. Nietzsche stood beside us taking notes, showing no intention of helping.
