1883 / Sils Maria, Switzerland
He Fa on Nietzsche
Wait for Me at the Comma
Nietzsche took me walking. I had underestimated what this intellectual activity would require of my shoes.
He Fa · Created with AI collaboration
Thinking and climbing were sharing the same oxygen supply.
1880s albumen print and large-format exposure vocabulary; contemporary AI fiction
When Nietzsche suggested a walk, I agreed too quickly. I thought walking was a courtesy, something like saying we should have dinner sometime. Sils Maria in 1883 did not accept that interpretation. He put on his hat and went out. I followed before I had properly put down my bag.
The path was beautiful enough at first to make me forgive its gradient. The lake lay on one side, the mountains on the other. I remembered sentences that would later appear on book jackets and prepared to discuss them somewhere suitable. He did not wait for a suitable place. He talked as he walked. Following him, I lost my breath before I had started to think.
I asked him to slow down. He looked back at me, then at my shoes. It is not that I dislike thinking, I said. At present, thinking and climbing are sharing the same oxygen supply. He did not laugh, but he stopped. He waited beside the path, holding a folded sheet of paper beneath his palm to keep it from the wind.
When I caught up, I asked where we had been. He repeated the beginning of a thought. I listened carefully while a small stone slid beneath my foot. I caught his sleeve; my body had approached him before my argument could. He steadied himself, waited until I was steady, then withdrew his sleeve. No school of thought was founded in the process.
Once we sat down, I told him about working in theatre. One group treated rehearsal as life; another reminded them that life had to go on. Some wanted something new to happen every evening; others only wanted today to end early. Which group are you in? he asked. I usually have to persuade both, I said. Spoken aloud, my occupation sounded unhealthy.
When do you finish? he asked. Thinking he meant our walk, I said immediately that now would be fine. He meant the work. I did not answer. He refolded the paper. Its corners did not meet, so he opened it and tried again. I suddenly wanted to film this: a philosopher who would fill so many enormous book covers, dealing with one small sheet that would not become tidy.
I told him that people in the future would love his sentences. Which sentence? he asked. I hesitated. Many I remembered might not yet have been written that summer; some might not be his at all. Finally I said people would shorten long things and place them where encouragement was needed. He looked towards the path. Perhaps what you need now is water.
We shared what water remained. I had wanted the conversation to continue for ever. At least, in my original plan, a philosopher was supposed to undertake this labour for visitors. But he began walking home. I discovered that I would have to perform the return journey myself. Having discussed something once did not excuse my legs from doing it again.
Back at his lodging, he showed me the green wallpaper. This felt more intimate than I had expected. Did you choose it? He nodded. Someone who must spend many difficult days in a room cannot live solely by leaving sentences to posterity. What the eyes meet every day, how the tablecloth sits beside the wall: these also require decisions.
I helped him shift the table to see a corner of the wall. A leg scraped across the floor with a long sound. He signalled me to be gentler. The large words we had discussed that afternoon no longer needed to return. We had found something we could both hear.
Before leaving, I asked whether we would walk tomorrow. Depending on the weather, he said. Then I will check my shoes first. Outside, I began writing down a question I had not finished that afternoon. Halfway through, I could not remember its second half. That was all right. At last I had left myself a sufficiently long comma.
The time and place
Nietzsche stayed in Sils Maria in summer 1883. The museum documents wallpaper he chose that year. The route, He Fa's visit and the table-moving episode are fictional.

1601 / London, performance day at the Globe
He Fa on Shakespeare
Please Swallow the Ending
I read one wrong line, and the Globe began packing itself away.
The cheapest standing tickets soon acquired private-box accommodation.
Early seventeenth-century woodcut vocabulary; AI fiction
Image record & citation
hf-img-be1f99226f7f
Oversized scissors on theatre seating steps
In a fictional theatre rendered with brown-black woodcut-like lines, two ruff-collared figures occupy opposite stepped seats around an oversized pair of scissors. Tiny audience faces fill wooden galleries above intersecting roof and stair lines, with a fallen hat at lower right amid dense cross-hatching.
Shakespeare pushed a sheet into my hand. They were one person short; I should go on and read it. I said I did not understand. Just read what is there. That instruction had got me into plenty of performances. I had not expected it to be in use in 1601.
On the Globe's stage, I read “Bring a chair.” A chair promptly fell out of my mouth onto my foot. The audience applauded. Through the pain, I asked Shakespeare what this paper was. He drew it slightly back. Something new, he said.
Once spoken, the lines grew into solid objects. I said sword. A sword hung from my tongue. I quickly closed my mouth and broke it in two. A child near the stage collected one half. Shakespeare crouched to inspect the break and complained that I had shortened his monologue.
The actor playing the king arrived and ordered me off. I read “Exit” from the paper. The floor suddenly withdrew. The front row's toes touched the stage. The second gallery bent towards the first. The theatre squeezed inward, fold after fold, like an accordion. The cheapest standing tickets soon acquired private-box accommodation.
Shakespeare grabbed my collar and jumped a closing gap. Who told you to read the stage direction? You did not mark it, I said. It was written for someone who could read. As I began to object, a beam folded down above us. We dropped together.
The words on the sheet queued to enter my mouth, impatient to finish the evening's work. I clenched my teeth but swallowed one “door.” Knocking immediately sounded inside my stomach. Shakespeare put his ear against it. How many are in there? This is no time to sell tickets, I said.
The final “Dismiss the audience” had already risen into the air like a pair of enormous iron scissors, ready to cut the compressed theatre apart. Shakespeare caught one end; I caught the other. Whoever let go would have to swim home through the Thames.
I remembered the red ticket stub in my pocket: no returns or exchanges. I did not dare read it aloud. Lying on floorboards that now stood upright, we each bit one side of the final line and chewed the ending back into our mouths. It tasted of ink and unpaid wages.
The theatre slowly flattened. The chairs returned beneath their occupants. The child still had the sword. The king complained about the delay and called for the next scene. I shook my head and held my stomach. Someone inside knocked three times. Shakespeare had already sat down with his pen, waiting to hear who it was.

1601 / London, an imagined performance day at the Globe
He Fa on Shakespeare
One of Everyone
The man who paid a penny to watch the play ended up on stage, still unsure who should pay him.
He Fa · Created with AI collaboration
Everyone told me to go. Nobody told me where.
Early seventeenth-century woodcut and letterpress vocabulary; contemporary AI fiction
At the Globe, I first paid a penny. The man collecting money put it in a box without giving me a ticket. In the yard, I saw someone eating beside the stage and felt relieved. More than four centuries later, we were still holding meetings about whether audiences could bring drinks into a theatre. This place clearly had no intention of reserving that question for history.
I wanted to discuss theatre with Shakespeare. He was easy to find that day: people kept calling his name, each time with a different problem. I had barely told him that I worked in theatre when he looked at my build and asked whether I could walk from here to there. This was shorter than the discussion agenda I had prepared. I said I could.
Someone put a coat on me. Its collar was stiff. Its previous wearer had left a strong presence behind. Who am I playing? A citizen. What does this citizen think? Follow those men first. At last I had a role without an interior monologue.
My job was to enter behind a group, listen to what was said, and leave with them. I earnestly asked when to go. An actor handed me his paper, which held very few lines. I turned it over; there was no complete script on the back. He reclaimed it, perhaps afraid I would lose the only part he knew.
I waited by the door a long time. On stage, someone spoke of loyalty, someone of betrayal, and someone said the same person's name in three different tones. I gradually understood the situation but not my cue. By the time the others entered, I was still at the door, a citizen who had not received the official notice.
Shakespeare gave me a small push from behind. I hurried on and the audience laughed. I did not know who they were laughing at, so I remained serious. The laughter grew. I had often thought that audiences needed guidance. Here I discovered they could find a mistake perfectly well on their own, then raise it together.
When it was time to leave, the man ahead turned and spread his arms. Thinking he was stopping me, I stopped. His speech required everyone to leave, while his body blocked my way. I looked at him, waiting for a less contradictory instruction. Someone in the yard shouted: leave the one with the glasses.
I did stay a little longer. I was not deliberately inventing a new form; the exit was blocked. A citizen who was never supposed to answer a question acquired a few seconds of decision-making power. Eventually I went around the other way and almost collided with someone entering. Backstage, someone swore with such precision that I immediately felt at home.
After the scene, I found Shakespeare and asked how the performance fee worked. Return the coat first, he said. Beneath it, my own clothes were wet with sweat. Why did you not leave? Everyone told me to go, I said, but nobody told me where. He watched me a moment, borrowed the paper beneath a cup, and wrote a few things down.
I would not claim to have inspired a masterpiece. He might simply have written: do not hire this man again. Still, since I had been on stage, could I get my penny back? You saw the play too, he said. I suggested that the view from the stage and the view from the yard ought to carry different prices. He put a coin on the table. As I reached for it, a young man collecting thread took it away.
The next scene had begun. Someone told me to move. I stood by the wall and held a wooden sword that was about to fall. We had not settled the money, but a relationship had formed quickly: if you stay long enough, someone will always hand you something.
The time and place
The Globe opened in 1599. Penny admission to the yard and eating during performances are documented. No particular play, payment agreement or performance date is claimed here.
He Fa's performance, backstage actions, payment discussion and all dialogue are invented. The image is not a surviving print from 1601.

sources.text:
1888 / The Yellow House, Arles, France
He Fa on Van Gogh
The Chair Refuses to Wait
Gauguin had not arrived. The chair prepared for him left first.
“Rescue first, draw later!”
1880s reed-pen and watercolour vocabulary; AI fiction
Image record & citation
hf-img-491f74a3e8e2
Tilting chair before yellow walls and blue doors
A brightly brushed fictional street scene places a person on a bent wooden chair with feet raised and one hand reaching left, while a red-haired figure reaches behind it. Yellow walls, blue doors and empty chairs recede across cobbles covered in small colour marks and golden leaves.
As soon as Van Gogh finished its fourth leg, the chair climbed off the paper, knocked over the ink bottle and ran. We chased it to the Yellow House doorway. In the middle of the street it paused, shook paint from its wooden legs and accelerated.
Arles, October 1888. Gauguin had not arrived, and the chair had evidently lost patience. Van Gogh pursued it with his pen. Wait, I said. You have not told me what it eats. Chairs do not eat. Then why is it heading for the restaurant?
The real chair by the door saw it and followed. Then the upstairs chairs, the neighbours' chairs, the chairs outside the restaurant. Wood began striking stone all along the street. Several people still sitting were carried away before they could get up, soup bowls in their hands.
I caught the painted chair from behind. It immediately stopped, apparently pleased to have found a passenger. As I relaxed, it flung me into its seat and ran on. Van Gogh kept pace beside me. I reached for his help, but he was studying the moving legs and muttering something.
“Rescue first, draw later!” I shouted. He put his pen behind his ear and caught the chair back. The chair dragged us round a corner, its rear legs crossing a gutter while the others crushed his shoes. Looking down, I saw familiar yellow paint spreading over the seat and staining my trousers into part of it.
It wanted to keep me. I tried to stand, but beneath my backside came the sound of wet paint pulling apart. Do not force it, Van Gogh said. Should I wait for it to dry? Ahead, a restaurant table stood up and blocked the door, apparently opposing this unauthorised expansion of the chair business.
Van Gogh crouched and drew a very long table on a sheet. Before adding legs, he asked me to hold it. I pulled the red ticket stub free of the chair and clipped down a corner of the sheet. He quickly added four stout legs and pushed the paper into the street.
The long table sprang up with a thump, blocking the whole road. The chairs braked and crowded round it, finding their places one after another. Mine joined them and finally released my trousers. Someone put their remaining soup on the table. Bread followed from the roadside. Van Gogh sat opposite me, his sleeves covered in ink.
What now? I asked. He was already drawing a bowl. I held down the sheet and suggested that the bowl should have something in it first. He changed two strokes. A freshly drawn fish leapt out, flicked its tail and knocked the red ticket into the soup.

1888 / The Yellow House, Arles, France
He Fa on Van Gogh
The Chairs Met First
Gauguin had not arrived. I came first to try his chair.
He Fa · Created with AI collaboration
Before I could become a guest, I had become one of a pair.
1880s reed-pen, ink and transparent-watercolour vocabulary; contemporary AI fiction
Van Gogh was inside the doorway, I was outside, and a chair stood between us. Neither of us could see the other's feet. We had tried three times and got stuck in the same place each time. Raise your end, I said. He lifted it; the back struck the frame. Not that end. Which end? he asked. I discovered that before living together, people should agree on left and right.
In October 1888, the Yellow House in Arles was waiting for someone. His name was Gauguin, and he had not yet arrived. I said I was He Fa and had dropped by on my way through. Van Gogh handed me the other end of the chair. The welcome was concrete. Before I could become a guest, I had become one of a pair.
He wanted painters to work together in the house. I understood. I too had gathered people somewhere to rehearse or make a film together. Whether they would leave together was something one discovered at the end. Van Gogh put the chair down and went inside to inspect the angle. Holding it alone outside, I found that one person's ideal can make another person stand very crookedly.
At last we turned it sideways and sent one leg through first. The chair entered without drama, without waiting for us to achieve an intellectual breakthrough. Van Gogh rubbed the new mark on the doorframe. I wanted to reassure him that people would one day study this room. But that could not replace the paint we had just scraped away.
The house was still incomplete. As he described where things would go, he moved the things already there to make space for things yet to arrive. Who is this chair for? I asked. Sit down first. I sat. It wobbled. We both looked down. This is not an aesthetic problem, I said. He went to find paper for the short leg.
The paper had writing on it. I stopped him: perhaps it was important. He turned it over, showed me the other side, then looked at me. Unwilling to impose posterity's archival habits on his present life, I helped fold it. Beneath the chair leg, it worked. I sat more comfortably, although I kept thinking about the word being pressed underneath.
He asked what I painted. I said I made films and theatre. How? I invited people and let things happen, sometimes writing them first, sometimes waiting for the people to change them. I made it sound easy, omitting the money, the chasing, the food going cold before filming began. He pointed to the other, empty chair. Then you must understand waiting for someone.
I understood a little. Before a person arrives, they are at their easiest to live with. You can arrange their room, imagine which wall they will prefer, even turn imagined arguments into stories you might later tell. When they actually enter, the first thing they ask may simply be where the water is. Van Gogh heard none of these thoughts. He was moving the chairs closer together, then apart.
I asked whether he wanted a rest. He agreed and handed me a small piece of bread. We ate on chairs that now had a use. I did not tell him what would happen later. I did not own the person yet to arrive, and knowing the outcome did not entitle me to turn every movement of his preparations into an omen.
Wind came through the doorway. A corner of paper protruded beneath the chair leg. I nudged it inward with my shoe. Van Gogh saw. Still wobbling? No, I said. At last he leaned against the back. For a little while we had nothing left to arrange.
Before I left, he asked me to hold the door. I did. Perhaps anyone who hopes others will stay first needs someone willing to hold a door for them. I did not say this aloud. It would have sounded too much like composing an ending for the day. I only asked whether the other chair needed moving.
The time and place
Letters document Van Gogh furnishing the Yellow House and awaiting Gauguin in October 1888. The chair-moving, folded paper and shared bread are invented; the chairs are not identified as the originals of particular paintings.
He Fa's visit and all dialogue are fictional. The image is contemporary AI-assisted work, not an original Van Gogh or a surviving record of the scene.

sources.text:
1964 / New York · the Silver Factory
He Fa on Andy Warhol
The One in the Camera Won’t Clock Off
I came for a screen test. The He Fa on screen got the job first.
New York, 1964. The other He Fa takes the chair first.
1964 black-and-white documentary and optical double-exposure character
Image record & citation
hf-img-0756445cc714
Silver studio and a figure crossing a screen
A fictional black-and-white studio shows a person holding an upright screen at left while a similarly dressed figure appears to step out beside a chair. A sunglasses-wearing person stands behind a camera at right, surrounded by foil-like reflections, portrait paintings, floor cables and film containers.
As soon as the camera started, the me on screen stood up.
I remained seated.
The Silver Factory, New York, 1964. Warhol had asked me to move as little as possible. The He Fa on screen plainly had not received the instruction. He straightened his shirt and gestured for me to get up. I tried to raise my hand; it grew heavier. He grew nimbler, stepping over the screen’s lower edge into the room, a strip of white light trailing from his sole.
“Sit back down,” I said.
He brushed my words aside and took my chair. The screen scooped me up like a bedsheet. I clung to its frame as my body grew thinner and my nose disappeared in profile. Only then did I remember that the film recorded no sound. I opened my mouth to shout. The machine was the only thing heard in the room.
Warhol came closer to inspect, then stepped back to adjust the shot.
The double pointed at me as though requesting the replacement of an inadequate prop. I pushed an arm out of the screen and grabbed the chair back, hoping to pull him in. He casually hung his coat on my hand. This He Fa was already better suited to New York.
I felt in my pocket. Everything had flattened except the stiff red ticket stub. While Warhol looked aside, I covered the lens with it. Something clicked, and every exchange stopped. I had one leg inside the screen and one outside. The double froze halfway through crossing his legs.
“We’re missing a section,” Warhol said.
On the back of the stub I wrote: Let me out first.
He took the paper, read it and nodded. I uncovered a sliver of lens. The double immediately moved. I covered it again; his smile froze across half his face. After three attempts, we reached an agreement: he would sit for me by day, I would come out at night, and each could use half the name.
Warhol labelled the film can “HE / FA.” The double objected to the order of the credits. I reminded him that he had not spoken a single word. Warhol pointed at the camera, indicating that neither had I.
At changeover I finally squeezed out of the screen, flexing my nose first and then my shoulders. The double settled inside, already better than me at checking his watch impatiently. I was about to leave when a second camera started at the other end of the room.
The He Fa on screen and I turned round together.
Sources & project notes
Warhol made the Screen Tests in 1964–66 as silent 16mm film portraits, usually projected in slow motion.
The time travel, fantastic events and dialogue are literary fiction; images are AI-assisted creations.

1964 / New York · the Silver Factory
He Fa on Andy Warhol
I Apply for Permission to Move
He told me to sit. I soon discovered that not acting required even more permission than acting.
He Fa · Created with AI collaboration
New York, 1964. The camera has not decided whether I am an actor. Fictional scene.
The character of a 1964 35mm black-and-white documentary production photograph
After I sat down, Andy was still arranging the light. I asked what I was supposed to play in this audition. He said I only needed to sit. I assumed he had already formed an opinion of my acting.
New York, 1964. The silver material on the Factory walls was as creased as a present opened and wrapped again. The camera was small; its tripod looked serious. I wore a shirt from a second-hand shop, worried that I did not look like an artist, then worried that I looked too much like someone trying to look like an artist. Andy adjusted the camera and asked me to move my chair to the right.
I asked whether I should introduce myself. I said my name was He Fa and that I worked in theatre. He nodded without inviting the second half of my prepared speech. Only later did I realise that the camera recorded no sound. Most of my résumé had lost its usefulness in this room.
Before filming, I asked if I could blink. He said to move as little as possible. This did not strike me as a complete answer. Whether blinking was an action or a malfunction mattered to an actor’s understanding of the job. Before I could clarify, the machine was running.
At first I devised a serious expression. Ten or fifteen seconds later, I worried that it was too serious. To appear natural I loosened the corners of my mouth and immediately felt that I was smiling. Drawing them back left me looking like someone who could not understand anyone. My face was frantically busy. My body remained politely seated.
The bridge of my nose began to itch. My glasses slid slowly downward. I could not tell whether anyone else could see this, but it occupied my entire attention. People on the other side of the room talked and laughed twice. I badly wanted to know whether they meant me. Andy supplied no answer from behind the camera. He moved to one side to check the light. The silver wall broke his shadow into pieces.
Finally I raised a hand and pushed up my glasses. Things became easier after that, like a game in which I had already committed a foul. I looked into the lens and remembered how often I stood behind a camera telling people to ignore it. Such an economical instruction: the speaker did the recording; the listener did the work of not noticing.
When the machine stopped, I immediately asked whether that movement meant we had to start again. Andy looked at me and asked whether I wanted to sit through another roll. I considered it for two seconds and said no. He said that would do, then.
The strip had taken less than three minutes to expose. Projected more slowly, it would run for roughly four. Before becoming a star, I had increased my output in time. I asked whether I had been selected. He asked, selected for what? Wasn’t this an audition? He smiled, as though I had just made a practical suggestion.
I got up to find my coat and discovered that someone else was already in my chair. They had no résumé to present and a calmer face than mine. Suddenly resentful, I wanted another chance. Just then a friend squeezed past with drinks and asked me to clear the way. My jealousy lasted half a minute before local traffic cancelled it.
Before leaving, I asked Andy how he would record my name. He gave me paper and a pen. I carefully wrote 何发, then the romanisation. It was my most cooperative movement of the entire audition. He put the paper beside the film can. Looking at the can, I imagined someone in the future pressing play: first watching me try hard not to perform, then watching me give in and adjust my glasses.
The time and place
Warhol’s Screen Tests were principally made from 1964 to 1966 on silent 16mm film and generally projected more slowly than they were shot. They were film portraits, not conventional casting auditions. The illustration imagines a 35mm documentary photograph of the filming session.
He Fa’s encounters, actions and conversations are literary fiction. Images are AI-assisted period scenes.

How Works Happen · Archival Research
How Works Happen: Theatre, Assessment and Agreements for Working Together
Eight encounters with P4 and US-period materials: who acts, how media take part, and how an action becomes a work.
Begin with a scene
In these materials, P4 is both a theatre space for working together and a platform offering space, documentation, organisation and planning. The public Personal Chronicle proposal brings watching, performing and filming together. To understand this practice, we need to see how people use a space, initiate actions and leave records, rather than simply list productions.
The lights go down, but singing comes from outside the stage. A performer in white descends from the upper floor; only later does the audience see a second performer, dressed in black, behind the gauze. Projections, bodies, written words, music and broadcasts keep redirecting attention. This opening is described in a retained Shadow Counterpoint press text. That account also records a difficulty: some spectators felt that the juxtaposition divided their attention and that the words did not clarify the story.

Three questions to carry through the materials
How do existing images, texts and bodily experience become actions that several people can carry out together? Who decides what an action means: makers, participants, a machine or assessors? When does an action begin and end, and how does its record let others enter it? These questions take concrete form in gauze and projections, translation interfaces, assessment documents, paper scripts and public project agreements. They are ways to compare particular materials, rather than a single theme imposed on every work.

Four windows in time
The first concerns early theatre collaboration. The 2016 Shadow Counterpoint texts describe a practical spatial problem: how existing images and music coexist with performance, and how spectators divide their attention. Two press texts credit He Fa and Aoshuang with planning and Yan Qin with direction. Preservation in He Fa’s archive does not make every contribution his.
The second concerns documented US-period work. A Fa’s review work list dated 28 April 2017 identifies the assessment itself as documentary work. Some Fafalish Library photographs carry a device date of 24 October 2017 and show paper, letterforms, computer operations and onlookers. They can be compared through questions of judgement and reading, but the materials do not establish that the assessment caused the later experiments.
The third concerns shared exercises around 2021–2022. Lisa workshop photographs show both two people standing face to face and exchanges around paper and materials. In Feedback, reading and physical actions alternate; in Outward Monologue, thread and a curtain alter what can be seen between bodies. Camera dates support the workshop records; directory labels supply the other two dates. These are different kinds of evidence, not a precise chronology.
The fourth is a public organisational proposal from 2023. The Personal Chronicle recruitment text connects an interview, project initiation, process documentation and a public presentation. Publication establishes that the procedure was proposed, not that every project completed it.
The US period is a parallel strand in He Fa’s practice, not an American phase of P4 as a whole. These windows organise a reading, not a complete institutional history.

Places do not form a single ladder of progress
These windows do not mean that He Fa first resolved images, then moved to bodies and finally to organisation. Images were already part of theatre, and US-period proposals also addressed shared work. Long Long Ago Group proposed that participants take turns hosting activities in their own regions while continuing to attend one another’s activities, and jointly seek alternatives when a venue was unsuitable. The surviving proposal establishes an intention, not its implementation. Like Personal Chronicle it treats organisation as a condition of making; a direct line of inheritance remains unproven.

Eight encounters, organised by questions
Begin with the Shadow Counterpoint reports to understand the practical difficulty of coordinating media. Then read the Fa’s review assessment and work list to see how an evaluation becomes part of a work. Fafalish Library photographs bring paper, screens and onlookers around the same table; the Lisa workshop moves between facing another person and gathering around materials.
Outward Monologue and Feedback show different bodily processes: thread and concealment in one, paper and repeated movements in the other. Out of Everyday Life places paper within a seated exchange, though its contents and any decisions remain unknown. Finally, the publication of Personal Chronicle sets out proposed beginnings and endings for projects. The first seven encounters have varying degrees of visual or documentary support; the eighth is first of all the publication of a proposal, not proof of subsequent delivery.

Relational Image Theory
· He Fa
Chapter 2 · The Person Who Says “I Love You”
A Sentence Changes Its Use
At the beginning of
Shoot Self with You
, Jia Rui says, ‘I love you.’ A little later, Zi Chou says, ‘The acting is terrible.’
[2-1]
¶
Between the two sentences, the listener shifts from one role to another. The first offers a declaration of love; the second looks back to assess that expression. Someone who was just reaching toward another person has become a performer being watched. He has finished speaking, yet what his words amount to has become a question again.
¶
Watch the passage: How a Declaration of Love Becomes a Judgment of Acting
Video · bilingual dialogue · stills · return to this paragraph
I do not want to find proof of a feeling hidden beneath the lines of this declaration. Discovering the actors’ private feelings would not make the scene easier to understand. What deserves attention is that two demands fall on the same person at once: he needs to speak to his partner, and he needs to make his speaking worth watching. The other person can receive what he expresses, or step outside it and judge his performance. Acting thus carries an asymmetry: I am still speaking to you, while you are already watching how I speak.
¶
This shift also means that what is ‘real’ in a film cannot be measured by intensity of commitment alone. If an actor cries, the tears really occur; what they express still depends on the action in which they appear. Someone who does not cry may also render a difficult grief precisely. Feelings and the ability to express them do not always arrive at the same moment. Demanding that they coincide completely can keep actors so busy proving what is inside them that they have no time to hear the person beside them.
¶
‘The acting is terrible’ can, of course, be a useful judgment. Without judgments about expression, rehearsal would struggle to continue. But a judgment needs to contain something that can be answered: what was unclear just now, which action came too soon, or who had not yet been given time to respond. If evaluation stays at the level of real or fake, performers can only keep offering themselves up, waiting for someone else to announce that this time they are finally real enough.
¶
I want the film to keep this shift visible. It allows viewers to see how intimate words become work, and how judgments about that work enter the process of people drawing closer. Declarations of love and evaluations each have their uses. When they meet, they can also interrupt one another.
¶
Shoot Self with You, still from the fixed 4K master. At the opening, three people occupy different distances within one frame.
Shoot Self with You, collectively created by the cast and crew; still from the fixed master.
Image record & citation
hf-img-ccc5fe5b40ab
Human Surrender / Shoot Self with You | Three bodily distances within one shot
Several people share a tightly framed, dim interior. A profile at the right presses close to the camera and is cropped by the edge; a seated person with glasses occupies the middle with a hand near the chin. Only part of another shoulder is visible at the left, creating markedly different bodily distances within one shot.
A Role Gives Someone a Position
A role allows someone to do something with others without first having to explain themselves in full. They can say a line that has already been written, carry out an agreed action, or begin by knowing whom to turn toward. Something difficult to say in ordinary life can sometimes take shape through this distance. Fiction gives action a starting point, and leaves the person a little room to retreat: this sentence is happening within the play, so I can try saying it.
¶
In an article written before the performance, Sun Jiarui describes how acting allowed him to meet people and become their friend, and how it became a way of feeling needed. He also writes about his dislike of himself in photographs, his surprise after agreeing to perform, and his intention to stop acting.
[2-2]
These parts should be read together. A role gives him a way in, but may also narrow that entrance. Others need this actor, and so he can remain part of their shared life. How else might he be needed once he leaves the actor’s position? That becomes a harder question to answer.
¶
What I see here is a dependence that enthusiasm can easily conceal in creative work. Doing things together produces relations, but those relations may then require a person to keep serving a particular purpose. Someone who is always ready with a reply is expected to keep replying. Someone willing to take on a difficult role is invited to do so again. The ability that first gave them entry gradually becomes the main way others recognize them. The more successful the role, the easier it is for the particular person to be hidden behind it.
¶
This does not mean collaboration should have no division of tasks. It is precisely through different abilities that people can work together. The problem is when a person’s assigned part comes to be understood as all that they are. If someone refuses to perform next time, do they lose a work arrangement, or also their place among the others? ‘We’re all friends’ cannot answer that question in advance. It depends on how people continue to see one another after someone stops serving a function.
¶
I therefore want to think of a role as a place one can enter and also leave. It should allow tentative attempts: speaking with someone else’s sentences and discovering one’s own voice; completing a task and discovering that one no longer wants to do it this way. The relations a role opens up deserve to be tested beyond that role.
¶
Knowing It Is Acting, Still Wanting to Argue Back
After the performance, Sun Jiarui wrote: ‘I know
He Fa
is acting, but I really do want to argue back.’
[2-3]
¶
This sentence makes the effect of performance precise. He recognizes it as acting, yet the wish to argue back still arises. Knowing that something belongs to a play does not exempt him from its effects. An actor can know perfectly well that the other person is speaking lines and still be angered or moved by what they say, or feel that an arrangement ought to change. Fiction has real effects precisely because the people taking part in it have not left reality: they are still spending time, waiting for one another, judging the action before them, and carrying it out with their own bodies.
¶
Yet we cannot gather all these effects under the phrase ‘getting into character.’ Getting into character is often understood as forgetting oneself, as if actors can only feel something real by temporarily losing the ability to distinguish what is happening. Jia Rui’s words retain that distinction. He knows he is performing, and he has his own judgment. The urge to argue back coexists with his awareness of the play. A person can participate in a framework while also judging it from within.
¶
This is part of what makes fiction interesting. It lets someone borrow another situation while retaining some distance from it. A person can try actions they would not ordinarily take and discover their limits in the attempt. Complete immersion is only one state of performance. Remaining aware, hesitating, or occasionally stepping out of a role can also produce powerful expression. A film can bring these different states together, allowing a character’s actions and an actor’s judgments to illuminate one another.
¶
Someone may ask: if real relations matter, why not simply talk directly? Because ‘directly’ has conditions of its own. The names we call one another, our habits, and our expectations in ordinary life already determine much of who can say what and how far they can go. Taking on another role can sometimes move those arrangements a little. People do not always have a complete self first and then search for the right sentences to convey it. Sometimes only after speaking and acting do they discover that this is how they respond.
¶
I value this discovery, but do not want to possess it. A maker can arrange a task that allows a sentence to be spoken. What that sentence later means to the speaker is something the speaker must go on understanding. The work preserves the expression, while the person’s interpretation continues to change.
¶
No Single Kind of Truth Can Answer Everything
At this point, several things that easily become entangled need to be separated. Whether a line was actually spoken is something a recording can help establish. To understand what someone felt while speaking, we need to hear their account. Whether that expression changed how people related to one another requires looking at what they did next. Whether the film gave these changes a forceful organization takes us back to its sounds, images, and rhythms.
¶
All four questions matter. When they are mixed together, a work can acquire a value from the weight of lived experience that seems to need no further explanation: someone was really distressed, so this passage must remain; the collaboration was unforgettable, so viewers ought to be moved. But viewers did not share those days. They are facing a film and need to establish a relation to it through what it gives them. A pause familiar to its makers may still be a blank for a stranger. Turning that blank into a waiting the viewer can feel is work the film’s form has to do.
¶
Conversely, a moving film does not prescribe how the people involved should remember what happened. Artistic success cannot account for every value of an encounter. Someone may cherish the film while remaining unhappy with a particular arrangement. Someone else may have no interest in the finished film yet cherish an afternoon of working together. These differences should be allowed to remain around the work.
¶
My position is therefore clear: art can actively create the conditions under which people meet. It need not wait for an entirely authentic life to appear of its own accord. Roles, sets, lines, and cameras can all give experience ways of being expressed that it did not have before. Art’s strength also comes from a limit: participants can always bring something that the arrangement has not yet included.
¶
When someone says ‘I love you,’ they borrow a sentence countless people have spoken, yet still address it, at this moment, to a particular person. The listener may answer, hesitate, or judge the performance. Where the next sentence takes this relation cannot be determined by the first sentence alone. The film’s work begins here: to preserve how a reply is awaited, missed, or changed.
¶

Chapter 3 · Once More
The Last Attempt Remains in the Body
“Once more” is one of the most ordinary things said in rehearsal, and perhaps one of the hardest requests to understand. What are we repeating? A sequence of movements, a line, a feeling that has already gone, or an approach that failed to begin just now? The person saying it may think the meaning is clear, but the person doing it has to decide what to carry into the next attempt.
¶
This suggestion also appears in
Shoot Self with You
.
[3-1]
I want to pause first over the word “again.” It points to the past but calls for a future action. The next attempt will not begin from nothing: the participants have already heard feedback, know that a particular action has failed, and may have become more familiar with their partners, or may already be tired. Repetition always carries something left by the previous attempt. Even when the lines and positions are exactly the same, what people have to deal with may have changed.
¶
Watch the passage: What Does “One More Time” Ask Us to Repeat?
Video · bilingual dialogue · stills · return to this paragraph
Starting again can therefore both correct and accumulate. A sequence that initially required thought can later be completed smoothly; an answer that could be tried at first may no longer appear because it has already been rejected. Repetition brings proficiency, and it also brings expectations. People gradually learn what will be accepted. That knowledge can help them work together, but it can also make them deliver the right answer before the other person has finished speaking.
¶
I do not place contingency in opposition to proficiency. If a partner unexpectedly changes speed, someone practised may have more room to respond; someone entirely unprepared may only be able to fall back on the actions they first memorized. What matters is what capacities practice has freed up, and what attention it has taken over. Once an action can be performed reliably, can the person still hear the difference between this attempt and the last?
¶
Sameness then has two uses. It can let people retreat into a result they already know, or provide a stable place from which small changes can finally be noticed. If everything changes on every attempt, change becomes harder to distinguish. Keeping some things in place makes it possible to see how others move. Freedom in creative work sometimes needs such fixed points.
¶
A rehearsal for Kill That Rose. First published in a performance countdown article on 11 June 2021.

What Counts as Finished?
A request that can be carried out can usually also specify when it has been fulfilled. Wait for the other person to finish before beginning your own line; walk to a particular place and pause; make a word audible to the back row. The actor can try, the director can explain, and the next attempt can be compared with the last. They may not agree quickly, but their disagreement has an object they can work on together.
¶
“Make it more real” may move that object out of reach. The actor has completed the action but must also prove that they are present in it; if they explain that they feel something, they may then be judged too deliberate. The more authenticity is demanded, the more the actor needs to watch how they appear. They try to enter the scene while checking from the outside whether they have entered it. A command to be natural can make people work ever harder to manage their naturalness.
¶
Gentleness and severity cannot distinguish good rehearsal here. A precise request can be demanding and frustrating, while broad encouragement may never give anyone something they can actually do. The artist should take on the difficulty of turning judgment into work. If an attempt lacks force, where exactly does it fall short? Are the actions unrelated, the words addressed to no one, or does the rhythm leave no time for a response? A feeling may not be immediately nameable, but the work should still begin with something that can be tried.
¶
I am especially wary of treating commitment as an unlimited resource. What an actor has already expressed may be judged not good enough, but that judgment cannot simply become a judgment of the whole person. It is this attempt that has failed; the person’s entire authenticity should not therefore be put on trial. Rehearsal needs to make room for an attempt that has not gone well, so that the next can be work rather than another act of self-defence.
¶
The strongest objection to this position is that art takes people precisely where no method yet exists. If every request is completely clear, would all that remains be execution? I agree that the unknown cannot be eliminated. A director may not be able to say in advance what they are looking for, but they can work with the actors to identify the differences that emerge in each attempt, and acknowledge that they have not yet found it this time. The question is who bears the unknown. An artist cannot preserve the ambiguity of their own judgment while demanding definite proof of the participants’ inner lives.
¶
Finishing does not always mean reaching an ideal result. Sometimes it means having seen clearly that continuing with this method will bring us no closer to what we are looking for. Only when we can end one method can we begin another.
¶
Letting the Lines Step Back a Little
In a 2018 interview, Ryusuke Hamaguchi discussed repeated script readings: first, without imposing a fixed tone, the actors read until they have thoroughly absorbed the words; then, during filming, they let their expression respond to the moment and their partners.
[3-2]
What interests me is the arrangement between these two stages. Repetition takes on part of the work of remembering, so that when filming begins, the actors do not have to devote all their attention to “What is my next line?”
¶
This suggests a limited claim: preparation can change how attention is distributed. When the lines are relatively secure, an actor may notice a partner’s hesitation and adjust the timing of their own entry. The text has not disappeared, but it has receded a little. The person has a chance to respond to what is happening. Listening here includes sound, but also waiting: allowing the other person’s expression on this attempt to arrive a little later, more quietly, or with a pause absent from the last.
¶
This arrangement can also lead to the opposite result. Once actors have memorized the text, they may be even more eager to complete the sequence they already know; what is called natural is merely the precise reproduction of a practised manner. A method’s name does not determine its effect. What needs to be observed is whether, after repetition, actors have more ways to respond to change, or are left only with smoother execution.
¶
There is an actual timeline connecting
P4
and Hamaguchi. In a 2023 article, Yun Jianhui recalled that we had already discussed Hamaguchi’s work in 2022; after
Shoot Self with You
began, the early crew studied
Intimacies
, and lines from that film entered the script in July of the same year.
[3-3]
This record shows that the film had become part of our shared work. For me, the question more worth pursuing is how those studies changed the way we worked. There is still a long way between liking a film and making its method work among another group of people.
¶
What I take from repeated script reading does not require every creative work to follow the same procedure. It draws my attention to a question that enthusiasm often obscures: how many things can a person handle at once while expressing themselves? Remembering lines, searching for emotion, attending to the camera, and guessing how pleased the director is can easily fill all one’s attention with one’s own tasks. Entrusting some of this to practice is meant to free up the capacity to attend to other people.
¶
Listening in art therefore needs to be arranged. It can begin by reducing certain tasks, fixing a standing position, or making a sentence clear. Asking someone to open up their whole self is often too much; enabling them to hear the sentence in front of them through to its end is sometimes already difficult.
¶
The Kill That Rose team, 2021. People sit together around a computer, papers and cups.

Allowing an Attempt to Have No Shape Yet
Another value of repetition is that it allows awkwardness to remain in the work for a while. When an action is new, the body often moves more slowly than the intention. Knowing that one wants to come closer does not mean already knowing how to stand, where to put one’s hands, or how to leave the other person enough support. If a complete action is demanded too soon, participants can easily choose a familiar performance posture that makes the difficulty disappear from the image.
¶
The difficulty may be covered over without the action having been resolved. A familiar way of performing intimacy may conceal how two people actually approach each other; an uneven attempt may instead reveal what needs adjusting. I am willing to give such attempts time. But awkwardness does not thereby acquire an inherent aesthetic value. A pause may contain a search, or it may simply reflect a lack of preparation. Creative work needs to discern whether, after the pause, the relation between the person and the action has changed.
¶
We can imagine a simple comparison: two people repeatedly practise taking the hand the other extends. One way of practising requires the action to match the demonstration every time; another first fixes where the extended hand starts, and lets the person receiving it adjust to its actual speed. The first can train precision, the second responsiveness. Both may be useful, and they may alternate within the same rehearsal. The distinction is concrete enough that proficiency and freedom need not be set against each other.
¶
This also changes how I think about “failed footage.” Whether an attempt is worth including in a film depends on what it changes. If viewers can see how two people adjust and begin to wait for one another, slowness has content of its own. If only embarrassment is shown repeatedly, while the participants gain no new action, extending the viewing may merely increase their exposure. Keeping failure requires a formal reason, just as keeping success does.
¶
Once more cannot cancel the previous attempt. What it can do is bring that attempt into a new action: I did not hear you out just now, so now I wait; I was eager to finish, and now I see that my partner is not ready; I thought it was a question of emotion, and now I hear the other person say it is a little hot. A small condition emerges, and what the next attempt needs to do changes with it.
¶

Chapter 4 · The Body Sets Conditions
First, Say It Is Hot
A Meng asks, “Can you hug me?” Zi Chou replies, “I can, but it’s a little hot.”
¶
Watch the passage: Yes, but It’s a Little Hot
Video · bilingual dialogue · stills · return to this paragraph
A Meng suggests turning on the air conditioner. Zi Chou says, “But that’s too cold.”
[4-1]
¶
Here, a hug encounters temperature. The answer begins with “I can,” immediately followed by “hot”; a solution is proposed, and brings another kind of discomfort. Before the matter has been reduced to whether or not there is love, the body has already supplied information that needs to be dealt with.
¶
I want to understand intimacy from this small point. We often treat the body as the executor of feeling: if two people want to come closer, their bodies should carry out that approach. Yet bodies have their own speeds and conditions. Heat, cold, tiredness, and an inability to bear weight can all change an action. These are not additional problems that arise only after emotion. Feelings take shape within these conditions: wait a little, change position, use less force, or perhaps it cannot be done today.
¶
The body’s limits also mean that two people cannot form a whole through willingness alone. What feels right to one person may feel hot to the other; the same action makes different demands on each. Completing something together requires these differences to enter the action, beyond merely obtaining the same answer. Willingness gives a direction; how exactly to proceed remains to be discussed.
¶
Awkwardness then has content. It brings the abstract idea of coming closer into contact with two actual bodies. For film, what is worth seeing extends beyond a complete, beautiful hug. How conditions slow an action, and how people deal with that slowing, may reveal their relation more directly. Film can give small mismatches time, allowing viewers to discover that intimacy has no single posture that suits every body.
¶
In this dialogue, the air conditioner remains a suggestion. For now, I leave this unfinished point open. Once a possible solution has been voiced, the action may continue, or it may need to change direction. The body’s demands have already changed the request.
¶

From Conditions to Interpretation
Next, Yun Jianhui asks, “Then can you hug me?” Zi Chou replies, “I can.” A Meng then presses, “Then—then why are there so many reasons?” and proposes an explanation of “complicated feelings.”
[4-1]
A third speaker has joined in: the exchange no longer follows a single line of questions and answers between the same two people.
¶
Watch the passage: From Temperature to “So Many Reasons”
Video · bilingual dialogue · stills · return to this paragraph
I am concerned with how “reasons” appear here. The earlier heat and cold pointed to the conditions of the action; the later question begins to probe why those conditions are being raised. The question moves from how to hug to what is going on with the person answering. The two kinds of question can help each other, but one can also displace the other.
¶
Understanding the other person’s feelings is, of course, necessary. Statements about the body do not always fully express what a person wants. Heat may simply be heat, or it may coexist with hesitation; sometimes people have not yet found the right words and can only begin with the part easiest to say. Serious engagement cannot give up interpretation. But interpretation should give the other person more opportunities to explain themselves, rather than arrive first as an already completed answer.
¶
We can compare two ways of asking. “Is there another difficulty?” leaves the original conditions in place and allows new ones to be added. “You are just making excuses” may instead deprive the original words of their effect: the speaker must first prove that they have no other motive before they can return to their immediate discomfort. The two questions leave different amounts of room to continue.
¶
Sometimes the strongest interpretation is also the one most likely to block a response. It can absorb hesitation, objection, and silence into a single judgment. If the other person says no, we think they are not yet willing to face it; if they cannot explain, we think we already see deeper than they do. Such understanding leaves the other person no room to correct it. We seem to be discussing their inner life, while actually coming into contact with less and less of it.
¶
This set of utterances in the film makes that danger available for thought, but does not settle the characters’ full intentions for us. Further questioning may also be an attempt to find a solution. My judgment concerns how interpretation is used: it should return to action and help us deal with the difficulty before us. Knowing that someone has complicated feelings does not relieve us of continuing to listen when they say they are hot.
¶
Being Recognized and Having One’s Needs Met
The person asking for a hug also has a body and wishes of their own. They may simply need a moment of closeness, or may hope to use that closeness to confirm their place in the other person’s heart. That need deserves to be taken seriously. Acknowledging the body’s conditions does not mean excluding the person making the request from the relationship.
¶
The difficulty is that both people’s needs are real, yet they may not be met at the same time. One person needs closeness, the other distance. If distance is understood as a rejection of the first person as a whole, intimacy takes on an ever heavier task: every action must prove that the relationship still exists, and every hesitation may be read as its disappearance. A limited request thus comes to demand an almost unlimited answer.
¶
I want to bring recognition back into finite actions. Hear the other person’s difficulty and allow it to change what was originally planned; when you cannot meet their need, state your own limits. We do not have to understand another person completely before beginning to respond in this way. Sometimes we do not know where their exhaustion comes from, but can already ease the immediate demand. Conversely, we may know a great deal about someone and still be unwilling to change our arrangements for a difficulty they have voiced.
¶
This does not turn every wish into an obligation for others. A refusal can also take a request seriously: I know what you want, but I cannot do it now; this matters to you, but I cannot fulfil it in the way you hope. Refusal brings disappointment and may change a relationship. At least it allows both people to recognize a specific limit, without requiring one of them to keep pretending.
¶
The desire for recognition often contains a deeper contradiction. I want confirmation from someone independent of me: their answer matters precisely because I do not decide it myself. Yet I am also afraid that this independent person will give an answer I do not want to hear. The more I need their confirmation, then, the more I may want to control the form it takes. The independence on which desire relies also becomes the part it finds hardest to bear.
¶
This contradiction cannot be removed by a single, thorough conversation. Intimacy needs to bear it repeatedly: the other person matters to me, while still not being identical to the person I expect. They can love me and also not want to perform a particular action at this moment. The wish does not thereby become ridiculous, nor does disappointment have to be erased; both need to coexist with the other person’s answer.
¶
The Eyes Return More Than My Image
In a 2026 research article, I used the motif “I cannot see myself in your eyes” to discuss approach and confirmation.
[4-2]
¶
Wanting to see oneself in another person’s eyes is, first of all, an understandable wish. I want my presence to mean something to them; through the way they look at me, I want to know that I am not bearing this relationship alone. But the other person’s eyes are also looking at their own world. They may notice things I have overlooked, bring back judgments I did not expect, and even change how I understand myself.
¶
Confirmation draws its force precisely from this difference. An image returned entirely according to my demands comes increasingly to resemble a result I have arranged in advance. I obtain the appearance I want, yet find it harder to believe that it is another person’s response. To dispel the doubt, I may demand more direct declarations, closer proximity, and more intense commitment. Each proof works for a while, then needs to be followed by another. The harder the other person tries to conform to me, the less certain I can be whether what I receive is them or my own demands.
¶
I do not want to call this longing narcissism too readily. A vulnerable person may also want a clear answer, and anyone in a relationship may need a moment of firm confirmation. The question is whether, after confirmation, we can still hear difference. When the other person states their own conditions, do we learn more about them, or feel that they have broken the assurance they just gave?
¶
This brings intimacy and aesthetics together at the same point. Looking at a face, we may seek only the expression we expect; watching a film, we may likewise seek only images that confirm our existing judgments. Viewing can therefore become narrower the longer we look. To stay a little longer and let an unexpected detail change my understanding is a capacity I want to practise in my work. It does not abolish judgment; it allows the person and material before us to revise it.
¶
However close bodies become, this work cannot be spared. A camera can enlarge a face, an arm, or skin and bring details before our eyes, but it cannot take the place of responses between people. A convincing image of intimacy can coexist with two different feelings. Writing and editing should both leave room for that difference.
¶
That is why the answer about temperature matters to me. Someone did not immediately produce the expected posture; they stated the conditions through which the action still had to pass. The relationship thus gained something more that could be worked on together: how two people approach, where they stop, and whether they continue.
¶

Chapter 5 · Who Can Tell the Director to Leave the Stage?
“We have four directors onstage.”
¶
During the public performance in
Shoot Self with You
, Zi Chou counts the directors: the actual director, the director in the film, the director in the play, and another “director who came from who knows where.” Soon afterward, I criticize the acting and tell Ricky, “Just get off the stage and be a spectator.” He answers, “Why? I’m not getting off.”
[5-1]
¶
Suddenly, the word “director” is no longer enough. Several people can hold the title. One gives an instruction; another can still refuse it. The title does not carry out their next action for them.
¶
Watch the passage: “We Have Four Directors on Stage”
Video · bilingual dialogue · stills · return to this paragraph
What interests me in this exchange is how an assessment becomes an instruction. To say someone is acting badly is to judge a performance; to tell them to leave is to change their position within the event. Whether they can still speak, and whether the others carry on, are both affected by this sentence. “Be a spectator” also has concrete consequences here: watching is offered as the position to take after leaving the performance. There is nothing inherently inferior about being a spectator, but in this statement, it is a position assigned by someone else.
¶
Ricky then says, “I know the acting is terrible, but you’re the one who asked me to come and act in this play.”
[5-1]
He does more than argue about the quality of the acting. He brings up why he came in the first place. Someone has been invited to take part, has given their time and taken on a role, and is now suddenly asked to leave the stage. The invitation collides with the assessment. The original arrangement needs to be explained again.
¶
Watch the passage: “But You Asked Me Here to Perform in This Play”
Video · bilingual dialogue · stills · return to this paragraph
This adds something else to what is happening. The people in the scene continue acting, while also arguing about how the play should continue.
¶

Knowing It Is Acting, Still Wanting to Object
After the public performance in 2023, Sun Jiarui wrote about it from his own position. He felt that the performance had stalled and that Xiang Yubin had moved it forward; I appeared, thought this was no good, and told her to leave the stage. He continued: “I knew
He Fa
was acting, but I really did want to argue back: this is good, it’s good just like this. But I had no strength left.”
[5-2]
¶
Jia Rui’s “it’s good just like this” also proposes a measure different from mine. I thought the performance needed to be interrupted; he thought that what had just emerged deserved to continue. Our two judgments did not become one simply because we were part of the same work. I cannot use my position as director to decide his understanding for him, nor can I automatically recast his objection afterward as compelling material that the work required.
¶
I want to keep this in the book. What most deserves attention in collaborative creation often emerges when someone refuses to understand it on my terms. That disagreement prevents me from deciding alone what, exactly, we have just accomplished.
¶
What Does a Change of Role Change?
P4
experiments with allowing established working roles to change. In a production statement from 2023, I wrote that actors could become directors, camera operators could become actors, those documenting could also act, and performers could also observe.
[5-3]
This expresses a way of working we hoped for: no one has to remain locked into a single function forever. When someone documenting the work steps in front of the camera, they have to face, in their own body, difficulties they previously watched. When performers help organize the work, they can also propose how they want to appear.
¶
The value of such changes depends on whether they alter the concrete next step. If someone is merely called a director but cannot change the task, propose cuts or revisions, or refuse to continue, the new title gives them little room to act. Someone who both films and performs may simply be doing more work, without gaining more opportunities to decide.
¶
A shift in working roles therefore needs a response from others. When someone proposes another way of doing things, the others have to make time for it. When someone says they cannot do something now, those present cannot treat this only as an obstacle for the performance to overcome. The measure of collaborative creation lies here: can another person’s presence change my original arrangement?
¶
This does not require every disagreement to end in concession. Someone still has to decide how the scene moves forward, and not all views can be accommodated at once. Judgment has to address what the disagreement is about. Ricky gives his reason for coming at someone’s invitation; Jia Rui believes that Xiang Yubin has already moved the stalled scene forward. These are concrete views that can be discussed and also opposed. Classifying them as obedience or disobedience would make the actual questions disappear.
¶
There is also a creative gain here. The original plan may not have room for everything a person can do. Outside their assigned role, they may propose a better method, or point out a problem everyone has grown so used to that they no longer notice it. If every change must first be imagined by the person who initiated the project, the others merely increase the number of people carrying it out. Working together matters because I, too, may follow a direction I had not foreseen and find my own work anew within it.
¶
Putting My Own Position into the Work
“Who can tell the director to leave the stage?” is also a question I ask myself. An actor can be interrupted; can a director’s arrangements be interrupted in the same way? When someone holding a camera wants a particular image, can the person being filmed make them change that wish?
¶
These questions cannot be resolved simply by filming the camera or letting the director appear onscreen. I can place myself inside the work while still deciding how others are seen. Revealing my presence only makes my position visible. What matters next is what kinds of objection that position will accept.
¶
In the public performance, at least the judgments and refusals have been spoken. They leave the film with material different from a complete performance: how a scene is stopped, how someone argues for staying and continuing, and how a participant later writes down an objection they could not fully express at the time. Film can bring these things from different moments together, so that the director’s judgment at the time is no longer the only point of entry.
¶
But I also have to acknowledge a distinction that collaboration cannot erase. Many people are present, yet the finished film still passes through selection. Who is given more time, whose hesitation is kept, which image precedes an objection—all affect how later viewers understand the dispute. Even if every piece of footage records something that actually happened, its arrangement still comes from specific decisions.
¶
Openness during creation makes the work of editing harder. Keeping a disagreement can let different judgments remain at odds. It can also be arranged so that all we see is a generous author and people who seem difficult to work with. Including someone who objects does not mean the film has taken care to preserve their reasons.
¶
The demand I can make is that those reasons remain discernible. Why Ricky refuses to leave the stage, and why Jia Rui thinks “it’s good just like this,” cannot be turned entirely into the emotional atmosphere of the scene. Later viewers should have a chance to disagree with me on those grounds. That possibility does not weaken the author’s work. It demands greater precision in the author’s choices: what have I kept here, and what have I deprived of a chance to answer?
¶
A collaboratively made film does not turn everyone into the same author. It can allow different people to remain different within the work. The director still has decisions to make, but cannot use those decisions to end the argument on everyone’s behalf.
¶

Chapter 7 · Behind the White Cloth
This disappearance had a procedure agreed on beforehand.
¶
Sun Jiarui describes it clearly in his account after the performance: cover everyone with the white cloth lying on the floor, go backstage, and quietly leave, so the audience sees only a piece of cloth remaining onstage. “It’s a magic trick.”
[7-1]
¶
Several people have to carry out this arrangement together. Someone picks up the cloth, someone is covered, and everyone leaves by the agreed route. To let an audience see a disappearance, a series of very concrete actions first has to be organized. The cloth has to hide the people; the backstage route has to be passable; what is onstage and where the audience sits have to form a certain relation. Disappearance is given a form that can be carried out.
¶
Within this staging, we know what to do next. Yet a question arises as the action nears completion.
¶
Jia Rui writes that, when they reached the exit, A Meng suddenly asked whether this was what he wanted: to go somewhere no one was, where no one could find him. The lines were not in the script. He answered, “Yes, yes.” Looking back, he still could not say whether he had wanted to finish the performance quickly or felt that she had indeed touched on something important.
[7-1]
¶
A planned disappearance left an answer that the plan had not resolved.
¶
Who Wants to Disappear?
A Meng’s question turns attention from the action to the wish. An exit performed by several people together suddenly requires an answer from one person: is this what you want?
¶
“How to do it” could be settled by discussion. What to cover the bodies with, where to leave, and what to leave for the audience could all be rehearsed beforehand. “Is this what you want?” calls for a different kind of answer. It brings the arranged action back before the person performing it and asks them to explain their relation to it.
¶
Sometimes the two coincide. By carrying out an action, someone may indeed express something they have long wanted to say. But an action can also accommodate other reasons: cooperating with a partner, following the rehearsal, bringing things to a smooth close, or simply finishing what is immediately at hand. A single “yes” cannot separate these reasons one by one. Jia Rui’s later account preserves their entanglement.
¶
This also makes me reluctant to call an unplanned question a direct route to someone’s inner life. It did change the event, because beyond the scheduled exit, something else now required a response. But what the questioner touched on still has to emerge gradually through the answer, the actions, and later understanding. The suddenness of a question does not automatically make the answer more truthful.
¶
In the film’s manually verified dialogue record, A Meng asks, “So is this what you want?” and Jia Rui answers, “Yes.” She then says, “No one can see you,” and he answers again, “Yes.”
[7-2]
Two affirmations have been spoken, yet the questions are not exhausted.
¶
What remains unfinished lies elsewhere: someone has answered without necessarily being able to grasp every reason for that answer.
¶
Understanding Continues After the Answer
Everyday life often asks people to know what they want before they act. Actual experience is less orderly. Someone may agree and only later discover that they cannot bear it, or refuse and only afterward realize what they are reluctant to lose. They may still hold several explanations much later.
¶
Jia Rui’s writing gives this concrete weight. He does not deny having said “yes,” nor does he erase his answer at the time. He tries to explain it, then stops within the explanation. Wanting the performance to end and being touched by the question are two possibilities he himself proposes. The account does not declare one true and the other false.
¶
I cannot choose for him from outside. Nor need this uncertainty be treated as an understanding he has not yet attained, as though asking a few more times would finally yield a pure cause. Some actions are moved by several forces from the outset. Reducing them to a single motive may produce clarity only by subtraction.
¶
This does not make every explanation equal. His statement that the exit under the white cloth had been agreed on in advance limits accounts of the whole ending as a sudden departure. His observation that A Meng’s question was not in the script also prevents the entire exchange from being classified as predetermined dialogue. His account provides facts sufficient to change our understanding without giving a psychological answer that accounts for the whole event.
¶
What I value is precisely the possibility of keeping both. Specific events can be clarified without closing off someone’s entire experience. A theory that calls every uncertainty profound loses its judgment; a film that treats every answer as a person’s final confession brings that person to an end too soon.
¶
At the beginning of his account, Jia Rui also writes that friends came to check on him and express concern. Some thanked him; some said he was sacrificing himself again. Yet he did not understand what he had done to deserve thanks, or what counted as sacrifice. What he could confirm was that he did get himself very dirty after every performance.
[7-1]
¶
This is a sharp point. People see the same performance and leave with different accounts. Gratitude and concern may be sincere and still miss the experience of the person involved. To see someone as sacrificing himself may praise his commitment while also placing him in a role he does not recognize. Caring about him requires hearing his hesitation about these accounts.
¶
The Cloth Does Not Fully Explain a Person
The white cloth also does practical work in the film. It changes how bodies are visible: clothing, faces, and individual positions become hard to distinguish, leaving raised shapes, folds in the fabric, and partial edges. For a time, individuals are gathered beneath a shared material.
¶
But the film does not show only this cloth. In the images near the exchange, backstage computers, control equipment, and crew members also appear. After the cloth fills the image, those people and pieces of equipment can be seen again.
[7-3]
The arrangement for disappearing and the activities that keep the event running thus enter the same passage of film.
¶
Watch the passage: Beyond the White Cloth, Backstage Work Continues
Video · bilingual dialogue · stills · return to this paragraph
