P4 Theater and You
2026-06-25
Theory and Methods
Not a Trichotomy but Three Axes: Film, Theatre, and Documentary
A three-axis account of film, theatre, and documentary through media ontology, epistemological contracts, and the politics of performance.
Media ontology, epistemological contract and performance politics of film, drama and documentary
Summary
"What is the difference between film, drama and documentary?" is usually understood as a horizontal comparison between the three art types, but this question implies a misplacement at the category level: film and drama first stipulate how the work is produced, preserved and presented, and therefore mainly belong to the category of media and art institutions; documentary first stipulates how the work points to historical reality, how to organize evidence and what factual responsibilities the creator should bear, so it mainly belongs to the categories of epistemology, pragmatics and ethics. Documentaries can be movies, or they can take the form of drama, sound, photography, interactive media, etc.; movies can be fictional or documentary; dramas can play fictional characters or present real testimonies and historical archives. Based on film ontology, performance research and documentary theory, this article proposes the three axes of "media tense-referential contract-performance construction" and the threshold model of "ethical accountability". By analyzing the documentary theater practices of "Summer Chronicles", "The Act of Killing", "Twenty-Four Cities" and Rimini Protokoll, this article demonstrates that: liveness and documentaryness are not absolute opposites, nor are performance and documentaryness mutually exclusive attributes; what determines whether a work is documentary is not whether it looks natural or whether the images are not staged, but whether the work makes verifiable claims about the real world to the audience, and whether it takes responsibility for the source of evidence, the method of re-enactment, the situation of the participants and possible consequences. Therefore, film, drama and documentary should not be understood as three mutually exclusive containers, but should be placed in a multi-dimensional and intersecting media coordinate system.
Keywords
Film; drama; documentary; media ontology; liveness; factual claims; performance; documentary ethics
1. The question raised: a category error concealed by parallel grammar
The three are not parallel categories, but answer questions at different levels.
In everyday language, "movie" is often tacitly equated with a feature film, "drama" is tacitly equated with a fictional performance on stage, and "documentary" is understood to be a direct record of reality. So the three seem to form a neat set of oppositions
Movies tell stories, plays stage stories, and documentaries record reality.
This statement is convenient, but it creates three misunderstandings in theory.
First, it reduces "film" to "fictional film" and ignores news films, ethnographic films, film essays, experimental films, animated documentaries, and a large number of image forms between fiction and non-fiction. Cinema in the academic sense is a broader institution of the moving image rather than a synonym for feature film.
Second, it associates "drama" with "unreality," as if performing on stage necessarily implies fiction. Yet testimony theatre, courtroom theatre, verbatim theatre, historical reenactment, political action theatre, and documentary theater can all make explicit factual claims about real people and historical events.
Third, it defines documentary as "reality itself" without creation, selection, or performance. This view not only ignores the role of camera position, editing, sound, subtitles, interviews and distribution context in constructing meaning, but also fails to explain why highly staged documentaries may still have epistemic value, nor why "mockumentaries" that use handheld photography, synchronized sound and interview styles still belong to fiction.
To be more precise, these three concepts are not at exactly the same logical level
concept
Top questions to answer
Main categories
movie
Through what moving image devices is the work produced, fixed, edited and projected?
Media-Device Category
Drama/Theatre
How do performers and audiences co-constitute an event in a specific time and space?
Performance-Event Category
documentary/documentary
How does the work point to historical reality, make factual claims, and bear the burden of evidence?
Epistemology-Ethical Categories
Therefore, the core proposition of this article is
Film and drama mainly stipulate the way the work exists; documentary mainly stipulates the responsible relationship between the work and reality.
The "main" here is very important. Of course, film and theater also have epistemological, ethical and political dimensions; documentaries have also formed stable production institutions, stylistic traditions and distribution systems. But from the perspective of conceptual distinction, film and drama are first and foremost a question of "how to present", while documentary is first and foremost a question of "why the reality is stated in this way."
2. Theoretical Genealogy: Recorded Images, Events and Accountable Statements
Film as a repeatable audiovisual object: projection, viewing and media installation.
(1) Film: from photographic traces to repeatable audiovisual objects
Classic film ontology often starts from the causal connection between photographic images and reality. Bazin believed that the particularity of photography was that the optical traces of objects could form images with less reliance on manual depiction; Cavell understood film as the automatic projection of a world in front of the audience. Unlike painting, photographic film seems to retain traces of something's presence in front of the camera (Bazin 1967; Cavell 1979).
However, it cannot be concluded that "film is a record of reality". First of all, photography only guarantees that a certain optical event has occurred, and does not guarantee that subtitles, narration, character identities, and causal explanations are real. Second, animated films, digitally composite films, and entirely computer-generated images still belong to film culture. Rodowick's discussion of digital cinema has shown that cinema should not be defined solely by the materiality of film or the indexicality of photography (Rodowick 2007).
Compared with "photographic traces", the more stable feature of film is that it processes one or more shooting, recording, design and performance activities into a relatively fixed, repeatable audio-visual object. A film actor's performance is not equivalent to any one complete action that occurs on set. It is often split into different scenes, camera positions and shooting times, and is finally recomposed by lens selection, editing, sound design and color processing. Performance in film is therefore a co-production of body, camera and post-production
"Composite Performance"
。
The basic time structure of the film is also formed from this: the audience usually watches the object that has been completed, selected and fixed. The audiovisual sequences seen by different viewers at different times can be substantially the same.
A film screening can certainly become a social event, and the audience's reaction can change the viewing experience, but these reactions usually do not reversely change the sequence of shots that have been completed.
(2) Drama: from textual works to co-generated events
"Drama" in Chinese includes at least two objects that are related but cannot be confused with each other: one is the drama text that can be read, published and adapted, and the other is the theater performance that takes place in a specific place. If no distinction is made, Shakespeare's play, a specific performance, and the entire performance tradition of the play will be mistaken for the same object.
Aristotle understood tragedy as imitation accomplished through the actions of actors rather than mere narrative. But modern theater theory further points out that theatrical performance is not about pre-existing script content being transparently put on the stage. The actor's physical state, audience reaction, venue acoustics, accidents, social environment and performance rhythm together constitute an event that cannot be completely replicated.
Peggy Phelan emphasizes the evanescent nature of performance
Fischer-Lichte used the "autopoietic feedback loop" to illustrate how actors and audiences influence each other.
The audience's silence, laughter, restlessness, and even departure may change the actor's rhythm, and the actor's actions will continue to reorganize the audience's attention and emotions (Phelan 1993; Fischer-Lichte 2008).
The same play can be performed repeatedly, but it repeats the structure, rules or score, not the same events.
However, treating liveness as the pure essence of theater uncontaminated by technology is equally problematic. Auslander points out that modern "live" experience has been redefined in the media environment of radio, recording, film and television (Auslander 2008). Video projections, remote actors, real-time data, live audiences and virtual spaces may all find their way into contemporary theatre. Therefore, site and mediatization are better understood as different degrees of organization rather than as either-or metaphysical oppositions.
The archetypal characteristic of drama is not that it is "absolutely without a medium," but that the main aesthetic object of the work still includes
An ongoing performative event with feedback possibilities and live contingency.
(3) Documentary: Not reality itself, but claims about reality
The core of the documentary is not "no processing", but how the evidence enters public judgment.
A fundamental turning point in documentary theory is to abandon the understanding of documentary as "raw reality." Grierson's famous "creative treatment of reality" has acknowledged that documentary not only uses the real world as its material, but also necessarily formalizes reality through composition, editing, narrative and sound.
Bill Nichols further understood documentary as a social practice, historical tradition, and way of viewing, rather than just a text with a certain fixed style. The poetic, interpretive, observational, participatory, reflexive and performative modes he distinguishes just illustrate that documentary does not have a single "objective appearance"; its theoretical framework also puts voice, persuasion, evidence and ethics at the center of documentary research. ([Indiana University Press][1])
Carl Plantinga's "assertive stance" and Noel Carroll's "presumptive assertion" theories provide more rigorous epistemological explanations
Documentaries invite viewers to understand the central statements in the work as claims about the real world, rather than as assumptions in a fictional game.
The so-called "real world" is not unmediated nature, but a world in which people, institutions, and events may be tested by historical evidence, witnesses, archives, and public discussion (Plantinga 1997; Carroll 1996).
Documentary identity cannot therefore be determined solely by the appearance of the image. Fiction can use interviews, surveillance footage, shaky shots, and news subtitles; documentaries can use animation, reenactments, models, dance, and dreams. What really matters is what kind of relationship is established between the work and the audience
alleged contract
。
This contract does not guarantee that the work will be correct. Documentaries may make mistakes, lie, or intentionally mislead. Precisely because it makes factual claims, we have reason to accuse it of being untrue. Characters in fictional works do not have real resumes, which does not constitute deception; documentaries fictionalize the identity of the interviewer, but make the audience mistakenly believe that the interviewer is a real witness, which constitutes a breach of the record contract.
From this we can distinguish three concepts that are often confused
reality
Refers to whether the characters and events discussed in the work are placed in the historical world
authenticity
Refers to whether specific statements, images, and explanations are credible
Documentary
It refers to whether the work places itself in the relationship between evidence testing and public accountability.
Documentaries do not have a monopoly on "truth." Fictional films and dramas can equally reveal deep emotional truths, social structures, and historical experiences. But documentaries bear a more specific obligation
When it says "this person exists", "this thing happened", "this image comes from a certain time and place"
The audience has the right to ask for evidence.
3. "Three Axis-One Threshold" Model
Three axes and ethical threshold model: media tense, referential contract, performance construction, and ethical accountability.
In order to avoid repacking film, drama and documentary into three closed containers, this article proposes a heuristic analysis model. Any work can be tentatively represented as
W = <M, R, P; E>
Among them, the three descriptive dimensions are media tense, referential contract and performance construction; ethical accountability constitutes a normative threshold. The notation here does not require a mechanical quantification of a work of art, but rather shows that several properties can vary independently of each other.
1. Media tense axis (M)
This axis examines what kind of objects the work mainly exists as
At one end is a fixed, copyable and replayable record object
At the other end of the spectrum are live events that rely on simultaneous participation of performers and audiences
The middle includes live movies, remote theater, interactive images, real-time generated performances and stage videos.
Traditional film is usually closer to the "recorded object" end, and traditional theater is closer to the "live event" end. But this is an archetypal difference, not an insurmountable boundary.
2. Referring to the Contract Axis (R)
This axis examines how the work asks the viewer to understand its statement
The fictional side invites the audience to engage in imagination "if these characters and events existed"
The factual side requires the audience to understand the core statement as an assertion about the historical world
It includes autobiographical fiction, historical drama, documentary novels, film essays and mixed fiction and reality.
This dimension has nothing to do with whether the work is "profound" or not. Fiction can have powerful historical insights, and documentaries can be superficial. The difference is whether the audience has reason to treat a specific statement as a fact that can be externally verified.
3. Performance construction axis (P)
This axis examines how well the creator organizes scenes, language, and character behaviors
The lower end includes long observations, incidental events, and unrehearsed interactions
The higher end includes scripts, rehearsals, role plays, reenactments, sets, and highly stylized mise-en-scène.
The key point is that the degree of construction is not inversely proportional to documentaryness. Low intervention does not automatically produce truth, nor does high performance automatically eliminate documentary value. Interview questions themselves shape responses, and observational photography excludes large amounts of information through framing and editing; conversely, reenactments can sometimes reveal memories, traumas, fantasies, and power structures that could not be recorded by the original camera.
4. Ethical Accountability Threshold (E)
Ethical accountability is not another style but a condition for the legitimacy of factual work. Include at least
Traceability of sources of archives, data and testimonies
Appropriate disclosure of levels of reenactment, synthesis, doubles, and fictionalization
Ongoing assessment of participant knowledge, risks, and power inequalities
Responsibility for contextual editing, translation, anonymity and identity presentation
Ability to respond to factual errors, harm consequences, and public questioning.
Therefore, even if a work is on the "factual" end, it does not mean that it is ethically qualified. Documentation is a commitment, and ethical accountability determines whether the work fulfills this commitment well.

This table shows that documentary is not a third medium next to film. "Documentary" in a narrow sense can be defined as
Documentary practice in the medium of film or moving image.
Documentary theater is

4. Systematic differences between the three
(1) Basic units of the work: lens objects, performance events and factual relationships
The basic aesthetic unit of a film is usually an audiovisual object that has been fixed and programmed.
Even if the filming process is full of chance, what the audience ultimately comes into contact with is still a edited version.
The basic unit of drama is a performance event. The script, director's plan and stage design can be relatively stable, but the time experienced by the actors and the audience cannot be completely reproduced.
A show can repeat the same lines every night without replicating exactly the same rhythms, missteps, moods, and viewing relationships.
The core unit of documentary is neither the lens nor the stage action itself, but the relationship between images, sounds, testimonies and historical reality.
Evidence relationship
. A shot may be real but redefined by false subtitles
An actor's reenactment may not capture the past directly, but it can serve as evidence of how someone remembers, denies, or imagines the past in the present.
(2) Time structure: has happened, is happening and is claimed to have happened
Time in traditional movies is consummated. Filming and editing often precede viewing, and the viewer is confronted with an already settled arrangement.
Traditional theater has a progressive nature. A performance is not a mechanical reproduction of an original event, but a re-realization in front of an audience. Even when the ending is written, the physical processes that bring it to fruition are still at risk.
Documentaries have
double time
The present when the shooting was taken and the historical time it refers to. The interviewer's current expression may become indirect evidence of past events; archival images not only record the past, but are also given a new argumentative position in new editing.
Documentaries do not bring the past back to the present intact, but reorganize how we can understand the past in the present.
(3) Performance mechanism: playing roles, generating roles and performing oneself
Fictional actors often openly admit that they are playing characters that do not exist in reality. A film actor's performance is broken up by the camera and editing; a stage actor must maintain character actions over a relatively continuous period of time.
Documentary participants are often mistaken for "not acting." In fact, people almost inevitably organize their own image when facing a camera, an interviewer, or an audience. Interviewees may choose to dress, suppress emotions, exaggerate experiences, or use language that is socially expected. Performing oneself is not the same as lying; social identity itself is presented repeatedly in different situations.
Therefore, what the documentary needs to ask is not "did this person perform?" but
Who is he performing for? In what power relations is it performed? What is the performance trying to prove? How do creators explain this performance through editing?
The characters in the documentary are simultaneously social actors, images and sources of evidence in the creator's narrative. Precisely because the three identities overlap, documentary ethics is far more complicated than "obtaining consent for a single filming".
(4) Narrative and evidence: logic of possibility and logic of justification
Works of fiction rely primarily on possibility, coherence, and artistic form to establish persuasiveness. The audience will not deny "Hamlet" because Hamlet does not have a birth certificate, because the work never asks the audience to believe that this prince did exist in Danish history.
Documentaries require not only narrative coherence but also justification. Footage, testimony, and data cannot just "fit the story" but must form a legitimate connection to the work's claims. Documentaries can create suspense, create characters, and use symbols, but aesthetic effects are no substitute for evidence.
This also means that "real material" does not automatically tell the truth. Archival images must be dated, located, photographed, and originally used; testimonies need to account for memory bias, interests, and trauma; and statistics need to be caliber. The form of documentary is not a decoration outside of reality, but the way in which evidence is organized into public knowledge.
(5) Audience position: viewing the chosen world, co-locating with events and examining factual claims
The movie camera pre-selects the viewing position for the audience. The lens determines the distance, the editing determines the sequence, and the frame determines what is visible and invisible. The audience can make critical interpretations, but they cannot really move their eyes outside the painting in the established version.
The theater spectator, although constrained by lighting, scheduling, and seating, usually has greater freedom of immediate attention: he can look at the actors who are not speaking, watch the stage machinery, or observe other members of the audience. More importantly, the presence of the audience itself may become a performance condition.
Documentary viewers are given another role: not only to watch, but also to judge. Documentary viewing implies a structure of public scrutiny-whose claim is it, why should it be believed, what has been omitted, and who bears the consequences? The ideal audience for a documentary is therefore not one who passively accepts "truth," but a critical audience capable of distinguishing between evidence, interpretation, and rhetoric.
5. Boundary Cases: How Performances Become Documentary Evidence
(1) "Summer Chronicle": The camera is not a transparent window, but a participant in the truth experiment
Chronicles of a Summer: Cameras, Street Questions and Reflexive Experiments.
Jean Rouch and Edgar Morin's "Chronicles of a Summer" (1961) is often regarded as an important work of cinematic truth-seeking. The film gets close to the work, emotions, war memories and political situations of ordinary people in Paris through street questions, collective conversations and daily follow-up shots. Lightweight camera equipment and simultaneous sound recording expanded the camera's ability to enter everyday environments, but the film's most important contribution is not to claim that technology has finally eliminated mediation, but to turn mediation itself into a problem.
Later in the film, participants watch footage and discuss which scenes are "real" and which characters are "overacted." Screenings that were intended to verify authenticity instead exposed conflicts between standards of authenticity: some believed that emotion was too dramatic, while others believed that restraint was inauthentic. Relevant research points out that the film ultimately does not prove that the camera can reach unperformed life, but instead transforms "how the truth is produced between the camera, participants and audience" into the theme of the work. ([The Criterion Collection][2])
According to the model of this article, the media tense of "Summer Chronicles" belongs to documentary film, and the referential contract is obviously factual, but its degree of performance construction is not low: the questions are raised by the director, the group is convened by the director, and the feedback from the screening changes the participants' understanding of their own image. Its documentary value comes precisely from the disclosure of these conditions, not from the non-existence of "zero intervention."
The film thus reveals a key principle
Reflexivity is not a way for documentaries to admit failure, but a way for documentaries to incorporate their own production conditions into the chain of evidence.
(2) "Killing Performance": Reenactment is not a copy of the past, but evidence of current ideology
"Killing Act": Genre film-style reenactment turns the perpetrator's current ideology into an object of evidence.
Joshua Oppenheimer's Acts of Killing (2012) invites perpetrators of mass killings in Indonesia to reenact their actions in the form of their favorite gangster films, musicals, and horror films. If measured by the standard of "the more staged shots there are, the lower the documentary quality", this work should almost be excluded from documentaries. But this judgment misses what the reenactment actually proves.
The reenactments in the film should not be taken as accurate forensic reconstructions of the killings. What it documents above all is how the past is understood, paraded, aestheticized, and rearranged in the present by the perpetrators. Genre film imagination, make-up, costumes and exaggerated performances expose official historical narratives, masculinity, film culture and self-deception. As relevant comments have pointed out, what the film reveals through the "film-within-a-film" structure is not the behavioral facts that the perpetrators are unwilling to admit - they often admit it publicly - but how they use performance to escape, transform or experience guilt. ([The New Yorker][3])
In this case, the performative construct axis is high, and the factual referential axis is equally high. The object of evidence for reenactment is not "how each action actually occurred in the past" but "how the perpetrator today imagines the past as a heroic narrative for viewing." Performance does not cancel documentaryness, but changes the object to which documentaryness is directed.
However, this approach also raises acute ethical questions: By allowing the perpetrator to occupy the center of the narrative, will the victim be suppressed again? Does the image expose violence while replicating its spectacle? These issues cannot be ended by declaring that the film "is real" but must be continually discussed at the level of risk, context, victim safety and political consequences. This suggests that a documentary's ethical accountability is not an automatic add-on after a work acquires the "documentary" label, but is part of its epistemological validity.
(3) "Tale of 24 Cities": Collective Memory, Actors' Testimonies and Disclosure Responsibilities
"Tale of 24 Cities": A hybrid structure of real interviews, actor testimonies and collective memory.
Jia Zhangke's "Twenty-Four Cities" (2008) revolves around the relocation, closure and replacement of a large factory in Chengdu by a real estate project. The film juxtaposes interviews with real workers and testimonies of composite characters performed by actors, and is generally regarded as a hybrid form of documentary and fiction; reports at the time also clearly stated that the film contains real interviews and performances by actors, and uses it to tell the history of the factory and its labor groups. ([The New Yorker][4])
The actor's testimony was not simply "fabricated." Synthetic characters are able to bring together intergenerational experiences that cannot be fully borne by any one interviewee, and form an emotional history of the disappearance of the socialist industrial community through performance rhythms, face culture, and celebrity memory. The problem is: when the audience cannot clearly distinguish between recorded testimony and comprehensive creation within the work, different materials will be given similar weight of evidence.
If the film is treated as a purely fictional film, the performance of the actors does not pose a problem; if it enters public history in the name of a documentary, the identity of the performers, the source of the material and the way the characters are integrated should bear a higher responsibility for disclosure. The theoretical value of "Twenty-Four Cities" comes from this unstable position: it forces the audience to distinguish between "evidence of historical facts" and "poetic synthesis of historical experience."
Therefore, this work should not be simply judged as a "true documentary" or a "fake documentary". A more accurate term would be hybrid documentary film, documentary essay film or documentary fiction. It not only preserves the testimonies of real workers, but also produces the symbolic form of collective memory through actors; its evaluation criteria must also include both aesthetic interpretation and factual disclosure.
(4) Rimini Protokoll: Documentation does not depend on the screen
Rimini Protokoll's "100% City" series: experts in daily life and urban demographics take the stage.
"My own performance" in documentary theater does not automatically equal the truth. It still requires representativeness and the responsibility of testimony.
The German theater group Rimini Protokoll often invites "everyday life experts" with specific life experiences, professional knowledge or social identities into performances, and transforms real-life mechanisms such as shareholder meetings, urban population structure, transnational call centers and war experiences into theater structures. Their official introduction clearly emphasizes that they collaborate with expertise holders outside the theater and create new perspectives on reality through interactive technology and spatial transformation. ([rimini-protokoll.de][5])
These performances illustrate that documentary can exist in live theatre. The performers may appear with their own names, occupations and experiences, and the performance materials may also come from data, documents and real systems. But the presence of the body at the scene does not mean that the testimony is automatically true. Real people can also misremember, conceal, exaggerate, or obey directorial structures; "acting in person" can only prove that someone is present at the moment, but cannot alone prove all his statements about the past.
The epistemological significance of documentary theater is that it transforms evidence from traces on the screen into a face-to-face witnessing relationship. The audience not only hears the statement, but also directly experiences the speaker's pauses, physical vulnerability, and social position. At the same time, directorial control over personnel selection, representation, and order of speaking remains.
Therefore, documentary theater is not "theater without performance", but
Theater that organizes factual material in a performative manner and requires staged statements to be tested by reality.
6. Stress testing of several boundary issues
Boundary judgment does not look at the appearance label, but looks at the viewing contract established by the work.
1. Is "Based on True Events" a documentary?
No. Historical dramas can be based on real events, but generally allow for the merging of characters, rewriting of dialogue, and reorganization of cause and effect. As long as the work does not require the audience to treat each scene as factual evidence, it remains primarily a fictional contract.
"Adapted from real events" only indicates that reality is the source of the material, but does not indicate that the work bears the documentary evidence obligation.
2. Why is a mockumentary not a documentary?
Because documentary style does not equal documentary contract. Handheld footage, interviews, timecodes and surveillance footage are just a few semiotic resources that can be used in any work. Mockumentaries often invite viewers to understand characters and events as fictional in their titles, releases, genre cues, or final reveals.
On the contrary, if the creator deliberately creates the illusion of a real news event and refuses to provide fictional tips for a long time, the problem is no longer just an artistic type experiment, but may become a communication deception.
3. Animated documentaries have no photographic traces, so why can they still be considered documentaries?
Because photographic causation is not a necessary condition for documentaryness. Animation can make claims about reality to viewers based on diaries, audio recordings, judicial records, memories and scientific data. The images are contrived, but the events, experiences, and interpretations expressed are still open to evidence testing.
Animated documentaries instead make the process of construction more visible: instead of mistaking the images for unmediated slices of reality, the viewer becomes aware of the visual form as an interpretation of the evidence.
4. Once a stage performance is filmed, is it still theater?
Stage performances and stage videos should be viewed as related but not identical objects. The original performance is a live event; the video transforms the event into an audio-visual work that can be watched repeatedly through camera position, scenery, editing and sound.
For the live audience, the actors, audience and space together constitute the theater event; for the video audience, the viewing object has been reorganized by the camera. Video can record drama, but it cannot fully preserve the unfilmed spatial relationships, audience feedback, and contingencies of the original event.
Live theater falls somewhere in between: the remote audience and actors may share time but not the same physical space, and the ability of the remote audience to respond depends on the technical design.
5. Does reenactment automatically make a documentary fiction?
No. Two statements must be distinguished
"This is the original image of the events of that year"
"This is a re-enactment of the events of that year based on certain evidence."
The latter does not have to pass off as original evidence as long as it clearly identifies its reenactment and explains what material it is based on. The problem is not the reenactment itself, but whether to confuse the evidentiary status of reenactments, speculation, and archives.
6. Do documentaries have to be objective and neutral?
It is impossible for a documentary to be completely devoid of standpoint. Camera selection, issue design, editing sequence, and distribution channels all have a value orientation. Objectivity should be understood not as "the absence of an author" but as a set of methodological disciplines that can be openly discussed: distinguishing fact from interpretation, presenting the limits of evidence, checking contrary material, avoiding deliberate falsification, and allowing claims to be criticized.
Documentaries can be strongly involved in politics, but the stronger the intervention does not mean that the requirements for facts are lower. Conversely, the clearer the public claim, the higher the burden of proof will generally be.
7. Discussion: From ontological purity to relational definition
There is a continuous "purity impulse" in the history of film and theater: film theory tries to find the unique material essence of film, theater theory tries to defend the unreplicable liveness, and documentary theory tries to find a realistic image that will not be contaminated by artistic processing.
But media practice continues to produce counterexamples. Digital films no longer rely on film; theaters make extensive use of screens and remote connections; documentaries can be animated, performed, and interactive; fictional works can also incorporate archives and real people. By insisting on finding a single necessary characteristic for each art, theory can only keep declaring new forms "not pure enough."
The model in this article adopts a relational definition. The identity of a work is not determined by one material alone, but by the following relationships
Work identity = media organization × referential contract × performance method × institutional context and ethical accountability
This definition does not mean that all boundaries can be eliminated arbitrarily. On the contrary, it makes the boundary judgment more stringent: when judging a work, you cannot just conclude by "like a movie", "like a documentary" or "someone is on the stage", but you must specify what attributes it has in which dimension.
From this we can also re-understand the concept of "reality". Works of art involve at least four different realities
existence is real
Whether the person, place or event actually exists
proposition true
Whether statements about them are accurate
Experience is real
Whether the work conveys a certain feeling that the subject has actually experienced
Structural reality
Whether the work reveals the social relationships behind individual experiences.
Documentaries especially bear the responsibility of the first two truths, and may also pursue the latter two; fictional films and dramas may not necessarily bear the factual obligations of specific propositions, but they may be more insightful than some documentaries in terms of empirical truth and structural truth.
Therefore, "fiction" does not equal falsehood, and "documentary" does not equal truth. The difference between the two is that they make different promises to the audience.
8. Conclusion
There is no simple, symmetrical dividing line between film, drama and documentary.
Film is first and foremost a media system that organizes moving images into repeatable audiovisual objects; drama is first and foremost a performance system that uses body, space, time, and audience feedback to constitute live events; documentary is first and foremost a practical way of making factual claims, organizing evidence, and accepting ethical accountability around historical reality.
Four conclusions can be drawn from this.
First
Documentary is not the opposite of film, but a mode of factuality possible within film and in other media.
Second
Drama is not synonymous with fiction.
Theater can present fictional characters and organize archives, data, testimonies and real identities.
Third
Rimini Protokoll《100% City》 ： 。
Performance is not the opposite of documentary.
Documentary characters necessarily present themselves in some way, and reenactments and role-playing can also produce knowledge. The real epistemological crisis arises from the obfuscation of archives, speculations, substitutions and fictions without disclosure.
Fourth
Documentation is not about the "realistic content" of a work, but how the work is responsible for its claims to reality.
Therefore, for any borderline work, four questions should be asked
Does it exist primarily as a documented object or as a live event?
Does it invite the viewer to adopt a fictional attitude or a factual judgment?
How does it organize performances, staging, reenactments and editing?
Does it take sufficient responsibility for the evidence, actors and consequences of dissemination?
In a prototype sense, the differences between the three can be condensed into one sentence
Cinema fixes and organizes the visible, drama organizes events that are shared together, and documentary assumes an arguable responsibility for reality.
But the most important theoretical conclusion is not to build higher walls around them, but to recognize that: while film and theater describe how works appear, documentaries describe the commitment of works to talk about the world. The three are not three closed categories, but media coordinates that can be superimposed and transformed into each other, and at the same time must accept different evaluation standards.

Theory and Methods
Physical Training for Brutal Drama: Not Madness, Precision
Many people misunderstand cruel drama, thinking that it requires actors to be more crazy, more painful, and more out of control.
Many people misunderstand cruel drama, thinking that it requires actors to be more crazy, more painful, and more out of control.
In fact, just the opposite.
Physical training in cruel drama is not training out of control.
But train accurately.
The more intense the stage state, the less it can rely solely on emotions.
Emotions can be draining.
The body will be hurt.
Audiences will also quickly recognize cheap exaggeration.
A truly powerful body is not a body that breaks down easily.
But a body that can control energy on the blade.
01 Train perception first, not performance
A lot of performance training begins with asking: What do you want to express?
Cruel Drama prefers to ask first: What do you feel?
Is there any weight on the soles of the feet?
Does the spine have any direction?
Where the breath gets stuck.
The sound comes out of the chest or is forced out of the throat.
The finer the body's perception, the more accurate the movements on stage will be.
Without perception, the so-called explosion is just chaos.
02 Repetition is not machinery, but approximation
Cruel drama values repetition.
Repeat an action ten times and the meaning changes.
Repeat this twenty times and the body will begin to reveal the real problem.
Repeating it to a certain point, the actor is no longer "acting out", but fighting against the action.
What the audience sees is no longer the form.
It is the true state of the body after time has consumed it.
Repetition is not for the sake of looking good.
Repetition is for approximation.
03 The sound must come out of the body
Screaming is not about being loud.
Whispering is not a low voice either.
The sound must have a physical source.
It can come from pressure in the abdomen.
Can come from vibrations in the chest.
Can come from tension in the back.
It can also come from an unnamed blockage.
If the sound is just an effect created by the throat, it will quickly turn into a performance voice.
The really stinging sounds are the sounds that the body has to make.
04 Training boundaries are more important than training extremes
In a cruel drama, actors cannot be treated as consumables.
Really serious training requires knowing boundaries.
Where is the controllable danger.
Where is the body really going to hurt.
Where is the emotional material that can enter.
Where must stop.
Cruelty without boundaries, just rough.
Only cruelty with boundaries can become a method.
05 Accurately establish the feeling of pain
The feeling of pain on stage does not depend on the actor actually being in pain.
It is established by structure.
Depend on rhythm.
By distance.
By body direction.
By the time the sound appears.
By the way the audience is forced to watch.
Therefore, the training of cruel drama is not to train people to be more like wounds.
Rather, it trains actors to be able to create the conditions for wounds to appear.
Not crazy.
Be precise.

sources.text:
P4 Theater and You
2026-06-25
Theory and Methods
Why silence on stage can be scary
Silence on stage is sometimes more dangerous than screaming.
Silence on stage is sometimes more dangerous than screaming.
Silence is not the absence of sound.
In theater, silence is often an amplified pressure.
When an actor stops talking, the audience doesn't really go into blank space.
We will begin to hear breathing.
Hear the friction of clothing.
I heard a slight noise from the chair.
I even heard my own uneasy judgment.
Silence makes viewing impossible to hide.
01 Silence exposes space
Lines focus attention on meaning.
Silence exposes the space.
How empty the stage is.
How far away are the actors from the audience.
How cold the light is.
Why standing alone makes people uncomfortable.
These things are often obscured in language.
When silence comes, they all emerge.
02 Silence makes the body bigger
When an actor speaks, the audience tends to follow the content.
When an actor is silent, his body suddenly becomes huge.
Where to put your hands.
Where the eyes look.
Have your shoulders dropped?
Is your breathing messed up?
All details will be magnified.
Cruel theater exploits this amplification, making the body the text.
03 Silence is not a pause
There are a lot of stage pauses just to create a rhythm.
Silence in a cruel drama is not a simple pause.
It's a constant pressure.
It's in no rush to bring the audience back into the story.
It leaves the viewer in an unexplainable state.
The longer this state lasts, the harder it is for the audience to remain on the sidelines.
04 Why we are afraid of silence
Because silence does not organize meaning for us.
It doesn't tell us what to laugh about, what to cry about, what to understand.
It gives the judgment back to the audience.
At the same time, it also returns the responsibility to the audience.
Why are you upset?
Who do you expect to speak first?
Why do you want the scene to pass quickly?
Silence forces the viewer.
05 Good silence requires structure
Silence on stage does not mean casual silence.
It requires structure.
There must be energy accumulation ahead.
Actors must be in physical condition.
The space must have a direction of pressure.
The audience has to be brought to a certain breaking point.
Otherwise, silence is just a cold moment.
The real silence is the moment when the theater withdraws its knife.
The knife is not in sight.
But the pressure remains.

Anxiety and Mourning in Human Surrender
An introduction to Anxiety and Mourning in Human Surrender, connecting Human Surrender, The Last Rehearsal, P4 Theater, psychoanalysis within the P4...
HS4G VIEWING NOTE / Human Surrender
Anxiety and Mourning in "Human Surrender"
FILM AS A ROOM THAT WATCHES BACK
Text | Du Lan
This article enters "Human Surrender" from the perspective of anxiety, illusion, castration tension, separation of character and actor, second-person call and the double meaning of "surrender".
VIEWING POSITION
Anxiety is not the theme but the average texture of the film
P4 Theater's "Human Surrender" (this film is a collective creation), the most interesting thing about the whole film is that it shows a kind of anxiety, or the whole film is in an anxiety, not only the lens, but also the sound design
The entire film continues at an even pace, making a sound like fingernails scratching on a blackboard, or something approximating that of body mucus.
In the basic plot of "a director directs a play", the "movie within a movie" becomes the essence of anxiety, which is the support for its illusion. The role of "director" in the film is the spokesperson of illusion - although he directly speaks about anxiety, his words about anxiety have become our only fulcrum.
It is this pivot that keeps us from drowning in the anxious substance of the drama. In those shots of the stage, rehearsals, and performances, we get a little respite.
VIEWING POSITION
Director: Let us avoid the illusion of being overwhelmed by anxiety
Which is to say that, amid angst, we need a director who, despite the script, is here to deliver dissatisfaction.
But with this dissatisfaction, the drama of anxiety has an external perspective, an illusion that puts us (as the audience) slightly closer to the anxiety itself.
This raises the question of castration, which, according to some viewers, is a play of acceptance-we accept our flaws, our ideal selves grow, and so on. But doesn't this complete acceptance of castration eliminate the tension of castration?
VIEWING DOOR / Audience entrance
If castration is fully accepted, the tension of castration is removed; what remains is not tranquility but the complete immanence of anxiety.
Without this tension, we are precisely in the complete immanence of anxiety.
VIEWING POSITION
Separation of sheets, characters and actors
Therefore, at the end, the actor covered himself with a sheet and would not come out no matter what. The actress asked: "No one can see you! Is this what you want?" The actor said: "Yes."
SCREEN STILL / Screen Notes
Figure 01｜The white cloth is not a simple mask, but saves the "invisible" as a boundary that is still present.
At this time, the real production team of the film appears on camera. The actor jumped out of the sheets, that is to say, the actor left the character behind, left the stage and went to the production team, while the character remained in the play.
In my opinion, this is the meaning of the title of "Human Surrender" - the character chose to surrender and stayed in some eternal space, while the actor left. Therefore, it can be said that the actor completed the mourning for the character and allowed the character to live in a sea of anxiety, so that he could escape.
SCREEN STILL / Screen Notes
Figure 02｜After the backstage went dark, the production team and on-site installations made the "end" look more like a separation than a seal.
VIEWING POSITION
The Creator leaves creation
To put it another way, the entire movie refers to the tense of "past". The Creator leaves creation, and thus the pre-history of the world, and in the film they are presented directly as anxiety.
So can we imagine such a perspective? Is there a second-person reference toward the actor in the self-ness of anxiety? (According to the English title of this movie
Shoot Self with You
I'll deal with it like this here)
VIEWING POSITION
Second person: the object faces the person who has not yet arrived
It is an impossible perspective of a thing, looking towards a person who has not yet arrived (it is not until the end of the film, with the actor's departure, that the actor becomes that "outside perspective"). In other words, things are materializing people, and things turn pure anxiety (pure anxiety cannot be counted as anxiety) into humanized anxiety.
SCREEN STILL / Screen Notes
Figure 03｜The actors and the audience are in the same position: they are not the ones who own the work, but the people who are projected into the world by the work.
Here, the actors and the audience are in the same position. The actors are the embodiment of the audience in reality, and they are projected into a world by objects.
In the world, anxiety becomes anxiety. From the worldless perspective of things, although anxiety is not yet anxiety, in its terror, it pushes us into a world. Therefore, it can be said that the second person of "you" is a call towards the future.
VIEWING POSITION
Two kinds of surrender
The word "surrender" can finally be spoken of. If the first type of surrender is the sinking of the character (sinking into the immanence of the script), the second kind of surrender is that the character cannot sink.
Just like the actors in the film who continue to act after they have acted, we can also imagine the audience in real life who want to watch it again and again after watching it. Then the reference of objects to people here has always remained open. This is where the film retains a certain unfinishedness (in other words, the second-person "you," which never comes yet), which still awaits the viewer to complete it, or surrender to it.
SCREEN STILL / Screen Notes
Figure 04｜The ending archive saves the names, but also the unfinished separation: the list is not a possession, but a late registration.
About the author
Du Lan
Lacanian psychoanalysis expert and psychological counselor. Now lives in Nanjing.

sources.text:
P4 Theater and You
2026-06-21
Theory and method
Human Surrender
What Remains of Psychoanalysis When Explanation Cannot Reach Pain?
A P4 essay on psychoanalysis, pain, explanation, and what remains when language cannot reach the suffering it tries to interpret.
PSYCHOANALYTIC FIELD ATLAS
Someone Is Finally There: Ofra Eshel's "Analytic Unity" and the Ontological Turn of psychoanalysis
PRESENCING / WITHNESSING / TRANSFORMATION IN O
FIELD NOTE
When explanation fails to reach the pain, what is left psychoanalysis?
VISUAL FIELD / Non-Human Atlas
Figure 01｜Analytical union is not the fusion of two people, but a temporary field of experience: two non-personal transparent fields bending towards the same dark center, but without occupying each other.
psychoanalysisThe most fascinating promise was once "making the unconscious conscious." A symptom is not meaningless, it has a history, it has desires, it has defenses, it has repetitions. If a person doesn't know why he is in pain, analysis will find out the obscured road bit by bit.
But Ofra Eshel is
The Emergence of Analytic Oneness
The question raised in is deeper, and more uncomfortable: if some suffering is not "something that is not yet understood" at all, but is "a catastrophe that has never been truly experienced by a subject," how useful is explanation?
What this book really wants to rewrite is not just a treatment technology issue, but the underlying image of psychoanalysis.
It pushes psychoanalysis from the discipline of "explaining hidden meanings" to the discipline of "making the experience that failed to happen finally happen".
In other words, Eshel is not discussing how the analyst can understand the patient more intelligently, but rather whether the analyst can be real enough, bear enough, be there enough where the patient can least exist.
that's what she calls
presencing
、
withnessing
and
analytic oneness
. These words may seem abstract, but they collectively point to a very concrete clinical reality: some people do not lack explanations, but never have a psychological environment that can survive with them during critical pain.
FIELD NOTE
Conclusion of this article
CORE ARGUMENT / Conclusion of this article
First, Eshel's "analytic unity" is not a gentle version of empathy, but an existential turn: the core of therapy shifts from "knowing the meaning of pain" to "making pain something experienceable."
Second, she inherits Winnicott's idea of "early collapse," arguing that many deep traumas are not the forgotten past, but disasters that have not yet become experienced; it keeps returning because it has never really passed.
Third, she uses Bion's
O
understand treatment as
transformation in O
Not to turn the unknown into knowledge, but to allow the emotional reality that cannot be fully known to gain a bearable form between two people.
Fourth, this theory is the most powerful and dangerous. It can penetrate the clinical darkness where explanations fail, or it can slip into fusion fantasies, therapist narcissism, boundary loss, and the obscuration of hurtful realities. To read Eshel, therefore, is to read both her courage and her risk.
FIELD NOTE
1. The End of Explanation: When Pain Has Not Become "My Experience"
VISUAL FIELD / Non-Human Atlas
Figure 02 | "Unexperienced collapse" is not a forgotten content, but a dark well that has not yet entered the subject's experience. The images use black holes, sound waves and shattered panes of glass to represent a past that is not yet a thing of the past.
Traditionalpsychoanalysis is great at asking the question: What does this symptom mean?
Dreams, slips of the tongue, repeated relationships, physical symptoms, silence, resistance, are all put into webs of meaning. The job of analysis is to translate, piece by piece, the desires, anxieties, defenses, and early relationships underlying the symptoms. This tradition is extremely powerful because it rejects pain as something accidental, absurd, and purely physiological. It insists that human suffering has structure.
But Eshel is concerned with a different kind of pain.
This pain is not because the meaning is too deep to be seen, but because when it occurs, there is simply no subject formed enough to say: "This is what I am experiencing." It is not repressed into the unconscious, but has not yet entered experience.
Not forgotten, but never established as "my past".
Winnicott said that the collapse the patient fears has often already occurred. It sounds contradictory: why be afraid of it if it has happened? It is this contradiction that Eshel captures. When collapse occurs, the subject is not yet capable of experiencing it, so it does not become a thing of the past. It stops in front of the patient's life like a future event, repeatedly approaching, repeatedly threatening, and repeatedly asking to be experienced.
This is the scariest thing about deep trauma.
People are not remembering something, but are being chased by something they have never experienced before.
It does not appear as memory, but as emptiness, deadness, insomnia, physical disintegration, perverse actions, suicidal despair, the inability to love and to be loved.
So Eshel said, psychoanalysis can't just ask "What does it mean?" It must also ask: Is it possible for this to finally be experienced? If a person did not have the psychological environment to withstand it, can today's therapy provide a new environment in which that unexperienced disaster becomes experienced for the first time?
FIELD NOTE
2. From explanation to presence: presencing is not "accompanying you"
The first keyword for Eshel is
presencing
. This term can easily be misread as "the therapist needs to be present," "be there for the patient," or "be more empathetic." But she had something more to say than that.
presencing
Not posture, not technique, not gentle persona. It refers to the analyst putting his or her own psychological existence into the patient's experiential world and becoming a supporting function that can be used in the treatment field.
The analyst does not merely hear the patient's pain, nor does he merely understand the patient's symbolism, but remains alive in the vicinity of the patient's painful area.
"Being alive" here does not mean being emotionally intense, but rather not retreating. The patient brings dead silence in, the analyst pushes it out without explanation
The patient brings in the hole, and the analyst does not rush to fill it; the patient brings in the state of being unable to think, feel, or believe in any relationship, but the analyst can still be there and bear the intrusion of this state into himself.
This is Eshel's rewording of psychoanalysis neutrality.
The analyst is no longer an observer from the outside or someone who cuts into the patient's mind with the tools of interpretation. The analyst himself becomes part of the therapeutic reality. Whether certain experiences of the patient can occur depends on whether the analyst actually enters that field of experience and does not disappear there prematurely.
This is extremely demanding for analysts. Because the truly difficult clinical moments are often not when patients speak out complex materials, but when patients throw themselves into the treatment room in a meaningless, lifeless, hopeless, and languageless state. Ordinary explanations are often too quick here. It is like building stairs in a place where there is no ground yet. The structure is beautiful, but there is no landing point.
The radical thing about Eshel is
She believes that the deepest healing is not to explain, but to finally let a person no longer be alone in that groundless place.
FIELD NOTE
3. From witnessing to co-presence: the radical nature of withnessing
The second keyword is
withnessing
. it's obviously responding
witnessing
that is, "witness".
Of course testimony is important. A pain seen, acknowledged, proven not to be an illusion has healing power in itself. One of the most painful experiences for many trauma survivors is that no one believes, no one hears, and no one testifies.
But Eshel believes that in the deepest clinical areas, witnessing remains at a distance. A witness stands somewhere, sees your pain, and acknowledges that it happened.
withnessing
This drags the analyst into a more dangerous position: not to see the pain, but to be with the pain; not to bear witness to the pain, but to bear it with the patient where the pain cannot be borne by the patient alone.
This is not about suffering for the patient, nor is it about possessing the patient's pain. It is more like the analyst's psychology temporarily becoming an extra organ, so that the patient's unprocessable experiences can be accommodated, felt, and lived out bit by bit between two people.
This idea is similar to Bion's container theory, but Eshel takes it even further. Bion says that the baby throws indigestible beta elements to the mother, who converts them through reverie into thinkable alpha elements and returns them to the baby. Eshel then asked: What if certain experiences are too early, too dead, too intangible, not even to the point of being "transformable into thoughts"?
At this point, the analyst cannot just understand the patient's projections. The analyst must allow himself to be drawn into that unthinking darkness and maintain some kind of usable life there.
withnessing
This is the meaning of: the analyst is not an external processing machine, but a shared presence.
FIELD NOTE
4. "Analytical unity" is not a merger, but a temporary field of experience
Eshel's most controversial concept is
analytic oneness
also known as
two-in-oneness
。
The word sounds dangerous because it conjures up images of the abolition of boundaries, the fusion of subjects, the therapist and patient becoming one. Eshel is certainly aware of this danger. In fact, it is only by acknowledging this danger that her concept can be truly understood.
analytic oneness
Not a merging of reality, nor a therapist crossing the line into the patient's life. It describes certain extreme clinical moments when patient and analyst form a field of experience that cannot be easily separated. This field is not "your psychology plus my psychology", but a temporary common psychological unit. It allows experiences that would otherwise not take place within the patient to finally take place in the analytic relationship.
It can be understood this way: In an ordinary relationship between two people, there is an "I" and a "you", and the two people respond to each other.
In the deep area that Eshel discusses, the problem is not just "how do I treat you", but the patient's "I" itself has not yet been established in certain disasters. Therefore, treatment must first form a more original bearing field, so that "I am experiencing" may appear.
That's why she takes psychoanalysis to an existential level. Therapy is not about first having a complete subject and then the subject understanding the content.
Therapy sometimes involves creating a place for experience to take place where the subject is not yet complete.
But it must be made clear: if this "unity" loses its boundaries, it will turn into a disaster. It is not a mystical union, a therapist's fantasy of omnipotence, an "I know you better than you" possession, or any justification for ethical transgression. It can only hold within a strict analytical framework: time, expense, location, silence, explanation, moderation, responsibility, supervision and self-doubt cannot be eliminated.
real
analytic oneness
It is not to cancel two people, but to allow a third field of experience to briefly appear on the premise that the two people still bear their respective responsibilities.
FIELD NOTE
5. Bion's O: Not to know, but to be
VISUAL FIELD / Non-Human Atlas
Figure 03 | Bion's O is not an object of knowledge, but changes the emotional reality of the observer. The measurement lines in the image curve around the black center, suggesting that the analyst is not outside reality.
Eshel's ability to organize these dangerous concepts relies heavily on late Bion.
Bion distinction
K
and
O
。
K
It is knowledge, something we can know, understand, and express.
O
It is the ultimate emotional reality, a reality that cannot be completely captured or completely objectified. face
O
the analyst cannot just know it, but must somehow become it, bear it, be changed by it.
This is what Eshel calls
transformation in O
meaning.
Common therapeutic changes can often be understood as
transformation in K
The patient goes from not knowing to knowing, from confusion to understanding, from symptoms to meaning. But Eshel believes that the deepest change is not a change in knowledge but a change in the state of being. A breakdown that has never been experienced does not automatically translate into an "early maternal failure" just because it is explained away. It must somehow be relived in therapy.
In other words, the patient does not get a correct theory about the trauma, but in the analyst's presence he is finally able to be in the reality of the trauma without once again being completely isolated, completely disintegrated, and completely disappeared.
This is why Eshel puts Winnicott and Bion together. Winnicott gives her the problem of "unexperienced collapse": some disasters occur without the subject being present. Bion to her
O
direction
In the face of emotional realities that cannot be intellectualized, therapy cannot stop at the level of explanation. Together, the two form Eshel's core proposition: the deepest change of psychoanalysis is when the unexperienced becomes experienced in the shared presence.
FIELD NOTE
6. Black holes, sleep, perversions and dreams: a clinical map of the entire book
Eshel's book is not abstract metaphysics. She repeatedly proves her concepts through extreme clinical material.
The "black hole" patient is one of the most important images.
The so-called black hole does not mean that the patient has an explainable gap, but that the entire relationship space is sucked into the dead silence.
. What the patient brings is not a clear conflict, but a devouring sense of lifelessness. If the analyst only explains, he will often be sucked into a sense of futility; if he rushes to make the patient "react", he will repeat the abandonment of the early environment.
The key to treatment is whether the analyst can stay alive in the gravity of the black hole, so that the dead silence is no longer just swallowed up, but becomes something that can be felt together.
The chapter where the analyst falls asleep in therapy is also poignant. Often the analyst falling asleep is seen as a mistake, a countertransference problem, a professional failure. Eshel does not excuse this situation, but she suggests a deeper understanding: sometimes the patient's dissociations, interruptions in consciousness, and psychological voids pass into the analyst's body.
The analyst's sleep is not simply absent, but may be the physical manifestation of some unthoughtful experience in the therapeutic field.
The point is not that "sleeping is a good thing"
Rather, it depends on whether the analyst can acknowledge, think about and take on this matter again after waking up, so that the originally isolated dissociation can enter a common field.
Seriously perverse chapters push the theory to the ethical edge. Eshel objects to viewing perversions solely as sexual deviations or Oedipal problems. What she saw was
A survival organization: When the inner sense of death is unbearable, people may use extreme physical, ritual, and sexualized repetition to resist mental breakdown.
Perversion is not the secret to happiness but may be the last device to avoid annihilation.
But here also emerges the most important warning of the book. In her work on sex offender material, Eshel admitted that she had penetrated deeply into the darkness of her patients without fully feeling the pain of her victims at the same time. This admission is extremely critical. it explains
withnessing
Not naturally correct. Being together brings understanding, but it may also create blind spots; going deep into the darkness can touch the patient's place of survival, or it may obscure the location of the injured person.
As for the chapter on telepathic dreams, it should be read with even greater caution. Whether readers accept the term "telepathy" or not, what is really worth grasping is its clinical structure: some patients encountered a care environment of "physical presence but psychological absence" in their early years. The mother is there, but not really there. So when the analyst becomes emotionally distant in therapy, the patient's early catastrophes are activated, and the dream acts like a boundary-crossing search mechanism, desperately confirming: Are you still there? Did you leave again?
This is not to ask us to believe in the supernatural, but to remind us that for some patients, the psychological absence of others is not a trivial matter, but a repetition of the collapse of the world.
FIELD NOTE
7. Compassion is not kindness, but shared suffering.
Eshel gets closer and closer to one word in the second half of the book: compassion.
Chinese is often translated as compassion, pity, and sympathy. But in Eshel's case, it's not a gentle moral sentiment, but closer to suffer-with
Suffer with others.
Mercy can stay high. A man stood on the shore, saw people drowning in the water, and said "I understand you are in pain." It may be sincere, but it's still safe. What Eshel calls compassion is even more dangerous: the analyst must allow the patient's pain to hit him or her, allowing himself to enter into that pain field to some extent.
This is not martyrdom or a show of self-sacrifice. True shared suffering does not require the analyst to lose judgment. Rather, it requires the analyst to retain an analytic function even after being struck by pain. The analyst can neither explain coldly nor indulge in empathic self-movement. She must maintain an extremely difficult tension between being involved and being able to think.
The most touching thing about Eshel is that she does not write about treatment as a triumph of light. Many times, therapy begins with being able to enter into a sense of death with the patient. It's not about explaining away death, it's not about telling patients "you actually want to live", it's not about trying to prove that relationships can be repaired
Rather, let the dead, unheld, unheard part be endured for the first time in another mind.
This is why her books feel heavy. She wasn't writing about "How psychotherapy can make people better," but instead
When a person has not really existed for too long, how can another person in therapy help him regain the possibility of existence.
FIELD NOTE
8. The real danger of this book
The more powerful the theory, the more rigorously it needs to be read.
Eshel's theoretical dangers are at least four.
First, fusion fantasy.
analytic oneness
It can easily be misread as "the fewer boundaries, the more real". This would destroy psychoanalysis the most basic ethical conditions. True unity is not a transgression of boundaries but a temporary field of experience that occurs within boundaries.
Second, the therapist is narcissistic. The analyst may imagine himself or herself as the only one with access to the patient's darkness, or even turn the patient's suffering into proof of his own "depth." Once this happens
withnessing
It will degenerate from shared suffering to self-sanctification.
Third, the actual harm is obscured. Particularly in material about violence, sexual assault, crime, and abuse, the analyst's understanding of the perpetrator's inner breakdown cannot replace an acknowledgment of the victim's suffering and realistic responsibility. Understanding is not absolution, and being together is not a withdrawal of ethics.
Fourth, evidence discipline is loose. Eshel's language sometimes verges on mystical experience, easily read as "the more unverifiable, the deeper." This is precisely what requires vigilance. Clinical depth cannot cancel reviewability, and theoretical imagination cannot cross factual boundaries.
So the right way to read Eshel is not to worship her radicality, but to preserve her cracks. She is truly important not because she gives us a perfect answer, but because she forces psychoanalysis to a question that cannot be easily answered: When explanations, meanings, relationships, and knowledge are not enough, what is left in therapy?
FIELD NOTE
9. Inspiration for public writing: Don't explain a person's darkness too quickly
The book also has implications for writing outside the clinic, especially how we write about trauma, intimacy, art, and human breakdown.
There is an impulse to explain in much public writing: Why is this person like this? What was his childhood like? What is his desire? What is his pathological structure? Where is the source of his trauma? This explanation is sometimes necessary, but it is also easy to do it too quickly. It turns pain into cases, people into structures, and overwhelming experiences into meanings that readers can consume.
Eshel reminds us: some darkness cannot be quickly translated. When a writer faces pain, the first responsibility is not necessarily to name it, but to maintain a presence that does not steal the pain. It's not about completing the meaning for the person involved, it's not about packaging the wounds into opinions, but it is about retaining the state of "it has not been experienced yet" in the language.
This is important for art criticism, psychoanalysis writing, and intimacy writing. A truly profound article does not explain every pain in an orderly manner, but allows readers to feel that there is a place here that has not yet been fully grasped by experience. Writing is not about illuminating the darkness into knowledge, but about creating a place next to the darkness where you can stay, breathe, and continue to see.
This is also the fundamental difference between Eshel and ordinary psychological chicken soup. Chicken Soup says: You want to be understood, you want to be healed, and you want to come out. Eshel said: It's not that some people can't get out, but that they never really entered the disaster that they should have experienced. Therapy is not about rushing him out, but about finally having someone who can go in with him and not leave him there.
FIELD NOTE
Conclusion: Someone is finally there, but cannot possess it
VISUAL FIELD / Non-Human Atlas
Figure 04 | Withnessing is not about annexing each other, but about two fields sharing a small dark center at the border: someone is finally there, but cannot occupy it.
Ofra Eshel's "The Emergence of Analytical Unity" really proposes an extreme proposition of psychoanalysis
When a person's pain is so deep that there is no language, no memory, no subject, no hope, psychoanalysis what is left?
Her answer is not some more elaborate explanation, not some gentler reassurance, but a way of being: whether the analyst can be there.
There, it is not a bystander; it is not a substitute; it is not a redemption; it is not a possession; it is not a dragging of the patient into the therapist's own meaning system. It means that where the patient is least able to be himself, another person still exists in a conscious, limited, and responsible way, making it possible for the unexperienced breakdown to finally be experienced together.
this is
presencing
The clinical weight is
withnessing
the ethical weight of
analytic oneness
The most moving and dangerous place.
So perhaps the best title for this book isn't "Analytical Unity" but: Someone Is Finally There.
But one last and equally important thing must be added: just because someone is there, it doesn't mean they can occupy it.
psychoanalysisThe deepest power is not to merge two people into one, nor to make the analyst the hero of the patient's darkness. Its deepest power is to form a common field within strict boundaries that can withstand disasters; in that field, things that have never happened as experience finally begin to happen.
It may be at this moment that a person takes possession of his past for the first time. Not because he finally knew the past, but because someone finally experienced the past with him.
