P4 Submission: The Cry of the People Without a People
An introduction to P4 Submission: The Cry of the People Without a People, connecting Actor-Generated Topology, AGT, The Grammar of Events, P4 Theater...
Look at the birds in the sky. They neither sow, nor reap, nor gather into barns. Even if people shoot them, you are worth more than hundreds of sparrows.
Zhang Youmin is a person who likes to visit ruins, not just because he is an excavator operator, nor just because he is not popular among people. When I was a child, six members of my family lived together. The weather in Zhang Laoer's village is always very cold, and his father's three sets of clothes are worn in turn by the three children in the family. He is not as strong and able to take care of the housework as the eldest brother, nor is he smarter and attracts more attention than the third child. When it was his turn, he would always drag his baggy clothes to the entrance of the village to play with friends, but his pants were too long and would pull down as soon as he ran. He was always caught when playing ghost hunting, and when it was time for him to catch people, the children would always hide in the village. Behind walls, on roofs, in ditches, and running away as soon as they are discovered. When I was in a hurry, I even kicked off my pants and didn't dare to run far. When he was arresting someone, he simply started wandering around the village, catching loaches and poking at ant nests...
He liked the cats in the village. The orange cats were often fed by the rich people who lived in the big courtyards and kept them fat. However, every time they fought, they could not beat the lean black cat with one blind eye. In the end, as soon as the black cat leaned over, the orange cat would jump away in a hurry. Every time when he got tired of playing, he would slowly look for the black cat in the village and watch it pounce on the wild pigeons on the trees. The wild pigeon cooed, but it stopped when its neck was bitten, and only warm blood flowed out.
At first it was difficult to find the black cat, and he always disappeared in a blink of an eye, but he kept looking, and gradually we were able to get along with him. The black cat moved at the top of the earth wall, lowering its body alertly as if hearing something, then relaxed, and suddenly jumped down in front of him. Lying on the wall, I glanced at him and he sat down.
He wanted to raise a cat, but he had no place, so he would occasionally meet the black cat in the wild. He had nothing to feed it, and the black cat never asked for petting. They usually kept some distance between each other and stayed for a while, while the black cat took care of itself.
The village has always regarded the black cat as an unlucky thing, because it is black, but it dares to walk alone and secretly kill Aunt Zhao's chickens. It worked accurately and quickly. When the second aunt lit up the lamp and rushed out with a broom, a pair of green eyes flashed, and its drooped wings disappeared at the other end of the courtyard wall.
The death of that chicken made Henwa very sad, because in his chaotic and unclear memories as a child, it seemed that the first memory was of a chick with yellow fluff that kept croaking, shaking its head and walking towards him. He watched the chick grow and remembered its body pulling out its hard, mature feathers. When his father went out to work and his mother worked in the fields, the chicken stayed with him and laid eggs into his little hands, although the eggs always disappeared. He once bullied this little chicken, when it had just learned to walk. He called it to come over but it didn't answer. So when he got angry, the young baby picked it up and threw it viciously into the trash can. It has a very good character. If you put your finger on it, it will never peck you. Instead, it will stick out its head for you to touch. Even after it grows very old, it still won't resist the baby holding it tightly in its arms sometimes.
The second aunt was very angry because some materials were missing from the banquet held by her son and daughter-in-law three days later. Marrying the eldest son is a laborious and expensive matter, but it is also necessary. The chicken was too old and could no longer lay eggs. She was looking forward to letting Bangwa kill it tomorrow, and then teach him how to bleed the chicken, pluck the feathers and remove the internal organs, and stew it for a while longer. After it was stewed, no one would think it was old. This careful and reasonable plan came to nothing because of the unworthy black cat.
The two of them shared the same hatred, and after the banquet, they planned to kill the black cat in the village. This decision was supported by other chicken-raising villagers. After their serious and lively discussions, a detailed battle plan was set up: let the hook lead it out, and everyone would work together to catch it. Hook is Youmin's nickname. He was not given by his family. He was called Hook because his pants would fall down and leak out of his butt when he ran.
In the village, some people are allowed to go, but some people don't go; at home, some people are allowed to go, because this is a rare thing to earn face, but some people don't go. So he grabbed his clothes and hid in the corner of the village like a black cat. This time, Henwa and the villagers never found him, but they caught the black cat not far from Henwa. It was still struggling before it died. People had never seen such a wild and untamed cat. It arched its back and bared its teeth, scratching anyone who dared to approach it. It avoided many heavy blows with sticks and captures in nets, and kept a distance from people. Some people jumped out of the hiding place, knocked away a villager, and ran towards the black cat. At this time, the black cat turned around and ran away. This time it ran without any care, and was caught by Erga, the dog trainer.
Some people watched it die among the dogs from a distance, the black color was drowned by the khaki howling, growling and biting. These dogs are trained never to bite, but have no mercy on any other creature that feels even remotely threatened. Reappeared, there was only bright red blood and white bones.
After the dogs were all locked up, he asked for some gnawed bones from the black cat that he could still find, and tried to make it look like a cat, but he couldn't make it, so he buried it in the corner where they usually stayed. At this time, Henwa saw it, came over and spat, "It deserves it, it ate our chicken. You still buried it, so ignorant, no wonder no one likes to play with you." He didn't answer, and he didn't feel sad, so he just sat there in a daze. The wild pigeons on the tree cooed, seemingly a little more wildly. They seemed to know that they were safer.
When he was a little older, he went to the city to work, moving bricks and building walls and cement, whatever he had to do. At that time he liked the city, where the people were beautiful, things were convenient, and the house was warmer. He used part of the money he earned from his first job to send to his family, and the rest bought himself some well-fitting clothes. After a few more times, he bought some bricks and mud and wanted to build a house for himself in the city, with a small second floor, like the rich people in the village, but it was demolished just two days after it was built.
He was angry: "Why demolish my house?"
A group of men in uniform came over and told him: The land under his feet did not belong to him, and the state stipulated that he could not build a house here.
"It's not mine..." he said, "Whose is it then?"
"It belongs to the country."
"Whose country does it belong to?" He wanted to ask who cares about this matter.
"The country? The country is you and me. When we come together, we are called the country. Anyway, there are regulations that do not allow random construction. Your building that has not been approved by the planning bureau is called private random construction. Do you understand?"
"Then which bureau should I approach for approval?"
"Don't worry, people will definitely not approve of this. The land in the city is very valuable, and the country uses it. If you want a place to live, rent it. Migrant workers like us can only rent a house to find a place to live. Land is very valuable in the city, and this newly built building is worth more than a hundred thousand square meters."
"But I built this building?"
"Did you build it? Did you pay for it?"
"No."
"You still say you built it without you. I think you are just moving the bricks here. They bought the bricks and the land, and you just put them on for them, and you still say you built it. It's true that you built it. The ownership belongs to them, and they just pay you a little money."
After that day, he fell in love with demolishing walls, and he always rushed to do demolition work. He doesn't understand the country, policies, and economic benefits, and he doesn't care about them at all. He just hates building things for people who don't know or care about him. His own sweat goes into the cement to form the appearance of a city, but they live comfortably. He felt that in the eyes of the foreman and the people walking on the street, he was like a brick, but the purpose of this brick was to lay cement on the upper floor. These people move in and decorate the outside and inside so that the ugly cement cannot be seen. No one cares about cement except the companies that can make money from them. And dismantling it yourself is like a kind of revenge, happy and powerful. He changed his name to Zhang Youming. He likes to wear black pants and black tops. He is as fashionable as many migrant workers, but he looks good in this outfit.
Zhang Youming often crowded with his co-workers in a temporary board house with six people. He likes to come out after dinner or before going to bed, use a flashlight to look at the ruins he demolished during the day, and then pick up whatever he wants. He picked up a long piece of wood and carried it back to the house with great difficulty, leaving it there after the project was completed. He also picked up a length of heating pipe with a T-shaped end, which he could swing easily.
The day he picked up the heating pipe, he rewarded himself with a piece of ham sausage, and while he was eating it, a black cat saw him. The black cat was not alert. It waited for a moment, then pounced on him and scratched his trouser legs, staring at the meat in his hand. There was no one around him. He looked at the cat expressionlessly, then suddenly smiled and threw the ham sausage to the ground.
The cat hurriedly pounced on it, biting into the packaging with its teeth and scraping the meat with its tongue. He looked at it, then suddenly took a few steps back and picked up the heating pipe.
Hit it and the cat will stop moving, splattering some blood. Seeing that no one was around, he waved a few more times and almost vomited. Then he leaned over, held his breath, stroked the cat's fur, and then tore open the cat's skin, took out the cat's heart, touched it, squeezed it hard, touched all the internal organs and intestines, and then threw it into the rubble. He lit a cigarette, got up and rinsed it, then threw the cigarette away and into the rubble.
On this day, he picked up something unusual. The thing glowed with a shiny metallic luster in the sun. It seemed to be very valuable. It was segment by segment, like a watch without a dial. It felt smooth and even had a vague strange feeling. He put the watch away and patted it. He felt relieved when he remembered that in a few days, his father would come to ask for tuition from the third child.
A few hours later, he woke up in the middle of the night and felt a vague discomfort, combined with the stimulation of blood, and he lay down dizzy. An increasingly strong sense of vomiting swept over him. He was dizzy, had unbearable abdominal pain, his arms and legs were weak, his gums were bleeding, and purple blisters appeared on his face and back. When his head was twisted slightly, a lot of strands of hair fell off his head, and he was sent to the hospital.
One day later, his father took the third child to the hospital, bought several kilograms of fruit in advance, and paid for the hospitalization fee with tuition. He felt very weak, with black stools, high fever, and even his nails and teeth were a little loose. Is this an illusion?
A few days later, he was transferred to another hospital many times, but no one could determine the cause of his illness. Even his father and brother lost a large bunch of hair while taking care of him in the hospital, and they felt even more nauseated and vomiting due to the fever. And what about him? Even the skin began to fall off in large areas. In the painful dizziness, he could vaguely see that the room he was in was falling off and shaking, and even the doctor began to feel uncomfortable. He was isolated.
Ten days later, he developed hair loss, sore throat, difficulty breathing, blood spots all over his body, and pus. Not a piece of his skin was intact, and the doctor's explanation was meaningless. In fact, the doctor was also coughing, vaguely, as if the whole hospital was coughing. He heard a gurgling voice, which was stuck together with the doctor's radioactive voice, as if the explanation was clear, but there was no way. He is gradually disintegrating, his organs are peeling off and melting, and the whole world is collapsing. The whole world, the world that goes its own way, the world that sucks blood and sweat, the world that is boring, lonely, hollow and cruel, the world that has been asking for everything collapsed at the moment he died, burying him, just like this world has always done.

Theory and Methods
From Sign to Event: Erika Fischer-Lichte's Thought and Influence
An introduction to Erika Fischer-Lichte's move from theatre semiotics to performance as event, embodiment, co-presence, and cultural interweaving.
From Symbol to Event: A Systematic Analysis of Erika Fischer-Lichte's Academic Thought and Influence
Introduction: Founder of Contemporary Performance Studies
Erika Fischer-Lichte is one of the most prolific and influential performance scholars of the late 20th and early 21st centuries. Her academic achievements have fundamentally reshaped German "Theaterwissenschaft" (Theaterwissenschaft) and even the global theater and performance studies disciplines. Her central contribution was to promote a critical paradigm shift that shifted the focus of scholarly analysis from dramatic texts to live performances as vital, embodied, and transformative events. This report aims to systematically analyze Fischer-Lichte's academic career, core theoretical contributions, evolution of his thoughts, and his far-reaching influence in the academic world.
This report believes that the trajectory of Fischer-Lichte's academic thought-from the rigorous semiotic analysis of dramatic codes, to the phenomenological aesthetic construction of performative events, to the political theoretical discussion of cultural intersections-not only reflects, but also actively drives a broader paradigm revolution within the entire humanities discipline. This revolution profoundly challenged the traditional boundaries between art and life, artist and audience, aesthetics and politics. In order to clearly present this line of thought, this report will first provide an overview of his main works and core theoretical contributions through the table below, and then systematically explore his academic foundation, evolving theoretical framework, important historical case studies, and their global resonance.
Table 1: Erika Fischer-Lichte's main works and core theoretical contributions
Year of publication (German/English)
Main works
Core theoretical contributions
1983 / 1992
The Semiotics of Theater
A systematic framework is established to analyze drama as a cultural system composed of symbols and codes.
2004 / 2008
The Transformative Power of Performance: A New Aesthetics
A "performative aesthetics" is proposed, the concept of "autopoietic feedback loops" is introduced, and the focus is placed on performance itself as a transformative event.
2005
"Theatre, Sacrifice, Ritual"
It explores how the integration of drama and ritual serves the construction of community in political performances and large-scale collective scenes.
2014
The Politics of Interweaving Performance Cultures
The "interweaving" model is proposed to transcend postcolonial criticism of "cross-culture" and emphasize the hybridity and political exchange of cultures.
2017
Tragedy's Endurance
Demonstrates a novel approach to theater historiography that closely links the performance history of ancient Greek tragedy with the evolution of German cultural identity.
Section 1 Academic Foundation and German "Drama" Tradition
Erica Fischer-Licht's academic influence is rooted in her profound educational background and central position in the German academic system. Her academic career is not only a series of personal achievements, but also a history that actively shapes the future of the discipline.
Detailed academic resume
Fischer-Licht's academic starting point is extremely broad. She studied drama, Slavic languages and literature, German linguistics, philosophy and psychology at the Freie Universität Berlin and the University of Hamburg. This interdisciplinary training laid a solid foundation for the breadth and depth of his future theory. Her teaching career began in 1973 and she served as professor of modern German literature, comparative literature and drama at the Universities of Frankfurt, Bayreuth and Mainz. In 1996, she joined the Department of Drama at the Freie Universität Berlin, which became the core base for the maturation and dissemination of her academic ideas. She retired in 2011 and was awarded the title of Emeritus Professor in 2022, marking a phased conclusion of her decades-long direct teaching influence.
In addition to teaching and research, Fischer-Lichte also plays a vital role in leadership positions in academic institutions. She served as President of the International Federation for Theater Research (IFTR) from 1995 to 1999, and has long chaired a number of top German and international research centers. These include the Collaborative Research Center "Performance Culture" (SFB 447) and the Graduate School "Inter-Arts" funded by the German Science Foundation (DFG), as well as the Kate Hamburg International Research Center "Interweaving of Performance Culture" funded by the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF). These leadership roles make her not only a creator of ideas but also an academic agenda-setter.
Her outstanding contributions have earned her a worldwide reputation. She was awarded an honorary doctorate from the University of Copenhagen and was elected as a member of the European Academy of Sciences, the Göttingen Academy of Sciences, the Berlin-Brandenburg Academy of Sciences, the Leopoldina Academy of Sciences of the German National Academy of Sciences, and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. In addition, she also won important awards such as the Berlin Science Prize, the German Theater Association's "Faust" Drama Award, and the Erwin Piscator Award for Lifetime Achievement.
The context of German "drama"
To understand Fischer-Lichte's academic positioning, we must place him within the unique tradition of German "theaterwissenschaft" (Theaterwissenschaft). Unlike the drama department under the British and American systems, which often includes practical artistic training, German drama studies is a purely academic research field, and its core tasks are theoretical construction and historical research, rather than cultivating artists. This context determines the theoretical orientation of Fischer-Licht's work, and her research is always committed to establishing a rigorous analytical framework and profound philosophical explanations for drama and performance phenomena.
builder of disciplines
What is remarkable about Fischer-Lichte is not only that she proposed far-reaching theories, but also that she demonstrated an outstanding ability to combine theoretical innovation with academic and political strategies. Looking at her resume, we can see that she is not only participating in academic discussions, but also actively constructing and leading platforms for these discussions. She has successfully transformed her theoretical conception into a dominant research paradigm by founding and chairing large-scale, long-term and well-funded interdisciplinary research centers such as "Performance Culture" and "The Intersection of Performance Culture".
This process has far-reaching structural consequences. Through these research centers, she was able to define core research questions, fund doctoral and postdoctoral projects, and train a whole generation of young scholars trained in her theory and methodology. This makes her thoughts no longer just personal academic opinions, but also institutionalized and systematized inheritance and development. Therefore, it can be said that Fischer-Licht not only participated in the "performative turn", but also institutionalized this turn through his strong academic organizational capabilities, ensuring his lasting influence in German and even international academic circles. Her career clearly demonstrates that the influence of a top scholar comes not only from the depth of his ideas but also from his ability to build an academic community and shape the future of his discipline.
Section 2 Semiotic Framework: Deconstructing Drama Codes
In the 1980s, Fischer-Lichte established an important position in the academic world with his foundational book "Semiotik des Theaters" (German edition 1983, English edition 1992). This classic text, hailed as "the most thorough, systematic, and convincing dramatic semiotics to date," provides an unprecedented set of rigorous tools for dramatic analysis.
core methodology
In the book, Fischer-Licht considers theater as a complex cultural system whose meaning arises from the synergy of multiple symbolic systems. Her analytical method is systematic and aims to deconstruct the various subsystems that constitute the "dramatic code". She examined in detail
• Actor's semiotic system: includes the actor's appearance (such as clothing, makeup) and his or her physical behavior, such as gestures, kinesics and proxemics.
• Symbol system of space: Covers visual elements such as stage design, scenery, props, etc.
• Non-verbal sound symbol system: includes auditory elements such as music and sound effects.
central argument
The core argument of "Theatrical Semiotics" is that the meaning of a theatrical performance is not singular or fixed, but is generated in the audience's perception through these multi-layered, simultaneously operating semiotic systems. Therefore, the goal of semiotic analysis is not to discover a unique and correct "meaning", but to reveal the polyphony and polyvalence of the meaning generation process itself. This methodology rejects the tradition of reducing drama to illustrations of literary texts, emphasizing the meaning-generating function of all non-verbal elements in performance.
The necessary foundation for a future revolution
Fischer-Lichte's academic career is often defined by his later theory of "performativity," which was in part a critique of text- and semiotic-centered modes of analysis. This seems to contradict her early semiotic research. However, an in-depth examination of his ideological trajectory reveals that this seeming contradiction is actually a profound dialectical development. As she herself later elaborated, "the semiotic and performative dimensions of a performance are different, although they are inseparable."
This assertion reveals the internal logic between her early and later work. First of all, "Drama Semiotics" provides the field of performance analysis with the most complete set of analytical tools for studying structured systems. It taught academics how to look at performances with analytical precision, going beyond mere literary criticism or impressionistic commentary. It can be said that she brought semiotic rigor to the study of drama as a comprehensive art form.
However, the limitation of the semiotic method is that its ultimate focus is still on "meaning" and "interpretation", that is, "what does the performance process mean?" It tends to treat the performance event as a "text" that can be "interpreted". After her most thorough exploration of the possibilities of the semiotic model, Fischer-Licht became acutely aware that the model could not fully capture the most central quality of performance: its liveness as a vital, embodied event and its direct impact on its participants, that is, the question "What does the performance do?"
Therefore, her "performative turn" is not a simple negation of her earlier work, but a transcendence based on it. She must first master and exhaust the potential of the semiotic model before she can deeply understand its limitations and convincingly propose a new paradigm focused on experience, presence, and transformation. The reason why she is qualified to announce the birth of a "new aesthetics" is precisely because she has thoroughly mastered the old aesthetic analysis tools. In this sense, her semiotic stage is an indispensable intellectual prerequisite for her later theoretical revolution.
Section 3 Performative turn: from text to event
Entering the 1990s, the humanities have experienced a profound "performative turn", the core of which is a shift from understanding culture as a "text" to be read to viewing culture as an "event" to be experienced. Erica Fischer-Licht was a key architect and promoter of this intellectual wave in the field of theater and performance studies.
From semiotics to performativity
Fischer-Licht explicitly shifts his theoretical focus from analyzing what a performance "means" (a question of semiotics) to what it "does" (a question of performativity). This shift implies a fundamental revaluation of what is studied. The core of the research is no longer a dramatic text that can be analyzed, or even a mise-en-scène that can be reproduced (
mise-en-scène), but the unique, fleeting, unrepeatable performance event itself.
Core Principles of Performativity Studies
Fischer-Licht established several core principles for the study of performativity that formed the cornerstone of her later theory
1. Bodily Co-presence: Performance is generated through the physical co-presence, encounter and interaction of actors and audiences. This is the ontological premise of performance as an event.
2. Transience and a strong sense of the present: The performance is short-lived, but everything that happens during the process has a strong sense of "here and now" (hic et nunc) and is deeply experienced by the participants.
3. The generative nature of meaning: Performance does not convey preset meaning, but generates meaning in the process of its occurrence. Meaning is the product of events, not its antecedents.
4. Eventality and liminal experience: The essential characteristic of performance is its "eventness". It provides participants with a special liminal experience, a state of "betwixt and between".
a methodological revolution
The transformation from "culture as text" to "culture as performance" is not just a shift in research focus, it actually triggered a profound revolution in research methodology. Analyzing a "text" (whether a literary work or a performance considered a text) allows the scholar to maintain an objective, detached stance. The research object is stable and can be reviewed and analyzed repeatedly.
However, when the object of analysis is transformed into an "event," this stability no longer exists. Research objects are fluid, ephemeral, and co-created by the researcher's (as viewer) own presence. This means that traditional analytical tools of literary criticism and art history are no longer sufficient. Scholars can no longer just play the role of a "reader" interpreting symbols.
This shift inevitably leads to a methodological crisis, which forces academic circles to find new ways of writing and analysis to capture and describe embodiment, ephemerality, and the subjective experience of events. Fischer-Lichte's books, especially The Transformative Power of Performance, not only proposed a new theory but also practiced a new research method. She confronts the difficulties and challenges inherent in translating lived, bodily experience into rigorous academic language and attempts to establish a new academic discourse for this purpose. This methodological revolution requires the researcher to transform from an external observer to a witness who reflects on his own participation in the event.
Section 4 A New Aesthetics: "The Transformative Power of Performance"
Erica Fischer-Licht's most influential book is undoubtedly Ästhetik des Performativen (2004), whose English translation is The Transformative Power of Performance: A New Aesthetics (2008). This book announces the birth of a "new aesthetics" that aims to transcend traditional aesthetic theories based on static subject-object relationships.
4.1 Autopoietic feedback loop: Reshaping the relationship between performance and observation
The "autopoietic feedback loop" is the core engine of Fischer-Lichte's new aesthetic theory. She borrows the concept of "autopoiesis" from cognitive biology and defines it as a self-referential, continuously changing and fundamentally unstable process generated by the interaction between actors and audiences.
The cycle works like this: actors act, the audience perceives and reacts (whether it's loud cheers, whispers, or just small changes in body posture), and these reactions are then perceived by the actors and other audience members, which in turn affects their subsequent actions and reactions. This cycle repeats itself, forming a continuous and unpredictable dynamic loop.
The introduction of this concept completely breaks the traditional binary opposition of "active performer/passive viewer". In a feedback loop, all participants are co-creators of events and share responsibility for their unfolding. Therefore, the process of performance is emergent and cannot be completely planned or predicted. Fischer-Lichte frequently cites Marina Abramović's performance work Lips of Thomas (
Lips of Thomas) as an example. In this work, when the artist self-harmed, the audience finally couldn't bear it and intervened and stopped the performance. At this moment, the audience transcends the boundaries of viewing and transforms into actors, profoundly embodying the subversive power of feedback loops.
4.2 Performance as event: materiality, liminality and transformation
Fischer-Licht's new aesthetics understands performance as a multidimensional event, the key elements of which include
• Physical co-presence: The basic condition for a performance to take place is that the performer and the audience share the same physical space at a specific time. It is this shared presence of bodies that forms the material basis on which the feedback loop operates.
• The performative generation of materiality: The materiality of performance - including its spatiality, body and acoustics - is not a pre-existing background, but is dynamically "generated" during the event. For example, space is not a static container, but is constantly being reshaped through the movement of actors and audiences, the intersection of gazes, and the spread of sound. Space "happens" rather than "exists".
• Liminality and transformation: By blurring the boundaries between art and life, aesthetics and ethics (as in the case of Abramovich), performance pushes participants into a "liminal state" - a critical state of "neither this nor that". It is within this unstable liminal state that lies the potential for change. This change may occur at the level of perception, attitude, or even self-perception. This is the true meaning of the book's title, "The Power of Change."
4.3 The emergence of meaning
Within this new aesthetic framework, meaning is no longer viewed as stable information encoded by the artist and decoded by the audience. The focus of analysis shifts from "understanding" and "interpretation" to "experience" and "perception". Meaning "emerges" in an unstable, multi-layered way from the dynamic interaction of feedback loops and the overall sensory experience of the event. The personal experience of each participant is crucial, and different participants will generate completely different meanings from the same performance.
The political subtext of "new aesthetics"
Although Fischer-Lichte's theory is constructed as an aesthetic, its core concepts - such as shared responsibility, co-creation, the blurring of role boundaries, and the negotiation of relationships in shared spaces - have inherently social and political dimensions. An in-depth analysis reveals that her "new aesthetics" is also a model of micro-political community.
The "autopoietic feedback loop" itself depicts a self-regulating community model in which each member's actions have an impact on the whole. Breaking the active/passive binary is a fundamentally democratic gesture that unilaterally devolves agency from the artist to all participants. Fischer-Licht clearly points out that when power struggles arise around "situation definition" this social process becomes a political process. She also emphasized that "the act of perceiving others is always a political act."
The performance event itself thus becomes a laboratory of social and political relations. It allows participants to experience a subjective state that is neither completely autonomous nor completely determined by others, which is precisely the profound definition of political subjectivity. This reveals that her aesthetic theory and political theory are inseparable. "Change" is not just personal or spiritual, but a new understanding of social agency and political possibility.
Section 5 Beyond Cross-Cultural: Performance Culture Interweaving Theory
With the deepening of globalization, cultural exchange has become a core issue in drama and performance research. In this context, Fischer-Lichte proposed the theory of "interweaving performance cultures", aiming to transcend the limitations of the traditional concept of "intercultural theatre".
Critique of "Cross-Cultural Drama"
Fischer-Licht offers a profound critique of the term "intercultural theatre". She believes that there is a postcolonial assumption underlying this concept, that is, culture is a static, closed entity with a certain "authenticity" that can engage in "encounter" or "dialogue". Not only does this model fail to get rid of the binary opposition of "the West and the Other", it also solidifies the idea of cultural ownership, as if culture is property that can be clearly divided and owned.
The concept of "interweaving"
To replace this problematic model, she proposes the concept of "interweaving". This concept asserts that culture is never isolated, but is always in a continuous process of change, exchange, and hybridization. In many cases, we are no longer able to clearly distinguish between "our" culture and what is "foreign" culture. The birth of modern drama itself is the product of this cultural interweaving process.
Intertwined aesthetics and politics
The theory of "interweaving" is not only a descriptive concept, but also has profound aesthetic and political implications
• Political process: The process of cultural interweaving is inherently political. It involves challenging cultural hegemony, undermining claims to "authenticity," and giving rise to new cultural diversity rather than homogeneity.
• Aesthetics is politics: In this framework, aesthetics and politics are no longer opposite poles. Fischer-Licht clearly stated that "aesthetics is politics". The performance event becomes a concrete site in which complex processes of cultural negotiation are materialized and experienced by the audience.
"Intertwining" as an "autopoietic feedback loop" at the macro level
There is a strong and unified logical thread in Fischer-Lichte's later thought, that is, the theory of "interweaving" can be understood as the application of "autopoietic feedback loops" at the macro-historical level. The two concepts share a striking structural similarity.
An "autopoietic feedback loop" describes how, at a micro level, two groups (actors and audience) interact in a shared space to create new, unpredictable events. "Interweaving" describes at the macro level, when two or more performance cultures come into contact, new hybrid forms are created through the process of appropriation, exchange and transformation.
Just as the feedback loop destabilizes the fixed roles of actor and audience, so does the theory of "interweaving" destabilize the stable categories of "own culture" and "foreign culture." Just as feedback loops are sites of political negotiation over situational definition, so too are "intersections" a site of political struggles over cultural identity, ownership, and representation.
Therefore, the theory of "interweaving" can be seen as extending the operating logic of "autopoietic feedback loops" from a single performance site to the grand scale of global cultural history. It applies the principles of dynamic, emergent, and politically charged interaction to the relationship between different performance traditions. This internal logical unity clearly demonstrates the coherence and systematicness of Fischer-Lichte's later thoughts.
Section 6 Application of Theory: Case Studies in Performance History
Fischer-Lichte's theoretical framework is not a castle in the air, and she demonstrates the powerful analytical utility of these concepts in practice through concrete historical research. Her historical works are the application and testing of her theoretical ideas.
6.1 Greek tragedy and German identity ("The Duration of Tragedy")
In his important book "Tragedy's Endurance: Greek Tragedy Performance and Cultural Identity in Germany since 1800" (Tragedy's Endurance), Fischer-Licht proposed a novel research approach to theater history. She believes that the history of Greek tragedy performances on the German stage since 1800 is actually the history of the evolving cultural identity of the German educated middle class.
Her research method is to reveal how performances of these classical texts were used to confirm, shake up and reshape Germany's cultural identity in specific political and social contexts by analyzing a series of key performances from Goethe's rehearsals in 1802, to their politicized use during the Third Reich, to social movements in the 1960s and new interpretations after the fall of the Berlin Wall. This work perfectly embodies her focus on performance, event, and reception. The meaning of tragedy is not contained in ancient texts, but lies in what each historical performance "did" in the local cultural context at that time, and how it performed its social function.
6.2 Ritual, Sacrifice and Political Drama ("Drama, Sacrifice, Ritual")
In Theater, Sacrifice, Ritual: Exploring the Forms of Political Drama, Fischer-Licht explores the fusion of drama and ritual in political performances in the 20th century, with cases ranging from Max Reinhardt's large-scale spectacles to the Nazis' Thingspiele and even the modern Olympics.
She pointed out that these large-scale collective performances often use sacrificial themes and ritual structures to deal with community-building issues arising from the loss of unity and the disintegration of communities in modern society. They are powerful tools for propaganda and mass manipulation. This research is directly related to her theory of "new aesthetics" because it examines performances that deliberately erase the boundaries between audience and participants in order to forge a strong collective identity. These cases vividly demonstrate how the "transformative power of performance" can be used for explicit political purposes, revealing the complex and profound connection between aesthetics and power.
Section 7 Acceptance, Criticism and Lasting Influence
As a groundbreaking scholar, Erika Fischer-Lichte's theories have not only received widespread praise, but also triggered in-depth discussions and criticisms in the academic community. A balanced assessment needs to examine both its far-reaching implications and the challenges it faces.
global influence
Fischer-Lichte's academic ideas have had a shaping impact on theater and performance studies around the world. She is the author of New Theater Quarterly (
He is an important contributor to top academic journals such as New Theater Quarterly, Theater Research International and Journal of Dramatic Theory and Criticism.
Her influence is particularly significant in China. Her books have been translated and become required readings at China's top drama schools, and her theoretical concepts, such as the "interweaving of performance cultures," are actively used by Chinese scholars to analyze and theorize local theater phenomena. This fully proves the cross-cultural applicability and strong vitality of his theory. One Chinese scholar even said that Fischer-Lichte's work "inspired a chain-reaction exploration of the meaning of drama" and regarded her as his academic mentor.
academic criticism
Fischer-Lichte's theory has also faced some important academic criticisms, which mainly focus on the following aspects
• Terminological ambiguity and lack of evidence: Some critics have argued that some of the terms she uses, such as "energy," appear analytically ambiguous. At the same time, her assertions about audience experience, such as that audiences are brought into a "fundamentally liminal state," are sometimes considered to be more assertions than based on sound empirical evidence.
• The return of semiotics: An important criticism points out that after she establishes the performance experience as a challenge to semiotic interpretation, she "recontextualizes it into a broadly semiotic framework", which to some extent weakens the radicality of her theory.
• Limitation of scope of application: Her theoretical model is mainly based on the analysis of European avant-garde theater and performance art, so it may not be fully applicable to all types of performances, especially some participatory practices. Some scholars believe that analyzing such practices requires different tools, such as "choragraphic communication".
• Ambiguity in the concept of "performativity": "Performativity" itself is a "travelling concept" that has multiple and even contradictory meanings in different disciplines and contexts, which may lead to ambiguity in theoretical applications.
A productive academic system
Despite the above criticisms, this has not diminished Fischer-Licht's academic standing. On the contrary, the existence of these critiques proves that her theory is solid and important enough to spark sustained and serious scholarly debate. Minor theories are often ignored, while important theories are repeatedly tested and questioned.
The academic literature that has developed around the limitations and inherent tensions of Fischer-Lichte theory is itself the best testimony to its importance. Scholars are using her concepts to analyze new cases (such as participatory performance) and to reflect on its theoretical boundaries. This dialogue process has been extremely productive and has pushed the field to refine its terminology and research methods. Fischer-Lichte's system of scholarship became a central reference point on which subsequent scholars had to build or argue. Her scholarly legacy is therefore not a set of unquestionable dogmas but a powerful but imperfect set of conceptual tools. Its influence lies not in its impeccability, but in its "generativity" that continues to stimulate new research and critical thinking.
Conclusion: The legacy of a transformative scholar
Erika Fischer-Lichte has made landmark contributions to the fields of theater and performance studies. Her core achievement is to lead the entire discipline's focus from a focus on dramatic texts to a complex and multidimensional understanding of performance itself-as a vital, embodied, co-created, and transformative event.
Looking back at the trajectory of her academic thoughts, we can clearly see a coherent evolutionary path: from the precise analytical system established in "Drama Semiotics" to the phenomenological and political insights proposed in "The Transformative Power of Performance", to the grand grasp of global cultural dynamics through the "Interweaving of Performance Culture" theory. This trajectory demonstrates the inherent, deepening logic of his lifelong academic work.
Ultimately, Erika Fischer-Lichte situates herself as much more than a theater historian or theorist. She is a truly transformative figure whose work provides a new language and a whole new set of questions for understanding art, culture, and even social interaction in the 21st century. Her legacy lies in her fleeting yet powerful performances that profoundly and lastingly redefined the very object of study of our discipline.

2025-09-27
Theory and Methods
The Aesthetics of the Event: Reading Erika Fischer-Lichte's The Transformative Power of Performance
A study of Erika Fischer-Lichte's performative aesthetics, the autopoietic feedback loop, bodily co-presence, liminality, and transformation.
The Aesthetics of Events: A Comprehensive Analysis of Erika Fischer-Lichte's "The Transformative Power of Performance"
Erika Fischer-Lichte's book The Transformative Power of Performance: A New Aesthetics is a landmark work in the field of contemporary theater and performance studies. The book was first published in German in 2004 as Ästhetik des Performativen, and was translated into English by Saskya Iris Jain in 2008 and published by Routledge. This work systematically proposes a new theoretical framework that aims to replace the traditional aesthetic paradigm. Its core lies in shifting the focus of analysis from stable and interpretable artistic "works" to fluid, unpredictable "events" that are co-created by multiple parties. Through this theoretical turn, Fischer-Lichte not only provided a powerful analytical tool for understanding avant-garde drama, performance art and cultural performances since the 1960s, but also profoundly reshaped the theoretical landscape of performance studies. This report aims to conduct a comprehensive and in-depth analysis of the book's core arguments, theoretical mechanisms, key case analysis and its academic impact.
Part One: Foundations of Performative Aesthetics
The opening section of this report will first establish the core paradigm shift proposed by Fischer-Lichte. Its discussion starts from prioritizing "events" over "works" and traces the historical and philosophical soil in which this new aesthetics is rooted, that is, the "performative turn", thereby constructing the foundation of the entire theoretical edifice.
From work to event: announcing a new paradigm
Fischer-Lichte's theoretical revolution began with a fundamental assertion: performance should no longer be seen as a stable, interpretable work of art, but must be understood as an _event_ that is fundamentally contingent, ephemeral, and co-created by its participants. This assertion marks a break with traditional aesthetic theory, which is deeply rooted in hermeneutics (the interpretation of meaning) and semiotics (the study of signs), and whose analytical premise is a static object that can be repeatedly examined.
Fischer-Lichte elevated performance art to the same status as traditional artworks, thereby heralding the birth of a "new aesthetics." The focus of analysis is no longer what the performance means, but what it does for the participants. This new aesthetic paradigm breaks away from the 19th century realist-psychological drama's obsession with "representation". The value of a performance no longer comes solely from its representation of a script or fictional character, but is generated from its own materiality and interactivity.
The essential characteristics of a performance "event" lie in its ephemerality, interactivity and the dissolution of a series of traditional binary oppositions, such as the complete blurring of the boundaries between artist and audience, body and mind, art and life. It is a process that "brings forth itself" and its development trajectory cannot be completely predicted or controlled. This transformation from "work" to "event" is not a simple change of terminology, but a fundamental reshaping of the ontology of performance. It moves performance from a category of "things" that can be analyzed retrospectively to a category of "experience" that requires phenomenological understanding in the moment of its unfolding. Traditional aesthetic theory, whether derived from painting, sculpture or literature, requires a stable "work" as an object of analysis. However, the nature of live performance is ephemeral and unrepeatable. Therefore, applying a work-based analytical model to performance is itself a category fallacy. Fischer-Lichte's theoretical contribution lies in her attempt to construct an aesthetic theory derived from performance itself, rather than rigidly applying theories from other disciplines. By defining performance as an "event," she internally unifies the theoretical framework with the fundamental nature of the medium. The far-reaching impact of this change is that if performance is an event, then the goal of art criticism is no longer to judge a finished product, but must change to the witness and analysis of a dynamic process.
Positioning the "Performative Turn"
Fischer-Lichte's theory did not appear out of thin air, but was rooted in a broad intellectual background-the "performative turn." This term describes a broad intellectual paradigm shift that has occurred throughout the humanities and arts since the mid-20th century, the core of which is a shift from a focus on "representation" to a focus on action, process, and eventfulness. It is this intellectual climate that makes Fischer-Lichte's "new aesthetics" possible and inevitable.
The genealogy of this theory can be traced back to the speech-act theory of language philosopher J.L. Austin, which believes that language can not only describe the world, but also do things. This concept was subsequently further developed in the gender studies of Judith Butler, who defined gender as a series of stylized and repeated bodily behaviors. Fischer-Lichte focuses her analysis on the profound aesthetic changes that have occurred in the visual arts, music, and theater since the 1960s, which she considers to be a key catalyst for her theory. During this period, the rise of "happenings", "Fluxus" and performance art directly challenged the status of traditional artworks as objects of contemplation, and instead pushed the artist's body, actions and the audience's on-site experience to the forefront.
Fischer-Lichte's unique contribution to the "performative turn" lies in her assertion that performative aesthetics aims to redefine traditional binary oppositions (such as subject/object, observer/observed) and to view theatrical performance as a "living event" rather than a semiotic text waiting to be decoded. She even traced the origin of this turn back to the establishment of ritual studies and dramaturgy at the turn of the 20th century, thus giving it a more profound historical pedigree. This series of arguments embodies Fischer-Lichte's theoretical ambition: she is not simply borrowing a popular term, but strategically repositioning the concept of "performativity." Although she acknowledges its roots in linguistics and cultural theory, she explicitly advocates for bringing the discussion of "performativity" back into the realm of art. She draws on a broad cultural "turn" to legitimize a particular "performative aesthetics." By the 1990s, the term "performativity" had become ubiquitous across numerous disciplines, leading in part to the generalization and dilution of its meaning. By anchoring his analysis firmly on specific artistic events, Fischer-Lichte is actually taking back the interpretive power of this core concept for performance studies. She argued that theater and performance art are not only cases of "performativity" but also "privileged fields" where its practical logic is most fully demonstrated and understood. This theoretical intervention made her work a foundational work for the revitalization of arts-centered performance studies.
Comparative framework: theatrical aesthetics vs. performative aesthetics
In order to more clearly reveal the revolutionary nature of Fischer-Lichte's theory, the following will systematically sort out the fundamental differences between traditional theater aesthetics and the performative aesthetics she advocated through a comparative framework. This table is not only a summary of the content, but also an inspiring analysis tool. It concretely makes an abstract theoretical argument concrete and makes its structural logic clear at a glance.
Features
Traditional drama aesthetics (work-centered)
Fisher-Richter's performative aesthetics (event-centered)
core object
Dramatic text; finished work of art.
Live, ephemeral performance events.
audience role
Interpreter; passive recipient of meaning.
Co-creator; active participant in the feedback loop.
meaning making
A hermeneutic reading of signs and symbols.
"Emerge" through sensory experience and interaction.
acting-viewing relationship
Separated by the "fourth wall" (representative).
Physical co-presence; direct, unpredictable interaction.
temporality
Repeatable; pursue consistency across sessions.
Unrepeatable; fundamentally dependent on the "here and now."
core focus
Performance _means_ nothing.
What does the performance _do_ to the participants.
Experience mode
Aesthetic distance; quiet observation.
Embodied participation; liminal experience.
physical status
A signifier that represents a character.
Phenomenal, material presence; the place where an event occurs.
The logic behind the construction of this table is that Fischer-Lichte's theory is established by "exploding a series of false binary oppositions." Tables are the most effective way to present this binary opposition and show how the new paradigm systematically disrupts the old paradigm. By juxtaposing concepts such as "passive recipient" and "active co-creator," "representation" and "co-presence," the table condenses the core argument of a complex 240-page work into its essential structural logic. This provides the reader with a clear, memorable framework for better understanding the more detailed discussions that follow in the report, as well as a conceptual map for exploring the entire book.
Part Two: The Engine of Performance: Autogenic Feedback Loops
This section will delve into the core mechanics of the Fischer-Lichte theory. It aims to explain how a performance event is generated and sustained through dynamic, self-regulated interactions between performers and audiences. This mechanism she named the "autopoietic feedback loop."
Shared bodies, shared spaces: the principle of co-presence
The cornerstone of the Fischer-Lichte system is the basic fact that actors and audiences must be in the same place at the same time. This is not an inconsequential logistical detail, but the ontological foundation of performance.
Performance occurs from the "bodily co-presence of actors and audiences." This shared "lifetime" forms the medium through which all interactions occur. This principle fundamentally challenges the concept of the "fourth wall" in traditional representational drama. In Fischer-Lichte's model, a completely closed fictional world is impossible because the reality of the audience's presence is always a decisive factor in the composition of the performance.
She cited communication theorist Paul Watzlawick's view that in a situation of shared presence, "one cannot not react to the other." Every cough, sigh or shift of attention of the audience is a perceptible event and will be immediately fed back to the performance process and have an impact on it.
Deconstructing autogenic feedback loops
The "autogeneic feedback loop" is the best-known concept from Fischer-Lichte's work. The term "autopoiesis" is borrowed from biology, meaning "self-creation" to describe the dynamic, self-generating, unpredictable cyclical process that constitutes the performance itself.
This cycle is a "self-referential and ever-changing" process. It is specifically manifested as: the performer's actions trigger perceptible reactions (such as laughter, silence, commotion) from the audience, and these reactions are in turn perceived by the performers and other audiences, thereby affecting their subsequent actions and reactions. Because this cycle is self-generating and responsive, performance events always maintain a certain degree of "unpredictability and spontaneity." Its process is extremely unstable and cannot be completely planned or controlled by any party.
Performance, therefore, is not the execution of a pre-existing script or plan; it "comes into being only in its process." Feedback loops are precisely the process by which performance _produces itself_. The "staging" created by the artist only sets the initial conditions for the activation of this cycle, while the real "performance" is the unique and unrepeatable event that emerges after the cycle is activated.
The dissolution of roles: from spectators to participants
The most radical consequence of spontaneous feedback loops is the breakdown of the traditional hierarchical relationship between the active artist and the passive audience.
Fischer-Lichte clearly "exploded the false binary opposition between actor and audience." Audiences are far from passive recipients; their reactions themselves form an integral part of the performance. All participants "share responsibility for what is happening." In extreme cases, this feedback loop can even lead to a complete role reversal. The analysis of Marina Abramović's "Lips of Thomas" in the book is the most typical example: the audience finally could not bear the performer's self-mutilation behavior and intervened, physically stopping the performance. At this moment, they "are themselves transformed into actors."
Avant-garde and experimental theater since the 1960s has often consciously exploited and highlighted the workings of feedback loops. They make this mechanism visible through strategies such as role reversal, creating temporary communities at the performance site, and facilitating physical contact between performers and audiences. Autogenic feedback loops are not only a descriptive model, but also a theory of agency. It reconceptualizes agency in performance as a distributed, relational, and emergent force rather than solely attributed to the author, director, or individual performer. Traditional theater models assume a clear hierarchy of agency: the author creates the text, the director interprets it, the actors perform it, and the audience receives it. However, the theory of feedback loops reveals that every participant jointly determines the direction of events, and no one has absolute control. This means that agency is no longer a property of individuals, but the product of interactions between individuals. In performance, the individual "experiences himself as a subject that is neither completely autonomous nor completely determined by others." This idea has important political implications: if agency in performance spaces is relational and co-creative, then performance itself becomes a model of a different kind of social and political process - one based on mutual influence and shared responsibility rather than top-down control. The "transformative force" of this book's title is therefore ultimately a political force.
Part Three: The Experience of Events: Materiality and Meaning
This section shifts the focus of analysis from the _mechanism_ of events to the _phenomenology_ of experiencing events. It aims to explore how the perceivable, material elements of performance create unique experiences, and how meaning itself is generated within this new aesthetic framework.
material performative becoming
According to Fischer-Lichte, feedback loops operate through the production and perception of materiality. Performance experience is fundamentally embodied and sensory rather than intellectual and interpretive. She breaks down this materiality into a few key components.
The materiality of performance is mainly reflected through three core elements: corporeality, spatiality and tonality.
• Bodily: The actor's phenomenal, material body - its presence, energy, sounds and even smell - becomes the primary focus of the audience's attention, no longer just its function as a character symbol.
• Spatiality: The way space is organized and used directly affects the relationships between actors and the flow of feedback loops.
• Tonality: This includes all auditory elements - vocals, acoustics, atmosphere, and especially rhythm. Rhythm "tunes" the bodies of participants and organizes the operation of feedback loops. Fischer-Lichte particularly emphasized rhythm as an organizing principle that effectively links materiality to cyclical, self-generated processes.
These material elements are not passive backgrounds, but "active forces" that trigger "physiological, emotional, energetic and motor responses" in participants. The materiality of the performance itself becomes "an agent in the self-generating feedback loop."
The emergence of meaning beyond semiotics
This section deals with one of the most complex questions in the theory: if performance is no longer a text waiting to be interpreted, how does meaning come about? Fisher-Richter proposed an "emergence" model.
Meaning is no longer a stable message transmitted from artist to audience. Instead, it "emerges" in an unstable, dynamic way over the course of events. In many cases, "understanding the artist's actions itself is far less important than experiencing the experiences generated by these actions." The audience's perception is in a constant state of flow, that is, "perceptual multistability". Their attention is constantly switching between different foci-for example, between the actor's physical body and the character he or she plays. It is in this instability and oscillation that meaning arises.
It is worth noting that although this theory is extremely subversive, some critics point out that Fischer-Lichte ultimately "coalesced" her theory to a certain extent back into a "broad semiotic" framework when she broke down events into physical, spatial and other components in her analysis and explored their relationships. This critical perspective adds necessary academic depth to understanding his theory. Fischer-Lichte's theory of meaning-making is anti-logocentric in nature. It challenges the supremacy of language and text that has long dominated Western drama theory, and instead locates meaning in embodied, sensory, and emotional experience. Traditional drama is text-led, and the meaning is mainly contained in the playwright's words. Fischer-Lichte's emphasis on materiality consciously shifts the core of experience to the non-verbal level: feeling the energy conveyed by a choir, the instinctive reaction to a painful body, or the sense of unity brought by a common rhythm. She also noted the difficulty of translating these "translinguistic images, fantasies, memories...feelings and emotions" into language after the fact. Her theory thus advocates a bodily, affective knowledge and meaning that exists before or outside of linguistic representation. This aligns her work with broader academic trends such as phenomenology and emotion theory, and poses a major challenge to purely hermeneutic or semiotic analysis methods.
Part 4: The power of change in practice: key case analysis
This section will situate abstract theory into concrete analysis, focusing on the key cases used by Fischer-Lichte to construct and illustrate his argument. These cases are not simple illustrations of the theory; they are the phenomena from which the theory itself is derived.
The Abramovich Case: Lips of Thomas as Liminal Crisis
This section will conduct a multi-dimensional analysis of Marina Abramović's 1975 performance art work, which is a core example in the book. The show is a crucible for testing all of Fischer-Lichte's core concepts.
According to the vivid description in the book, the performance included: Abramovich ate a kilogram of honey, drank a liter of red wine, cut a five-pointed star in his abdomen with a razor blade, whipped himself, and finally lay naked on a cross made of ice until the audience couldn't bear it and intervened. The power of this performance stems from the fact that it creates a situation in which the audience is "suspended between the norms and rules of art and daily life, between the imperatives of aesthetics and ethics." They face an unavoidable choice: continue to watch as art spectators, or step forward to intervene as similar people?
Initially, the audience's reaction was a physical signal of horror and dismay. This feedback continues to increase the tension in the scene until it reaches a critical point. This crisis cannot be solved by any conventional behavioral patterns. In the end, the audience decided to lift Abramovich from the ice cross, an action that constituted the climax of the entire incident. At this moment, they are no longer spectators, but become actors, ending the performance through their own initiative. This perfectly illustrates the "power of change" referred to in the book's title.
The Politics of the Gaze: Coco Fusco and Guillermo Gómez-Pena's Caged "Indians"
To demonstrate the political dimension of his theory, Fischer-Lichte analyzes another key case: Two Undiscovered Amerindians Visit..., 1992 by Coco Fusco and Guillermo Gómez-Peña.
In this performance, the two artists lock themselves in a cage and act as "undiscovered" Aboriginal people for the audience to visit. The performance was designed to induce the audience to perform actions that "embodied the colonial gaze." Many spectators regard them as spectacles, feed them, take photos with them, and completely enter the role of watching "others".
Fischer-Lichte used this case to illustrate one of her core points: "The act of perceiving the other is always a political act." The performance demonstrates "the transformative power of the gaze directed toward the Other, which can either recognize the Other as a shared subject or reduce it to an object." This makes the performance-viewing relationship itself a field full of ethical and political tensions. The selection of these cases is highly strategic and argumentative. By focusing on radical, body-centered, and often painful performance art, Fischer-Lichte deliberately selects examples that traditional theater theory cannot adequately explain. A traditional aesthetic theory based on representation and interpretation will be powerless when faced with "The Lips of Thomas". This show isn't "about" pain, it's pain itself. Its significance does not lie in a symbol, but in the ethical crisis it creates in the hearts of the audience. Similarly, Fusco and Gomez-Pena's works are not a "reproduction" of colonialism, but an "enactment" of the colonial gaze in real time, using the audience's own behavior as the main material. Through these extreme cases, Fischer-Lichte not only demonstrated the failure of the old paradigm, but also highlighted the explanatory power of his new theory. Her theories were not rigidly applied to these works, but emerged from some of the most challenging artistic practices of the late 20th century.
Part Five: The Reenchantment of the World: Meaning and Critical Context
The final section of the report will synthesize the book's arguments, explore its claims about the ultimate purpose and power of performance, and situate the work within its critical context.
Performance as liminal experience
Fischer-Lichte defines the "transformative power" of performance as its ability to lead participants into a state of "liminality"-a threshold state of "betwixt and between."
Drawing on anthropological concepts, performance events can place participants in a state where conventional social rules, roles and identities are temporarily suspended. Abramović's performance is a typical example of throwing the audience into the liminal crisis between aesthetics and ethical norms. In this liminal state, participants are able to experience themselves and their relationships with others in new ways. They are open to the possibility of transformation-whether it is a shift in perception, a shift in self-awareness, or a shift in understanding of social reality.
The Reenchantment of the World
This section explores the grand theme revealed in the title of the final chapter of the book: "The Re-Enchantment of the World."
By focusing attention on the materiality of bodies, objects and spaces, performance can make the ordinary extraordinary. It transforms the everyday banality and allows participants to perceive the world with a re-intensified intensity. In a world often seen as disenchanted, rationalized, and demystified, performance offers a mode of experience that reintroduces wonder, presence, and serendipity. It allows people to re-experience a world that is vibrant, dynamic and full of potential.
Critical reception and academic impact
Any professional scholarly report must contain a balanced assessment of the influence of the work analyzed and a response to the criticisms it has faced.
The Transformative Power of Performance is undoubtedly an "important reference" that has profoundly shaped academic debates in the fields of theater theory and performance studies. Concepts such as "autonomous feedback loops" have become core vocabulary of the discipline. However, the book also triggered a series of important academic criticisms
• Some scholars have pointed out that despite its radical premises, the theory ultimately returns to a semiotic framework by breaking down events into analyzable components.
• Some concepts, such as "energy", have been criticized as being more assertions than adequate explanations.
• It is also argued that Fischer-Lichte's way of thinking is sometimes too binary and that the feedback loops themselves could be distinguished and analyzed in more detail.
Finally, as Marvin Carlson points out in the book's introduction, an important contribution of this work is to bring a "refreshing continental perspective" to a field long dominated by Anglo-Saxon scholarship. The book's final argument about "reenchantment" positions performance not just as an artistic practice but as a crucial cultural and even quasi-spiritual practice. It suggests that in a secularized world, performance can take on the role once played by ritual: providing an intense, transformative community experience. The book frequently draws parallels between performance art and religious or ritual practices (such as comparing Abramović's self-mutilation to asceticism). The concept of "liminality" is borrowed directly from ritual anthropology. Descriptions of the performance experience are also imbued with ritualistic language of intensifying energy, shifts in consciousness, and the creation of temporary communities. The final claim of "reenchantment" thus combines all these threads. It suggests that this "new aesthetic" is not just a new way of analyzing art, but a way of understanding how performance can provide a modern, secular form of "enchantment" by making the material world present and powerful again. This has greatly improved the landscape of Fisher-Richter theory, moving it from a purely academic discussion to a profound level of cultural concern.

P4 Theater and You
2025-09-26
Theory and Methods
Drama is written in the sand.
These were words I first heard from an elderly drama teacher when I was 15, and they have become increasingly important and fascinating to me throughout my...
Drama is written in the sand. --Luke Percival
These were words I first heard from an elderly drama teacher when I was 15, and they have become increasingly important and fascinating to me throughout my career. It revealed to me the spiritual dimension that theater can give.
From a purely factual standpoint, drama is really nothing more than writing in the sand. The small salary you can earn in theater is quickly spent; the fame that many people crave in the first place is fleeting and easily forgotten. As for the plays themselves and the themes they explore, they also cannot change the world or human nature. In fact, you could even say that theater is a completely meaningless activity. But precisely in this realization, a question arises: What is the meaning of these 2,500 years of meaningless drama?
As I grew older as an actor and later as a theater creator, all my illusions and pathetic dreams about theater evaporated. I began to realize that not only was the drama meaningless, but also my own existence, my so-called identity, was based on a construction of meaning, and this construction ultimately led to a huge and unanswerable question mark. "From nothing, to nothing," said King Lear. The urge to perform, combined with the self-hatred rooted in my Catholic upbringing, pushed me to great despair in the early 1990s. My life was meaningless and worthless, and the drama I had chosen so passionately failed to create happiness for myself or anyone else. My depression was bottomless.
But the desire to find answers is even stronger. Unconsciously, I was forced to search more intently and frame my questions more precisely. The loss of the measurable utility of theater on a material level and the letting go of the obsessive desire to create utility are actually quite liberating. True, drama is meaningless when measured by output. Yet man has always ritualized his need for meaning in drama; universal texts that explore the meaning of life and human suffering, classics that ask the same questions, continue to fascinate us, even though no writer or playwright has ever succeeded in giving a complete answer. Since the answer is beyond human understanding, it is unlikely to be found. So is there any point in continuing to search? Is it this "search for meaning" itself that keeps us alive? Is it what provides theater creators with adrenaline and creativity? Is it what drives the audience into the theater? Without this inquiring curiosity, there would be no art, no religion, no drama...and perhaps, no beauty. Isn't the meaning of drama just exploration itself? It is the "not knowing" that wants to know, which leads us to realize that many things you once believed to be true are "not so." And what it is, you can't explain. This longing for truth cannot be proven, cannot be touched, cannot be put into words. The only thing we know for sure is that it appears in the quest itself. Theater cannot provide any form of answers. It forces artists and audiences to accept silence and emptiness, throwing them back to a life without explanation and logic, and teaching them to trust this search with their bare hands - this fact itself seems to be the only meaning of meaningless things. This is precisely the spiritual path that theater follows-to the rejection of any concept, answer, or judgment, to the acceptance of silence. A path to the realm of nothingness. This is often a central theme in Shakespeare's plays; a path paved with loss and letting go, ending in a purified insight, or, if you prefer, self-actualization.
What is liberating or self-fulfilling about this path?
Realizing that there are no "answers" frees you from the obligation to always have an answer ready, or at least be owed one. It allows you, as a dramatist, to work from a position of "not knowing," to trust your intuition, your energy, and-most importantly-to trust what the moment has to offer and the people around you. It gives you and those around you the freedom to "find", and the answers lie within the inquiry itself. It is a quest driven not by individual responsibility but by collective process, liberated from seeming certainties and preconceptions, and undertaken with an open mind and an eye for wonder. It creates space for us to see "what is" and deal with it with the freedom of an ignorant child. It gives the actor the freedom to act and react with "what is" rather than "what should be", a performance style born of respect and concern for others, an awareness of interdependence, and the courage to surrender fully to it, rather than imprisoning oneself in a solitary frenzy. This method, this way of acting, brings freedom, air and inspiration, and it creates the joy of performance, and even the joy of life, on the theatrical stage. This is the flip side of depression, the flip side of the consequences of the desire for results and success. It is from this joy and collectiveness that performances are born that are "unique" because of their extraordinary energy; performances that depict a world that can only be created by this particular group, rather than from the conceptual mind of a tortured individual. These performances are born out of respect and focus on what is happening to others, a focus shared by the audience and the actors. It is an extraordinary devotion in this noisy world, one that creates a sense of ritual communion and non-aloneness as audience and actors search for the "meaning of meaninglessness"; a moment of consolation, of shared suffering or laughter in the realization that there are no answers to so much senseless suffering and violence, but only understanding and perhaps a moment of compassion.
This "writing in the sand" is not a formula for success. It is like a mantra, a repetition of the same questions to which the same silence is the ultimate answer. It is a silence that holds great power, though: it is catharsis, a moment of shared awareness and understanding of human suffering. As long as humanity fails to put this compassion into practice in daily life, drama will continue to write its spell in the sand. And repeating those mantras day after day, obeying this ritual, is the only task of the dramatist. The rest are all delusions. The joy, or liberation, is not in what drama or life has to offer you, but in what you give over and over again, without leaving a trace. This is the insight created by Writing in the Sand.
Luke Percival September 4, 2003
Theater is writing in the sand.
Luk Perceval
