From a purely factual perspective, theatre is indeed no more than writing in the sand. The little money you can earn in theatre is quickly spent. The fame that many initially aspire to soon disappears and is easily forgotten. As for the plays and the themes they deal with, these are not capable of changing the world or humanity either. In fact, you could argue that theatre is an en entirely meaningless activity. But precisely in this realisation lies the question about the meaning of 2500 years of meaningless theatre.
As I grew older as an actor and subsequently as a theatre-maker, all my illusions and pathetic dreams about theatre dissipated. I came to realise not only that theatre was meaningless, but also that my own existence, my so-called identity, had been founded on a construct of meaning that ultimately leads to a huge unanswerable question mark. "From nothing to nothing", says Lear. The urge to perform and the self-hatred instilled in me by my Catholic upbringing drove me to great despair in the early 1990s. My life was meaningless, worthless, and theatre -for which I had chosen so passionately- had not been capable of creating happiness for either myself or any one else. The depth of my depression was great.
But the hunger to find an answer was even greater. Without my realising it, I was being forced to search more attentively, to formulate my questions more accurately. The loss of a materially measurable effect of theatre, as well as the letting go of the compulsive desire to create an effect, was actually quite a liberation. Indeed, in terms of yield, you could argue that theatre is utterly meaningless. And yet, man has always ritualised his need to give meaning in theatre; the same universal texts asking the same questions about the meaning of life and human suffering continue to fascinate us, even though no author or playwright has ever succeeded in formulating an adequate answer. As this answer lies beyond human comprehension, it is unlikely ever to be found. So does it make sense to continue looking for it? Is this "search for meaning" what keeps us alive in the first place? Is it what provides the theatre-maker with adrenaline, with creative power? Is it what drives spectators to the theatre? Without this inquisitiveness there would be no art, no religion, no theatre… and probably no beauty either. Is the meaning of theatre not the search itself? The "not knowing" that wants to know, which leads to the realisation that much of what you believed to be it "is not it". And whatever it is instead, you are unable to designate. The reason for this hunger for truth is not demonstrable, not tangible, impossible to put into words. All that we know for certain is that it manifests itself in "the search" itself. The mere fact that theatre is unable to provide any form of answer, that it forces the artist and spectator to accept the silence and emptiness, and throws them back into life without explanation, void of any logic, and teaches them to trust empty-handedly in the search - this would appear to be the only meaning of the meaningless. Precisely this is the spiritual path that theatre follows towards the rejection of any concept, answer or judgement, and the acceptance of silence. A road to nowhere. This is so often the central theme in Shakespeare's plays; a road that is paved with loss and letting go, and that ends in a chastening insight or, if you will, self-realisation.
What is so liberating or self-realising about this road?
The awareness that there is no "answer" releases you from the obligation always to have an answer ready or at least to owe an answer. It gives you the freedom as a theatre-maker to create from a position of "not knowing", to trust on you intuition, on your energy and -most importantly of all- on what the moment has to offer, on the people around you. It gives you and those around you the freedom to "search", whereby the answer lies hidden in the search itself. It is a search that is driven not by an individual responsibility but by a collective process, liberated from quasi certainties and preconceptions, with open visor and wonder. It creates space to look at what there is and to handle it with the freedom of an unwitting child. It offers the actor the freedom to act with and react to what there is rather than what there ought to be, a style of acting that originates in respect and attention for the other, in the awareness of dependency and the courage to give in to it completely, not to lock yourself up in egomania. This approach, this manner of acting offers freedom, air and inspiration, and it creates pleasure in preforming on the theatre stage, pleasure in life, if you will. It is the flip side of depression, a consequence of hunger for effect and success. Out of this pleasure and collectiveness are born performances that are "unique" precisely because of this extraordinary energetic quality; performances that depict a world that can only be created by this particular group of people, not the conceptual mind of a single tormented individual. These performances are borne by respect and concentration on whatever is happening to the other, a focus that spectators and actors share. It is an extraordinary form of devotion in this bigmouth world that creates a ritual solidarity, a non-loneliness, between spectators and actors in their search for the "meaning of the meaningless"; a moment of solace, of common suffering or laughter at the realisation that there are no answers for so much meaningless suffering and violence, but only understanding, and perhaps a moment of compassion.
This "writing in the sand" is not a formula for success. Like a mantra, it is the continuous repetition of exactly the same questions to which exactly the same silence is the ultimate answer. Albeit a silence with enormous power: the power of catharsis, a moment of shared awareness of and understanding for the suffering of man. As long as humanity is not able implement this compassion in the practice of daily existence, theatre will continue to write its mantras into the sand. And to repeat those mantras up until that day, to be subservient to this ritual, that is the only task of the theatre-maker. All the rest is idle hope. The joy, call it liberation, lies not in what theatre and/or life offers to you, but in what you yourself offer, time and again, without leaving any trace. That is the insight this "writing in the sand" creates.

The Third Body of Analysis: An Integrated Exploration of Thomas Ogden's Theory of the "Third Presence"
Part One: Basic Principles of "Third Presence"
Over the course of the development of psychoanalysis theory, the understanding of the therapeutic relationship itself has undergone profound evolution. From initially viewing it as a field of one-way projection to later recognizing the complexity of two-way interactions, this evolution reached a theoretical peak in the work of contemporary psychoanalysis scientist Thomas Ogden. The concept of "the analytic third" or "analytic third" proposed by Ogden is not only a redescription of the therapeutic relationship, but also an ontological reconstruction. It conceptualizes the invisible and dynamic interactive space between the analyst and the analysand in the analytic situation as a "third subject" with its own vitality. This part aims to lay down the core theoretical framework of "Third Presence", from its basic definition, internal dialectical movement mechanism, to the way it is generated and perceived in clinical situations, to reveal this complex and creative theory in depth step by step.
1.1 Defining the intersubjective field: a third subjectivity
The core definition of "third presence" is that it is a psychological entity that is jointly created by both analysts and transcends the sum of individuals. It is not a static space or metaphor, but a dynamic and subjective existence.
core definition
The "third presence" is defined as "the jointly created unconscious life of the analytic pair". It is an "intermediary, intersubjective analytic space" that emerges through unconscious communication processes between analyst and patient. This space is not just the intersection of two people's thoughts, but what Ogden calls a "third subjectivity" that seems to "take on a life of its own in the interpersonal field." This positioning itself marks a profound theoretical shift: the focus of psychoanalysis shifts from the archaeological excavation of the individual's internal psychological world to the participation and understanding of a new, living psychological reality in relationships. This nascent entity becomes a unique field in which "thoughts, fantasies, and emotions that might otherwise remain silent are mobilized and revealed."
This change in theoretical framework means that the goal of psychoanalysis is no longer just for the analyst to "understand" the patient's inner world - an epistemological task; but to participate in and understand a new "being" in the therapeutic relationship - an ontological investment. This ontological overtone runs through Ogden's language, speaking of a "co-created unconscious life" and an "analytic third subject." This is not the language of a mere epistemological tool, but the language of existence itself. When the theory emphasizes that this "third subject" is "unpredictable by prior knowledge of either party," it directly challenges the traditional notion that the analyst is merely discovering existing facts within the patient's mind. Rather, analyst and patient are co-creating something entirely new. This ontological commitment also explains why it is difficult to fully grasp the concept from a purely scientific or neuroscientific perspective, because the latter usually presupposes bounded, independent individual bodies and minds. The "third presence" exists in the space "between bodies/individuals" and is a relational reality that cannot be reduced to individual components. Therefore, the "third presence" is not only a tool for understanding the patient, it is itself the medium of the analytic process, a new form of existence that must be experienced, felt, and ultimately understood only retrospectively. This is in line with Ogden's later focus on "ontologypsychoanalysis".
Co-creation and asymmetry
Although the "third presence" is a product of co-creation, its formation process is not entirely reciprocal. The form and content of this "third" element are "primarily determined by the patient's internal object world, his unconscious fantasies and defense systems." This reveals an inherent asymmetry in the therapeutic relationship: the analyst's subjectivity is consciously and disciplinedly deployed in service of the exploration of the patient's inner world. Although a co-creator, the analyst's role is that of a container and translator whose personal experience is used to understand and symbolize the unconscious dynamics directed by the patient.
an emerging psychological entity
The "Third Presence" is described as a "new interpersonal field" or "third subjectivity" that "emerges spontaneously from the interaction of two minds and cannot be predicted based on prior knowledge of either party." This emphasizes its emergent and unpredictable nature. It is not a simple superposition of the existing characteristics of the analyst and the patient, but the product of a qualitative change, a completely new psychological entity. It is in this entity that experiences that have been repressed, dissociated, or never spoken gain the possibility of existence.
1.2 The Dialectics of Subjectivity: An Elucidation of Winnicott's Thoughts
The "third presence" is not a static structure, but a process of continuous movement. The core engine driving this process is what Ogden describes as a dialectical movement: participants exist both as independent individuals and simultaneously as part of an intersubjective unity, and there is a continuous and dynamic tension between these two states.
core dialectics
Ogden sees the core of the entire psychoanalysis enterprise as tracing "the dialectical movement between individual subjectivity...and intersubjectivity, the 'third presence'". This is the dynamic core of the theory: a constant oscillation between being an independent subject and being part of a co-created third subject. The vitality and depth of the analysis process come from the experience, endurance and understanding of this dialectical movement.
Winnicott's Paradox
Ogden explicitly extends D. W. Winnicott's famous paradoxical assertion that "there is no such thing as an infant [apart from the maternal provision]" to the analytic situation. He proposed: "In the context of analysis, there is no analysand who is divorced from the relationship with the analyst, and there is no analyst who is divorced from the relationship with the analysand." This argument is not to eliminate individuality, but to emphasize that at the psychological level, the subject is co-constructed in relationships.
dynamic tension
The key to this paradox lies in its dynamic nature. Ogden clarifies: "The mother-infant unity coexists in a dynamic tension with mother and infant as independent beings." Likewise, in analysis, the experience of fusion between analyst and analysand is in constant tension with their experience of independence. The task of analysis is therefore not to try to "sort out the elements that constitute the relationship in order to determine which qualities belong to whom" but rather to "describe the specific experiential nature of the unconscious interplay between individual subjectivity and intersubjectivity." The foundation of subjectivity is established in this inter-subjective dialectical relationship between "recognition" and "recognition".
1.3 The Generation of "Third Presence": Contemplation, Asymmetry and Retrospective Understanding
If dialectical movement is the theoretical engine of the "third presence," then the analyst's inner experience, especially his "reverie," is the key instrument for perceiving and understanding the operation of this engine. This section will focus on the specific mechanisms of how the "third presence" is formed and perceived in clinical practice.
The Analyst's "Contemplative" Role
The analyst's main access to the "third presence" is through his own "reverie experiences." This includes mental activities that may seem irrelevant to the patient and may even be considered distractions, such as "narcissistic self-absorption, distraction," "banal reveries," somatic delusions, and even complete daydreams or fantasies. In Ogden's theoretical framework, these are not disturbances that need to be overcome, but rather the analyst's mind unconsciously processing and giving form to unspoken experiences in a "third presence." They are the analyst's unconscious work of symbolizing the patient's unlanguageable experience.
Tolerate "uncertainty"
In order to be able to access and make use of this contemplative material, the analyst must be able to "withstand his or her own uncomfortable feelings and feelings: for example, feeling lost, frustrated, angry, or confused." This requires a special ability on the part of the analyst to "sit with unformulated experience" and to resist the urge to seek certainty or explanation prematurely. This ability to withstand uncertainty is the prerequisite for the "third presence" to emerge and be understood.
retrospective understanding
A "third presence" is not "an event experienced in the same way by both participants." Its meaning and structure often "can only be truly constructed and thought about in retrospect, often long after the experience has occurred." This is a crucial point: experience precedes understanding. Analyst and patient first "live" in the "third presence" and can then, at some point, usually through the intervention of the analyst, come back to understand what they have experienced together.
This reorientation of the analyst's inner world elevates the analyst's subjective vulnerability-his capacity to be lost, confused, and moved by his own contemplation-to the level of a core technical principle. The classical psychoanalysis technique emphasizes the neutrality and anonymity of the analyst and aims to create a projected "blank slate." The analyst's personal emotions, the "countertransference," are often seen as obstacles to be managed and overcome through self-analysis. Ogden's model, however, fundamentally overturns this view. The analyst's most private, seemingly irrelevant thoughts ("banal reveries") are precisely the source of data for the perception of the unconscious life of the "third presence." The task of the analyst is therefore not to eliminate its subjectivity but to "surrender" to it and exploit it. This requires a high tolerance for uncertainty and discomfort. This means that the "analytical attitude" is no longer one of detached observation, but one of deep, receptive immersion. The analyst's personality, style, and life experience are no longer obstacles but sources of his or her unique ability to interact with patients. This transforms the use of the self from a general therapeutic principle into a specific psychoanalysis technique: the disciplined use of contemplation to symbolize the co-created unconscious field. The analyst must be vulnerable enough to be shaped by the "third presence" in order to understand it.
Part 2: Clinical Practice of "Third Presence"
The vitality of a theory lies in the validity of its clinical application. Ogden's concept of the "third presence" has been so influential precisely because it provides a powerful framework for understanding and dealing with some of the most subtle, complex, and confusing moments in clinical practice. This section will delve into the manifestations of "Third Presence" in specific clinical work, and demonstrate how this theory can be transformed from an abstract concept into concrete therapeutic actions by analyzing Ogden's own detailed case materials. We will examine the manifestation of the Third Presence, its pathological "conquering" form, and the ultimate therapeutic goal of working beyond it.
2.1 Detailed case study: "The Stolen Letter"
To illustrate how the "Third Presence" operates in reality, Ogden provides a detailed clinical case in his book called "The Purloined Letter." This case involves him and a patient named Mr. L. Through a microscopic analysis of this treatment process, we can clearly see how theory is transformed into practice.
patient status
Mr. L exhibited a profound state of emotional numbness, detachment, and mechanization. He felt as if he was living outside an untouchable scene, unable to feel intimacy even with his wife and children. His dreams were filled with "paralyzed men, prisoners, and mutes," and a key one involved him struggling to split open a stone and discovering undecipherable hieroglyphics carved within. The dream accurately captures his central dilemma: meaning seems within reach, but ultimately proves hollow and hopelessly seductive. This state of "dead silence" sets the tone for the nature of the "third presence" that is about to be co-created.
The Analyst's Meditations as the Emergence of the "Third Presence"
During one therapy session, the analyst's attention was drawn to an envelope lying on the table next to him. The envelope had been there for some time, but at that moment it suddenly came alive as a psychological event. The analyst's thoughts revolved around the envelope in a series of meditations. These meditations were not random distractions, but the "third presence" was giving concrete form to Mr. L's unspoken experience
• Details of the envelope: The analyst first noticed the machine-made lines on the envelope, which disappointed him, as if the intimacy of the letter was false. Then he noticed the uncanceled stamp and Mozart's name on it. This "same" name in different languages made him feel a little familiar. Finally, he realized that the address on the envelope had been typed on an old manual typewriter, and this personal, imperfect imprint made him feel a sense of human warmth. These seemingly irrelevant details are precisely the "third presence" that uses concrete sensory forms to present the core conflict of analysis: the tension between mechanical/dehumanization (machine lines, the fantasy of batch mail) and humanity/personality (Mozart's name, the unique imprint of a manual typewriter).
• Garage fantasy: The analyst's mind then wanders to an anxious fantasy: his car is in a garage, and he must end therapy on time to pick up the car before the garage closes. He vividly imagined being turned away by his ruthless garage owner and feeling intense helplessness, anger, and loneliness. This fantasy is not just a trouble in the analyst's personal life, but a direct experience of Mr. L's core emotions in the "third presence". The analyst is "living out" Mr. L's unspoken despair of being trapped in an emotionless, mechanical world (symbolized by the patient's "brain-dead" mother).
analyst intervention
The point is that the analyst does not directly explain his musings or fantasies. He did not say to Mr. L: "I think my garage fantasy represents your feelings about your mother." On the contrary, because he had been changed by the experience of "third presence", he was able to
Speak from this shared experience rather than about this experience. His intervention was descriptive rather than explanatory. He told the patient that he imagined their time together must have felt like a "funless, obligatory exercise, a bit like clocking in and out at a factory" to Mr L. He then added that he felt that Mr. L sometimes felt so hopelessly suffocated in therapy that it must have felt like "suffocating in something that looked like air but was actually a vacuum." This intervention is powerful because it arises directly from the sense of mechanicality and suffocation experienced by the analyst in his garage fantasies and envelope musings.
patient transformation
Mr. L's reaction was immediate and profound. His voice became "bigger and fuller," something the analyst had never heard before. He immediately linked the analyst's words to his own fear of suffocation at night and became aware for the first time that the air in the therapy room made him feel stuffy and suffocating. This intervention broke the impasse and allowed repressed, pre-verbal bodily sensations to enter the realm of consciousness and speech. During the following session, Mr. L reported a dream in which he was underwater and discovered that he could breathe. This is a powerful symbol of a profound psychological transformation taking place. The dead, suffocating "third presence" has been transformed into a living, breathing liquid medium.
2.2 "Conquering Third" and Projective Identification
The "third presence" is not always a creative and transformative space. In some cases, it can become a closed, pathological system, what Ogden calls "the subjugating third."
definition
Ogden reconceptualizes projective identification as a specific form of "third presence." In this form, "the individual subjectivities of analyst and analysand are conquered by a co-created third analytic subject." This co-created subject is the "conquering third". It refers to a powerful, unconscious pattern of interaction in which both parties are trapped and lose the ability to feel and reflect as independent subjects.
deadlock theory
In this state, both analyst and patient are trapped in an unconscious dynamic loop from which they cannot escape. This provides a highly explanatory model for understanding the enactment of impasse, resistance, and compulsive repetition in therapy. In Mr. L's case, the sense of dead silence, machinery, and hopelessness that pervaded the treatment before the intervention could be understood as an experience of a "conquering third". Both parties unconsciously play out roles in this script, a numb patient and an analyst who also feels powerless and wandering.
saturated signal
When the analyst fails to recognize that he or she is experiencing a "conquering third," this may be a sign of "an oversaturated state within the therapist." This means that the therapist has become so completely overwhelmed by this co-creative dynamic that he or she has lost the psychological distance necessary to do reflective and symbolic work. At this point, the analyst is no longer an observer and interpreter of the "third presence" but merely a prisoner of it.
2.3 Therapeutic goal: transcending the "third presence" through mutual recognition
If the "conquering third" is the dilemma in therapy, then the ultimate goal of analytic work is to find a way out of this fused, conquered state and to regain individual subjectivity.
target
"Successful analytical work involves the transcendence of the 'conquering third'". This is the core therapeutic action within this theoretical framework. The purpose of therapy is not to eliminate the "third presence" but to transform its "conquering" qualities into an experience that can be thought about and understood.
mechanism
This transcendence is achieved through "mutual recognition of the analyst and the analysand as independent subjects." In Mr. L's case, when the analyst was able to put into words their shared experience of suffocation, he did two things simultaneously: first, he acknowledged Mr. L's unspoken pain (acknowledging the other); second, by speaking, he separated himself from that experience and reestablished himself as an independent subject capable of thinking and feeling. It is this act of "acknowledging the independence of the other's thoughts while maintaining a connection with them" that breaks the closed cycle of the "conquering third".
Regaining subjectivity after transformation
The result of transcending the "third presence" is "the re-appropriation of their (transformed) individual subjectivities." Importantly, participants did not simply return to their previous state. They have been profoundly changed by the experience of living a "third presence" together. When one is "given back" to oneself by another, this is itself a creative act that shapes a "becoming for the first time, a more fully human, a more reflective subject." Mr. L learned to breathe underwater in his dreams, and instead of returning to land, he learned to survive in a new, once deadly element. This symbolizes that his subjectivity has been transformed and enriched, rather than simply repaired.
Part Three: Theoretical Mapping: Positioning the "Third Presence"
No important theoretical concept exists in isolation. In order to fully understand the connotation and significance of "third presence", it must be examined within a broader psychoanalysis ideological picture. This section aims to draw a theoretical map that clarifies the relationship between "third presence" and other core concepts in psychoanalysis (such as transference-countertransference, therapeutic framework), and carefully distinguishes key differences between it and different versions of the concept of "third" proposed by other theorists (such as Jessica Benjamin and Jacques Lacan). Through this comparison and positioning, we can more clearly grasp the uniqueness and contribution of Ogden's theory.
3.1 Beyond transference-countertransference
"Third Presence" is not simply a new term added to the traditional concept of transference-countertransference, but a fundamental reconstruction of the entire phenomenal field they describe.
a single intersubjective whole
Ogden explicitly redefined transference and countertransference, not as "separable entities arising in response to each other," but as "two aspects of a single intersubjective whole generated by the analytic pairing, experienced separately (and independently) by the analyst and the analysand." The "third presence" is exactly this "whole". In this framework, transference is no longer simply a repetition of the patient's past, and countertransference is no longer simply the analyst's reaction to such repetitions. Both are manifestations of the "third presence", a co-created and dynamic unconscious field, at the level of individual experience.
From "double psychology" to "co-creation"
Traditional transference-countertransference models often imply a "two-person psychology" perspective, in which one person's past is projected onto the other. The "Third Presence" model advances this perspective into the framework of "co-creation". The focus is on an emergent relational process that is "not clearly bound to or identifiable as 'belonging' to either the analyst or the analysand." The material of analysis is no longer simply attributed as "this is the patient's" or "this is the analyst's" but is understood as the product of this "third subject."
Countertransference as Entrance
As mentioned in Part 1, the status of countertransference, and especially of the analyst's musings, is radically changed. It is no longer just a response to transference, but an "indispensable path" to "understanding and interpreting the transference-countertransference" field. In other words, countertransference is the analyst's direct experience of the "third presence." The analyst uses his or her own feelings, fantasies, and bodily sensations to access and understand this co-created unconscious space.
3.2 Analysis of "Third Nature": Ogden, Benjamin and Lacan
In the psychoanalysis literature, "the third" is a concept that has been elaborated by many theorists from different angles, which can easily cause confusion. It is therefore crucial to carefully distinguish Ogden's "third presence" from Jessica Benjamin's "intersubjective third" and Jacques Lacan's symbolic "third."
• Ogden's "Analytical Third": This is an emergent, co-created, unconscious subject that arises from the interaction of the analytic dyad, particularly through the process of projective identification. It may be both generative and "conquering". It is a mental entity that actually "exists" during the analysis process.
• Jessica Benjamin's "Intersubjective Third": This is a developmental achievement that represents a "potential space." In this space, "a sense of connection with each other's ideas" and "acceptance of each other's independence and differences" can coexist. It is created through mutual recognition and "surrender" and is the goal of a healthy intersubjective process that aims to transcend the doer/done-to binary. It describes more the quality of a relationship than a psychological entity.
• Jacques Lacan's symbolic "third": the Name-of-the-Father, which represents law, culture and language. This "third" is structural and exists before the individual. It does not arise from the mother-infant binary relationship, but intervenes in it, giving it order through triangulation, thereby preventing it from falling into the imaginary relationship of symbiotic fusion. It is the symbolic order itself.
To demonstrate the differences between these concepts more clearly, the table below compares them along several core dimensions
Features
Thomas Ogden's "analytic third" Jessica Benjamin's "intersubjective third" Jacques Lacan's symbolic "third"
Origin
Emergence from the unconscious interactions of analytic dyads.
Achieved through a developmental process of mutual recognition and surrender.
exists prior to the duality as a symbolic order (language, law, culture).
nature
A co-created "third subjectivity" or psychological entity with a life of its own. It can be "conquering".
The quality/experience of a "potential space" or intersubjective relationship. A relationship status.
A structural principle, the "Name of the Father," introduces a symbolic dimension.
Function
Giving form to unformed experience; the medium of the analytical process itself. Therapeutic work involves transcending its conquering form.
Allow connection and separation to coexist; get rid of the "agent/passive" complementarity.
Separating the mother-infant dyad, preventing psychosis, and structuring the subject's relationship to reality and desire.
treatment goals
A transformed subjectivity is achieved through experiencing, symbolizing and ultimately transcending the "third presence" through mutual recognition.
Create and sustain a "thirdness" as a medium of authentic connection and recognition.
Place the subject appropriately in the symbolic order; analyze the relationship between the subject and the "third".
3.3 "Third Presence" and Therapeutic Framework
If the "third presence" is an invisible psychological space, then the therapeutic frame is the tangible structure that accommodates this space. There is a dialectical relationship between "container" and "contained object".
Frames as containers
"Analytical frame" or "therapeutic frame" refers to a series of stable factors that constitute a therapeutic situation, including fixed time, place, cost, analyst's neutral stance, etc. The function of this framework is to create a safe, secure, and protected space that is essential for the emergence and exploration of the "third presence." The framework establishes a clear boundary between the "inside" of therapy and the "outside world."
"Third Presence" as the Accommodated Object
The "third presence" is a dynamic unconscious process that unfolds within the analytic space created by the frame. It is an "invisible spiritual space that transcends the physical space in which it occurs." It is the stability, predictability, and safety provided by the framework that make it possible for analyst and patient to withstand the often chaotic, intense, and confusing experiences of the "third presence." Without a sturdy container, the dynamic, yet sometimes destructive, unconscious content cannot be safely experienced and transformed. Therefore, the framework is a prerequisite for the existence and work of the "third presence".
Part 4: Critique, Evolution and Future Vision
A viable theory lies not only in its explanatory power, but also in the critical thinking, subsequent development, and ability to respond to new challenges it triggers. Since the "Third Presence" theory was proposed, it has not only profoundly affected clinical practice, but also become a source of further theoretical exploration and cross-field application. This section will first examine the socio-historical critiques of Ogden's theory, then trace its evolution and application in different fields, and finally provide a comprehensive review of its lasting influence and future significance in contemporary psychoanalysis thought.
4.1 Social and historical criticism
It is an important critical perspective to examine psychoanalysis theory in the historical and cultural context in which it was produced. Some researchers have made a profound analysis of the "Third Presence" theory from this perspective, believing that it is not a universal and eternal psychological discovery, but a product of specific intellectual history and social social formations.
connection with romanticism
A key criticism has been that Ogden's theory bears striking conceptual similarities to the ideas of the German Romantic philosopher Friedrich Schelling. This similarity manifests itself in several ways: a conception of subjectivity as a creative act of self-positing; and a conception of a new, larger entity that emerges through a dialectical process. This connection shows that Ogden's theory is deeply rooted in the specific context of Western intellectual history. Its emphasis on creation, experience, and generative characteristics echoes the Romantic trend of thought' admiration for individual subjectivity and organic wholeness. This criticism is not intended to devalue the theory, but rather to position it from a purely clinical theory to a cultural product with a specific philosophical pedigree.
product of late capitalism
This criticism further extends to the socio-economic level, arguing that the theoretical model of the "third presence" reflects the internal logic of late capitalism. According to this analysis, the encounter of psychoanalysis is constructed as an "exchange process dependent on the production and consumption activities of the analyzed participants." In this model, "analytic work takes the form of the production and consumption of a 'third'" specifically through "the exchange of private contemplative experiences between analyst and analysand." This is a very challenging perspective, which interprets the profound psychotherapy process as the production and exchange of "psychological goods" that is isomorphic to the logic of consumer society. From this perspective, the "third presence", a space full of creative and transformative potential, may also be regarded as a psychological form that is in line with contemporary society's constant pursuit of novel experiences and personalized products.
4.2 Contemporary applications and extensions
The influence of the "Third Presence" theory has transcended the traditional psychoanalysis diagnosis and treatment room, and has been applied to a wider range of fields, and is facing new theoretical evolution with the development of technology.
organizational psychology
The concept has been successfully applied to the analysis of organizational change and dynamics. In organizational settings, the "third presence" is viewed as that psychological space that can "repair and integrate broken human systems." It represents the place where true understanding and change can occur when deeper emotional connections are established between members in dyads, groups, and communities. Consultants or leaders can use this concept to promote organizational health by focusing on and addressing the unspoken, co-created unconscious dynamics within the organization.
The "artificial third": the role of artificial intelligence in psychotherapy
A recent and far-reaching development is the conceptualization of generative AI (such as ChatGPT) as an "artificial third" in the therapeutic relationship. This raises a series of profound questions: How does a non-human entity reshape the intersubjective field? How does it challenge humanity's monopoly on language, empathy and understanding? When the operating logic of this "third" (algorithm, training data) is largely opaque, how can the ethical boundaries in treatment (such as autonomy, informed consent) be redefined? The emergence of the "artificial third" forces us to rethink the core nature of human interaction, consciousness, and therapeutic relationships. It also raises a new topic for the future development of the "Third Presence" theory.
4.3 Concluding synthesis: the lasting impact of the "third presence"
Taken together, Thomas Ogden's "Third Presence" theory has had a revolutionary impact on contemporary psychoanalysis thought and practice. It is not only an exquisite clinical tool, but also a new world view of psychological reality and the therapeutic process.
paradigm shift
The introduction of "third presence" marks the decisive shift in the psychoanalysis paradigm from "single-person psychology" to "double-person psychology" and profoundly places "intersubjectivity" at the core of the theory. It ultimately establishes the idea that psychological reality does not exist in isolation within individuals but is continuously co-created in relationships.
Redefining the analyst role
This theory completely reshaped the understanding of the role of the analyst. The analyst is no longer a detached, objective interpreter but an engaged co-participant. His entire being-including his personality, analytical style, life experiences, and especially his capacity for contemplation-became a central tool in therapy. This transition requires the analyst to develop a high level of self-awareness, a tolerance for uncertainty, and the courage to remain emotionally vulnerable and open.
a living dynamic process
Ultimately, the concept of "third presence" transforms psychoanalysis from a static archaeological process (excavating the past) into a living, fluid, and often surprising co-creation process. The goal of therapy is no longer just to gain "insight" but to generate new and more dynamic forms of subjective experience. It is not a theory about repairing trauma, but a theory about "becoming" - co-creating a new self in a profound encounter with the other, and in the process, making life itself more abundant and real.

The Grammar of Events: Actor-Generated Topology (AGT) and the Birth of the Postmodern Subject, Part II
AGT Part II tests event emergence through P4 Theater, Hamlet, The Matrix, Human Surrender, topological crisis, and fidelity.
The Grammar of Events: Actor-Generated Topology (AGT) and the Birth of the Postmodern Subject, Part II
The Emergence of Events
Emergence
Topological crisis, liminal space, betrayal, transition.
Part II: Theoretical Verification and Dialogue - Placing AGT in a Wider Constellation
Introduction
In Part I, like engineers drawing a blueprint, we systematically constructed the theoretical edifice of Actor-Generated Topology (AGT). We defined its core axioms, coding mechanisms, and dynamic model. But even the most perfect blueprint has to pass through actual construction and weather before its value can be proven.
The task of this part is to place this newly built theoretical edifice of AGT within a broader constellation of complex phenomena and deep thought, testing its structural firmness, explanatory generality, and dialogic potential. We will first return to AGT's native soil - P4 Theater - and anatomize how an event is concretely catalyzed and generated. We will then turn AGT's searchlight toward two cultural texts of very different styles but equal depth, Hamlet and The Matrix, using them to pressure-test its cross-textual explanatory force. Next, taking P4's own complex work Human Surrender as an example, we will show how AGT analyzes contemporary cross-media practice. Finally, we will place AGT within the coordinates of contemporary thought, entering an equal and critical dialogue with mainstream personality theory and post-structuralist philosophy, so as to mark its distinct theoretical niche through reference and collision.
Chapter III: The Genesis of Events - P4 as an Engineer of Topological Dissonance
Introduction
In Chapter II, we established AGT's core dynamic law: topological resonance and dissonance. We argued that any profound transformation of subjectivity arises from an irreconcilable topological dissonance between one's internal default code and the code of the situation one inhabits. Yet in everyday situations, such violent dissonance is rare. Social norms, personal habits, and psychological defenses together build a powerful buffer that keeps us, most of the time, running in a low-energy autopilot mode relatively resonant with the environment.
How, then, can a subversive event happen? The task of this chapter is to enter the concrete laboratory of P4 Theater and anatomize P4's engineering blueprint as an event catalyst. I will argue that P4's practice is neither mysterious art nor accidental improvisation. It is a precise topological engineering. Its core technique is the coordinated, extreme coding of the three layers of Situation E - rules r, space s, and network n - consciously and maximally designing topological dissonance with participants' everyday default codes, thereby pushing them into topological crisis and liminal space, and finally creating the ripest conditions for an event to emerge.
3.1 The Engineering of Topological Crisis: How P4 Systematically Designs Dissonance
Introduction: From Allowing Failure to Designing Failure
The prelude to an event must be a profound topological crisis. In everyday life, however, our internal default code is like an old soldier hardened by battle: it has developed extremely powerful psychological defenses, enough to help us avoid or normalize most direct collisions that might produce crisis. We are skilled at filtering information, maintaining social distance, and following scripts of etiquette in order to preserve a stable and safe inner world.
Many participatory art projects are satisfied with creating an environment that allows failure. They build a tolerant atmosphere and tell participants that it is fine to make mistakes. But that is often not enough. An actor attached to their default code has an entire operating system devoted to avoiding situations in which mistakes might happen.
P4 Theater's radicality lies in going far beyond allowing failure. Through a sophisticated social alchemy, it consciously and systematically designs failure for participants: that is, it designs an impasse in which their everyday default code will necessarily fail. It does not wait for crisis to occur; in an engineering sense, it catalyzes crisis. This engineering of topological dissonance is P4's core technology as an event catalyst. The construction of the impasse is not a single attack, but a carefully choreographed and escalating hunt.
3.1.1 Coding Rules r(p): Symbolic Subversion from Norm to Game
P4's first attack always points to the software layer of our internal operating system: the grammar of social interaction on which we rely. P4's core rules are essentially game rules, r(p), designed to systematically abolish and subvert the normative rules, r(n), that participants rely on in everyday life: one should greet people politely, should not interrupt others, should avoid embarrassing silence, and so on.
Case analysis: the apparently simple rule of remaining silent throughout is enormously subversive. It instantly abolishes language, humanity's most important and safest social tool. For an actor whose default code, in the Form dimension [II], relies on the Discipline [N] module ("I should say a few polite things according to etiquette") or the Lurker [V] module ("I can analyze and control the situation by asking questions"), the entire library of forms is suddenly emptied. Their preset program for how to act is completely invalidated.
Dynamic analysis: this mismatch of rule codes at the symbolic level directly attacks the participant's Form dimension [II]. The system can no longer call on its familiar [N] or [V] modules to formulate an action plan. This symbolic topological dissonance immediately triggers enormous inner anxiety: What should I do? Do I look stupid? It forces participants either into complete paralysis or into the risk of trying unfamiliar, bodily, intuitive Player [P] interaction.
3.1.2 Coding Space s(p): Physical Coercion from Convention to Chaos
P4's second attack points to the hardware layer of our operating system: our body and its relation to physical space. P4's choice of non-fixed sites, especially extreme spaces such as the 510 office, is a deliberate manipulation of spatial coding. It throws participants out of familiar conventional spaces, s(n), such as cafes and conference rooms, each with clear and predictable norms of use, and into a chaotic space, s(p).
Case analysis: the dense topology of space. In a sixteen-square-meter office, twenty strangers are forced into bodily proximity. This chaotic space, s(p), uses an irresistible physical force to dissolve the core strategy by which participants, in the Execution dimension [III], use the Lurker [V] module to maintain a safe distance.
Dynamic analysis: physical topological dissonance. Here, observation loses its detachment, because the object you observe is breathing next to your ear. Bodily boundaries are constantly infringed. Preverbal embodied signals - temperature, smell, slight muscular tension - replace language as the main channel of information exchange. This physical dissonance makes every attempt to gain safety through withdrawal futile. It forces every actor to exist in a present and interventionist mode.
3.1.3 Coding Network n(p)/n(v): Relational Reorganization from Dispersion to Radiation
P4's third attack points to the network interface of the operating system: the patterns through which we relate to other actors. P4's victim situation is an intricate switch in network coding.
Case analysis: the victim situation. At the beginning of an event, the relational network among participants is usually distributed, n(p): everyone is an isolated node. But when the Architect designates one participant through the rules as the victim, for example by requiring them to maintain a painful posture, the topology of the entire network is suddenly reconstructed into a radiating network centered on that victim, n(v).
Dynamic analysis: relational topological dissonance. In this new network topology, all other participants are forcibly placed in the position of observers. This directly challenges the Discipline [N] module that seeks safety by blending into the group, because now everyone's inaction is visible. At the same time, it sharply increases the ethical debt of the Lurker [V] module, because observation is no longer neutral; it becomes a cold form of complicity.
Section summary: P4's impasse is not a mysterious atmosphere, but a high-intensity field of topological crisis jointly constructed by the three codes of rule r(p), space s(p), and network n(v), and systematically dissonant with participants' everyday codes. Only at the moment when all default programs fail can a new space full of possibility open.
3.1.4 A Dialectical Supplement: P4 as a Model of Topological Flexibility
After anatomizing in detail how P4 systematically designs topological dissonance and manufactures crisis, we have to add a crucial dialectical point, in order to avoid reducing P4's practice too rigidly to a single violent aesthetic that only produces crisis.
If we treat P4's practice itself as a meta-actant, we find that it does not possess only one fixed [P]-type or [A]-type topological code. On the contrary, P4's practice is itself a model of high topological flexibility. Its strength lies in its ability to call flexibly on all four force modules according to different creative ideas [I], designing very different kinds of Situation E.
When its aim is rupture, it designs a Player [P]-led crisis laboratory. This is the mode analyzed in detail above, whose purpose is to induce topological transition.
When its aim is construction, it designs an Architect [A]-led co-creation workshop. For example, in the form-building phase of Human Surrender, the core is a rigorous Architect [A] process that organizes chaotic materials into a cross-media narrative network.
When its aim is reflection, it designs a Lurker [V]-led collective archive. In Love Drama, for example, by collecting audience narrative samples, it transforms the field into a Lurker [V] database for observing and analyzing contemporary emotional patterns.
When its aim is stabilization, it may even introduce a Discipline [N]-led ritual space. After many intense emotional experiences, P4 guides participants into a simple, Discipline [N]-style collective action or vocalization, providing a stable anchor for a temporary community that has just passed through a storm and helping it land softly.
Therefore, the engineering of dissonance analyzed in this section, although P4's most radical and subversive chemical weapon, is only one element in P4's large arsenal. P4's real essence does not lie in a preference for any single force such as chaos, but in its deep understanding and command of the full spectrum of mutual generation and dialectical tension between order [A/N] and chaos [P/V].

3.2 Liminal Space: Generating within Neither-This-Nor-That
When topological crisis successfully erupts and the old default codes by which participants maintain everyday identity collapse, the P4 field truly becomes an extraordinary liminal space, full of danger and creative potential. We need Victor Turner's core anthropological concept in order to define and describe this crucial intermediate state with precision.
Turner defines liminality as the threshold state in ritual when an individual has been stripped of an old social identity but has not yet acquired a new one: neither here nor there. It is a zone of suspension outside structure, betwixt and between structural positions, charged with sacred danger and creative potential. In P4's artificial liminal space, its distinctive topology and psychodynamics become clearly visible.
3.2.1 Suspended Structure: P4's Anti-Theater Techniques
The generation of liminal space first depends on the systematic suspension of everyday social structures. P4 accomplishes this through its core anti-theater techniques.
Breaking the fourth wall suspends the structural opposition between actor and watcher. In P4, there is no safe audience seat. Every body is potentially watching and being watched at once, making identity based on traditional theatrical roles impossible.
Nonprofessional participation suspends the structural opposition between professional and amateur. The value of participants' actions is no longer determined by theatrical skill, but by reality and presence. This creates an equality based on existence rather than technique.
Through these techniques, P4 creates a structural vacuum. No matter what social position participants occupy in the outside world, they are temporarily returned to naked, equal, pre-structural human material.
3.2.2 Quantum Superposition: Chaotic Activation of Internal Modules
When external structure is suspended, the actor's internal default code also becomes invalid. At this point, the inner operating system enters an extremely unstable state that we call quantum superposition.
Phenomenological description: at this stage, all four primary action-force modules inside the actor - A, N, P, and V - are activated at the same time. They no longer follow a default, orderly calling sequence, but collide and combine randomly. This is exactly the chaotic state experienced by many first-time P4 participants: excited and frightened, wanting to enter and wanting to flee.
A typical inner monologue might be: I should do something to break the silence, but I do not know the rules and I am afraid of doing it wrong. I want to first see what others do, Lurker [V], but if I can come up with a good idea, maybe I can take hold of the situation, Architect [A]. These four contradictory impulses emerge simultaneously in a single instant, producing temporary paralysis of action and a sharp rise of internal energy.
3.2.3 The Budding of Communitas: Connecting through Shared Vulnerability
Yet it is exactly this apparently chaotic and paralyzed stage that creates the conditions for a new and profound human connection. Turner points out that in liminal space, relations among people also change qualitatively. They are no longer defined by social structure, but enter a direct, equal, affectively connected state of communitas.
Communitas in P4: within the P4 field, once everyone has been stripped of everyday masks and faces an unsettling impasse full of uncertainty, a sense of recognition based on shared vulnerability begins to germinate.
The root of connection: here, connection no longer depends on shared interests or social background, but on something more originary: a glance asking for help, an awkward bodily contact, a common wordless silence. Inside this structural vacuum, a direct I-you human relation beyond social role becomes possible. This budding communitas is the crucial emotional hotbed from which events can emerge.
Chapter summary: by systematically suspending external social structures, P4 introduces participants into a liminal space in which the inner operating system enters quantum superposition. This anxious, seemingly chaotic middle ground is precisely a creative hotbed. By forcing participants to face their fundamental inner tensions and begin weaving the first threads of communitas through shared vulnerability, it prepares the necessary conditions for the next phase: the brilliant emergence of micro-events.
3.3 The Emergence of Micro-Events and What Follows
In the chaos and tension of liminal space, amid the faint spark of communitas, a micro-event may - though need not - emerge. Here I strictly adopt Alain Badiou's definition of the event and miniaturize it: it is a ruptural emergence that cannot be explained or contained by the established rules of the situation, and that opens truth for those present. It is the instant in which the impossible becomes possible.
3.3.1 The Occurrence of an Event: An Unforeseeable Grace
In the P4 field, this micro-event may take many forms
A successful resolution of an ethical game: as mentioned repeatedly above, an intervener bravely breaks an impasse and rescues the victim in an unexpected way, neither simply attacking nor submitting, instantly reshaping the ethical structure of the field.
A collective, wordless bodily resonance: without any command, all participants suddenly enter the same rhythm of breathing or a harmonious pattern of collective movement, as if a single organism had awakened.
A sentence spoken into the right silence, changing the whole atmosphere: after a long silence, a participant may say something extremely plain that nevertheless strikes everyone's heart. Like an act of naming, it gives the entire chaotic experience a new shared meaning.
The occurrence of this event has the character of grace. It cannot be fully designed or predicted by the Architect, nor can it be forced by the pure will of the Player. It is a crystal accidentally and almost miraculously generated through the complex interaction of many actors, human and nonhuman, inside the chaos of liminal space. It is not anyone's work; it is the field's self-generation.
3.3.2 The Consequence of an Event: The Opening of a New Truth
The emergence of this event marks the birth of something truly new. Like lightning, it instantly illuminates the falsity of the situation, for example the default belief that strangers are necessarily alienated from one another. In a profound event of collective resonance, that belief is proven false. The event gives everyone present a new reference point with which to anchor their own existence. It opens the possibility of a new truth: we strangers can connect this deeply. The question is no longer simply, How should we act? It becomes a more decisive question: will we remain faithful to the event that has just happened?
3.3.3 The Birth of a Community of Comrades in Adventure
After an event occurs, those who choose to remain faithful to the truth it opens constitute a real community. In P4's context, this is not a therapeutic community seeking comfort and belonging. It is closer to a group of comrades in adventure.
Shared secret: they have witnessed a miracle together, a secret that cannot be fully understood by the language of the external situation. This shared secret is their strongest bond.
Shared mission: their connection is based on a common, perhaps wordless mission: after returning to the everyday world that does not believe in miracles, how can they continue to guard and practice the fragile truth opened by the event?
This community of comrades in adventure is the most precious thing P4, as an event catalyst, can generate.
3.4 The Birth of the Subject: Three Responses to the Event
In section 3.3, we witnessed the brilliant emergence of the micro-event as grace. Yet the occurrence of an event does not by itself guarantee any lasting transformation. After lightning, night may return immediately. The true force of an event lies not in the instant of its occurrence, but in how it is maintained and extended by what comes after.
The event is like a stone thrown into a still lake. It breaks the stability of the situation, and by its undeniable presence sends a silent but absolute summons to every actor involved. This summons does not demand one specific action; it demands an ethical stance. How an actor responds to that summons determines not only their future trajectory, but also retroactively defines the meaning of the event itself. It is at this moment of response that a subject in the strict sense - an existence no longer fully defined by the situation, acting for a truth - becomes possible.
I argue that in the face of the event's summons, there are three fundamental and mutually exclusive postures of response: reaction, betrayal, and fidelity.
3.4.1 Posture One: Reaction - Returning to a More Rigid Entrenchment
Reaction is a posture that tries to deny the occurrence of the event, normalize it, and translate it back into the old language of the situation.
Phenomenological description: after a deep collective resonance in P4, a reactive participant may immediately say, This is just some kind of group psychological effect; psychology has explained it already, or, It is no big deal; everyone will forget it tomorrow. Through an existing cynical knowledge framework - a defensive use of the Lurker [V] module - they dissolve the event's singular and subversive kernel of truth.
Inner dynamics: this posture is born from fear. The actor cannot bear the uncertainty brought by the event, nor its fundamental challenge to their existing worldview. To preserve the stability of the inner operating system, the default code, they retreat into an even more rigid and defensive entrenchment. It is a defensive refusal of the new, and its result is to miss the possibility of topological transition while possibly reinforcing the old code.
3.4.2 Posture II: Betrayal
Treason is a more complex posture. At first, it was attracted and inspired by the "event", even when it claimed to be "faithful" to it, but retreated from the old logic in the face of the hardships that followed it, which sustained this "truth" in the daily "situation".
Secular description: A participant who experienced deep connections at the P4 site and returned to everyday life, faced with the apathy of his colleagues or family contradictions, may find it too costly and too "idealistic" to sustain that "real". He/she may try to practice at some point (e.g. through a genuine dialogue), but after a setback quickly chooses to give up and to put on a daily social "mask".
Inside dynamics: this is an opportunistic gesture. The actors turned back and forth between the passionate possibilities opened up by the "event" and the customary sense of security provided by the "situation", and ultimately chose the latter. He/she betrays the possibility opened up by "events", which often lead to a long and endless sense of inherent conflict and guilt, making it more unstable to expand the code.
3.4.3 Posture III: "Fidelity" opens up a difficult "sustain"
Faith is the only truly creative gesture that can lead to the birth of a new subject matter. The subject acknowledges the occurrence of the "event" and makes a fundamental determination that this "event" will be used as a new "justification" or "reference point" in all future operations.
Secular description: a participant loyal to the P4 "event" who returns to everyday life and who does not naively think that the world has changed. Instead, he/she would use that "real connection" as a yardstick to look at and challenge the hypocrisy of everyday relationships and try to build new, small but real connections. His/her actions have since been "lighted" by that "event".
Inner dynamics: this is a gesture that combines love, love for the truth of events, and courage, determination to bear the consequences. The so-called "loyalty" is not blind to a particular dogma, but an ongoing and difficult process of "surrendering". In every new "situation", the subject must constantly think and practice: "What does that `event' mean to this concrete action of my own today?" It is in this process that a `subject of the Event' was forged.

Chapter V: Positioning of AGT in the system of theoretical coordinates
Introduction
Actor-Generated Topology (AGT) was not born out of a theoretical vacuum. It is a creative response to the existing legacy of the theory of personality and action, its value and originality, which must be demonstrated in dialogue and collision with established frameworks. The birth of a new theory, like the brightness of a new star in the universe, can be precisely located in its coordinates and brightness only by cross-referencing with other stars.
The task of this chapter is to place AGT, the new star, in a system of theoretical coordinates consisting of three mainstream personality classification schemes (MBTI, Big Five, Type IX) and a whole post-structured ideology cluster (ANT, Deleuze, Lacan, Badiou), for an in-depth comparative and critical analysis. We will argue that AGT is not intended to simply "replace" these classical models, but rather to provide a unique insight into personality and action from a completely new dimension based on "genetic grammar", thereby deeply complementing, challenging and ultimately enriching our existing theoretical landscape.
5.1 Dialogue with the dominant personality theory: Open the "black box" and explore mechanisms for generation
Actor-Generated Topology (AGT) is not intended to launch a zero-sum game to completely negate the great value of mainstream personality theory. On the contrary, AGT recognizes and respects the contribution of each model in its own dimensions: MBTI provides a easily transmitted classification of cognitive preferences, the five largest individuals provide scientificly rigorous behavioural characterizations, and the nine individuals provide in-depth motivational insight.
However, AGT has opened up an entirely new analytical dimension through its unique "generated grammar" perspective. It occupies an ecological position where other models are not systematically explored. This section will provide an in-depth comparative and critical analysis of how AGT responds to the core challenges left by these classic models: How it counters the static labelling of MBTI; how it opens the descriptive "black box" of the five large persons by means of a mechanism of generation; and how it provides an analytical "external scaffold" for the in-depth motives of the nine-person personality, which are hard to prove.
5.1.1 AGT vs. MBTI: from "personal card" to "operational production process"
Core differences: process orientation vs. result orientation - verbs and terminology
The fundamental difference between Miles-Briggs type indicator (MBTI) and AGT lies in its core philosophical questions. The core of MBTI is classification and attribution, and it tries to answer the question "What are you?". It provides a static, noun-like label (e.g. "INTJ") that summarizes the long-term results of individuals' cognitive preferences. It depicts a relatively stable personal "portrait". And the core of AGT is generation and process, and it tries to answer the question, "How did your actions come about?" It provides a dynamic, verbed flowchart (e.g. [A-A-N-V]). AGT doesn't care what you end up with, but how you become every move you make. If MBTI provides a "personal identity card" that facilitates rapid mutual recognition, then AGT provides a detailed "production process statement" on how this "business card" is designed, printed and used in different social contexts.
AGT's Advantage One: Paradoxical Legitimacy and Structural Interpretation
The dichotomy logic of MBTI, while bringing clarity, has also paid a great price - it is difficult to deal with the deep contradictions in the body. How can a person who has been convicted of being "thinking" make decisions that are "emotional" in certain circumstances? In the context of MBTI, this is often seen as an uncontrolled outbreak of its "disadvantaging function" and as an expression of "in maturity" or "underdevelopment". However, in the framework of AGT, contradictions are no longer a "defect" to be overcome, but rather the normality of the system, which is the core source of its complexity and vitality. Through its multi-dimensional code structure, AGT provides a legal and structural explanation for this contradiction.
For example, let's analyze an actor whose name is "A-V-P-A"
Its conceptual dimension [A] (architects) may be extremely rational and programmatic, pursuing a clear and orderly goal (T/J qualities close to MBTI).
The form dimension [V] (scrambling) is expressed in the tendency to avoid risks (a rational extraction) through extensive observation and information gathering when planning.
However, its implementation dimension [P] (player) may be impulsive, emotional and even unconventional (f/P qualities close to MBTI).
Ultimately, its receiving dimension [A] (architect) will try to re-integrate this contradictory operation into a rational and structured narrative. The AGT clearly reveals that the actor's "reasonable" and "emotional" are not mutually exclusive "types", but rather the different energy modules that are called upon in the different dimensions of the process of generating its actions. His inner conflict was not because he was "not enough T" or "not enough J", but because of his [concept A] desire for order and the confusion impulse of [implement P], which was an eternal and dramatic structural tension. AGT has moved from a psychological problem that needs to be "corrected" to a dynamic structure that can be analysed and understood.
AGT's Advantage Two: Beyond Types, Seeing Individuals in Situations
MBTI's greatest risk lies in its "barnum effect" and its tendency to label. Once classified as "INTJ", an individual may act unwittingly according to the description of the label (self-fulfillment prophecy) or use the label to find an excuse to avoid a mission that he is not good at ("I am an I, so I cannot speak publicly"), thereby limiting his possibilities. AGT, for its part, has liberated individuals from the type of cage through its large volume of 256 prototypes and its dynamic concept of "topological resonance". It recognizes that a person may have a "default code", but emphasizes its enormous potential to "scramble" by using non-default modules under different situations under E pressure.
It does not see a fixed "INTJ", but rather an actor who may have set up by default [A-A-V-V] (a typical "reflective strategist" that fits the description of INTJ).
But AGT is more interested that in a "crisis" situation like P4 Theater, the [A-A-V-V] may be forced to make a leap forward from [V] to [P] in the implementation dimension in order to respond to a sudden state of emergency, showing an unexpected, improvising, life-threatening operation of his own.
Summary: By deconstructing static types as a dynamic, inherently contradictory process that can "leap" in circumstances, AGT provides deeper and more empowering theoretical tools for understanding the complexity, plasticity and context of the human personality. It encourages us not to ask "Who I am" but "Who else I can be".
5.1.2 AGT vs. Largest Five Personalities: from "Contribution List" to "Cooking Cooking Book"
Core differences: Generating models vs. Descriptive models - Big Five / OCEAN Model, which opens the "black box", are among the brightest results of contemporary academic psychology and are the "gold standard" for personality research. Through rigorous terminology assumptions and large-scale cross-cultural factor analysis, it has been able to extract five stable personality dimensions: experiential openness, due diligence, Extraversion, Amity and Neuroticism. Its excellent scientific rigour and robust predictive effectiveness make it the cornerstone of understanding the differences in human behaviour. However, the top five are an excellent descriptive model. It's like the chemical cyclical table of elements, which tells you very precisely what the composition of the "personal element" of a person who is "highly due diligence, low-extrapolity" is, and on that basis predicts his possible behavioural tendencies in various situations. However, it is, to a large extent, a "black box" - it explains how these "elements" interact, combine and ultimately generate a specific action with less capacity. It provides a list of the "constituents" of the personality, but it does not provide the "cooking" of these elements in a dynamic process of life, in which "cooking" is a complete "cooking".
AGT's Advantage One: Explaining the phenomenon of homogeneis
AGT, on the other hand, is a production model whose central purpose is to open the "black box" and provide it. 5.1.3 AGT vs. Type IX personality: from "the abyss of motivation" to "the grammar of action"
Core differences: starting point for analysis - invisible "why" vs. Visible "how"
Enneagram is a deep personality system rooted in ancient wisdom and enriched in modern psychology. What is unique is that it does not stop with the appearance of behaviour, but rather points directly to the invisible inner engine of each type of behaviour - "core fear", "core desire" and "core weakness".
The starting point for the nine personality is the intrinsic, a priori "motive": it tries to answer the ultimate question: "Why did you do it?" It believes that it is understandable to understand the root causes of all external behaviour when one's core fears are understood (for example, the core fear of Observer No. 5 is "incompetence, ignorance"). The starting point for AGT is an external, observable "flow of action": AGT has suspended its quest for the ultimate "why". It does not predetermine any a priori "core fear" or "desir", but analyses an individual in [Idea-Form-Execution-Reception], like a linguist who analyses unknown languages. The observed and documented patterns of behaviour displayed in these four dimensions in order to infer their intrinsic operating logic in reverse. It answers: "How do you do this?"
AGT's Advantage One: Providing an "extraordinary structure" for "motives"
Instead of denying the existence of deep motives, AGT provides these invisible "motives" with an analytical "extranometric structure". According to AGT, the "core fear" or "core desire" of an actor is necessarily reflected in a systematic and identifiable pattern in its combination of extended codes. Let's take the example of the Watcher of the 9th personality. Its core fears are "incompetence, ignorance" and its core desires are "incompetent and knowledgeable". The AGT code clearly "translates" the core motivation of the 5th to "program" its entire operating system.
The precision of distinguishing subtypes: AGT can also more precisely divide subtypes of the same nine personality type. For example, the code of another personality number 5 may be [V-A-A-V]. AGT clearly reveals that it also stems from the fear of "countering ignorance", the path by which the two personality 5 "examining" it can be a purely inward "understanding" or a very structural "creation".
AGT's Advantage Two: Universal Syntax: Beyond Human Centralism
The nine personality is strictly limited to the deep psychological and spiritual dimensions of human beings. The grammatical framework of AGT, which is derived from the web theory of its actors (ANT), naturally has the potential to transcend anthropocentricism. AGT analyses not the "single", but the "grammatic of action", which is available to any "actant" capable of implementing the sequence of actions.
We can do the same thing by "expanding code" for an organization, an art project or even an artificial intelligence
A rigid, bureaucratic company whose code might be [N-N-N-N]. Its "core fear" is "disturbed and out of control".
A radical and mistested start-up enterprise whose code may be [P-A-P-P]. Its "core desire" is "subversive and growing".
A large language model AI whose code may be close to [V-N-A-N]. Its "core motivation" is defined by its program as "to generate the most relevant answers on the basis of given data".
Summary: If the nine-person personality provides a deep "motive map" of the internal dynamics of the human soul, then AGT provides an accurate set of "actional syntax" about how this map was drawn in the real world. By shifting the focus of analysis from the invisible "why" to the visible "how", AGT not only enhances the objectivity of analysis but also extends the application of the personality theory from the individual human being to all complex systems that can act.
5.2 Resonance with post-structuralism: as a interlocutor, not a cornerstone
Actor-Generated Topology (AGT), although an independent theoretical system dedicated to the construction of a universal "action syntax", was born out of the "air of thought" provided by the forefront of contemporary philosophical thinking. AGT is not a simple "application" or "derivative" of these thoughts. On the contrary, the relationship between AGT and them is a profound mutual interpretation and questioning. This section will clarify the complex resonance between AGT and several key thinkers of post-structuralism, but will always insist on the theoretical thrust of AGT - they are "interlocutors" rather than "legislators" of AGT. In this dialogue, AGT will demonstrate how it has "operationalized" these profound philosophical concepts into a set of analytical tools and, conversely, used its own grammar to ask them new questions.

AGT's most direct theoretical bloodline from Bruno Latour's ANT. AGT fully inherited ANT's "relationship theory" (action before essence), the concept of "actant" (extensive symmetry between humans and non-humans) and the importance attached to "assemble" (e.g. situation E). It can be said that the whole world view of AGT is based on the post-humanism cornerstone of ANT. However, AGT also completed a necessary "creative betrayal" of ANT. The ANT of Latur, to a large extent, is a "external" descriptive science. It is extremely good at "tracing" and "characterizing" how an existing network of heterosexual actors is assembled. However, it often maintains a methodological distance from the "inner" and contradictory "black box" within the network, especially among human actors. It is here that the AGT theory of "events". It boldly claims that the "inline black box" itself is equally open to learning and networking. AGT is an attempt to "microstrate" and "internalize" the ambitious sociological analysis tool of ANT to analyse the networks within individual actors (and their combinations). It tries to answer that little ANT question: how does an actor "generate" his tendency to engage in outside network formation?

5.2.3 Dialogue with LAC and "enabling"
If Deleuze is the "sult mate" of AGT, Lacan is its "hard mentor". Lacan's theory, which injects deep, negative dimensions into AGT's seemingly fluid course of action, is about "Lack", "Jouissance" and "the Real".
