Introduction
1.1 Origin of research: P4 Theater as a "problem"
On the map of contemporary Chinese drama, the ten-year practice of P4 Theater (2015-2025) constitutes a unique and difficult-to-classify "problematic" existence. It is not a traditional theater troupe with a fixed cast and performance venue, but more like a mobile, project-centered art laboratory and social energy aggregate. Its uniqueness is clearly reflected on multiple levels: it wanders around abandoned factories, offices, park lawns and even online spaces, taking the unstable field itself as the core element of creation; it is open to society for recruitment, and the identities of participants are constantly switching between audiences, creators, and actors, making the generation process of the work full of uncertainty; most importantly, it repeatedly emphasizes the capture of "truth", the embrace of "failure", and the dissolution of all established authority in its discourse and practice. In the concluding article, its founder He Fa described it as a generated university, a winding maze, and a hard drive engraved with life. This poetic summary exactly reflects the complexity and non-fixedness of its form.
Facing such a practice form as P4 Theater, the traditional drama analysis framework seems to be stretched thin. Neither the "script-centered theory" that focuses on the text nor the "director-centered theory" that emphasizes the authority of the director can explain the decentralized and co-created production model of p4. Even the recently emerged theories of Participatory Art and Immersive Theater often encounter difficulties when facing p4. Mainstream immersive theater often strives to provide consumers with a carefully designed and smooth "experience", while p4's practice is full of rough textures, uncomfortable tension, and even treats "errors" and "failures" as inherent components of its methodology. Therefore, P4 Theater is not only an art case worth studying, but also constitutes a "question" that challenges the existing theoretical framework: How does P4 Theater reconstruct the relationship between creators, participants and performance space through its unique practice, and in the process generate a new and instantaneous community? Behind its seemingly chaotic and even contradictory operations, is there an inherent generation mechanism that can be analyzed?
1.2 Core argument: topological transformation from position to relationship
In response to the above questions, this study puts forward a core argument: the key to understanding the revolutionary practice of P4 Theater lies in completing a fundamental shift in analytical perspective, that is, from a "Position" topology based on fixed identity to a "Relation" topology based on dynamic connections.
The underlying logic of traditional drama analysis is a "positional ontology" - it presupposes a series of stable social "positions" such as "writer", "director", "actor", "audience", etc., and the relationship between them is determined by these preset positions. Your identity determines your actions. The practice of p4 subverts this logic and presents the characteristics of a "relational ontology": in a carefully designed field, your current actions, who (or what) you choose to connect with, and the way you connect, in turn define your function and temporary "identity" at the moment. Your actions define who you are.
To clearly illustrate this topological transformation, this study will construct a two-level theoretical framework. At the macro-ontological level, this article will introduce Bruno Latour's Actor-Network Theory (ANT), viewing the p4 field as a heterogeneous network "assembled" by human and non-human actors-including participants, space, objects, rules, light, sound, etc. At the micro level of analysis, this article will propose an original analysis tool - the "architect-NPC-player-peeper" four-element dynamic model. The model is not a fixed identity label, but four fluid "functional positions" that actors in a network may occupy. By tracking individuals' "jumps" between these functional positions, and how nonhuman actors enable or impede these transitions, we will be able to reveal the sophisticated, self-generated network dynamics hidden beneath P4 Theater's seemingly chaotic surface.
1.3 Research methods and significance
This study will adopt an interdisciplinary and comprehensive research method, mainly including
Theoretical construction: Integrate and develop actor network theory, Lacanpsychoanalysis, ritual theory and participatory art criticism to form an original, multi-level analytical framework.
Text analysis: Conduct an in-depth interpretation of textual materials such as recruitment copywriting, creative self-narratives, participant feedback, and interview records published publicly over the past ten years in P4 Theater, using them as the key entrance to its internal operating logic and discourse system.
Case ethnographic analysis: Select typical cases such as the evolution of "510 Space" to conduct detailed, ethnographic micro-analysis to confirm and enrich the theoretical model with embodied experience and specific situations.
The significance of this study is reflected in the following two levels
Theoretical significance: First of all, this study attempts to provide a new analytical framework for participatory art and experimental theater research that goes beyond aesthetic judgment and phenomenon description and has sociological and philosophical depth. Secondly, by carefully applying ANT theory to artistic practice cases, this study will promote the application and development of ANT in the field of humanities and art. Finally, it is committed to promoting interdisciplinary dialogue in theater theory and sociology, psychoanalysis and other fields, and exploring new possibilities for artistic research.
Practical significance: An in-depth analysis of P4 Theater can provide other experimental and community art groups with reference models of organization, creation and mobilization. More importantly, in the context of globalized urbanization and increasing social atomization, p4's exploration of how to "generate connections" and how to build a "community of losers" provides valuable practical reference and profound social enlightenment for us to rethink the possibilities of contemporary youth's public life, the nature of social relations, and the liberating role that art can play.
1.4 Overview of thesis structure
This paper is divided into four chapters in addition to the introduction and conclusion.
The first chapter will systematically build the theoretical framework of this article. On the basis of a critical review of traditional theater topology, actor network theory will be introduced as a "meta-theory", and the "quaternary model" as a core analytical tool will be elaborated on, while defining the functions of "interpretive lenses" such as Lacan, Turner, and Bishop.
Chapter 2 will focus on the function of "architect" and analyze how p4 completes the initial "assembly" and "problematization" of the entire actor network through the politics of rules, space, and recruitment.
Chapter 3 will go deep into the dynamic generation process of the network, using the "quaternary model" to trace how NPCs catalyze, how players play, and ultimately the complete "translation" chain that leads to the emergence of "community".
Chapter 4 will enter the level of critical reflection and explore the "ethics of failure" in p4 practice, the regeneration of new power, and the possible ethical risks in the pursuit of "truth."
Through the above progressive analysis, this study hopes to provide a comprehensive interpretation of the complex cultural phenomenon of P4 Theater with both theoretical depth and empirical details.
Chapter 1 Theoretical Framework: Assembling an Analysis Toolbox
In order to effectively analyze the complex practice of P4 Theater, we must first get rid of the inertial constraints of traditional theater theory and actively "assemble" a more adaptable and penetrating theoretical toolbox. The purpose of this chapter is to systematically construct this theoretical framework consisting of three levels: "metatheory", "analytical tools" and "interpretive lens". It will first conduct a critical review of traditional theater's "position"-based topology to establish the starting point of our research; then, introduce actor-network theory (ANT) as the ontological foundation of the entire study; on top of this, elaborate on our original "four-dimensional dynamic model" as a core analytical tool; and finally, explicitly integrate the theories of Lacan, Turner, and Bishop as an interpretive lens to deepen the analysis of specific issues.
2.1 The Specter of "Position": A Critical Review of Traditional Theater Topologies of Power
The internal structure of traditional drama, no matter how changeable its aesthetic style, often follows a stable social topology based on "position". This topology is defined by a linear, hierarchical chain of power: screenwriter → director → actor → audience. In this chain, each role is assigned a relatively fixed "position", which determines its function, scope of power, and relationship with other positions. The screenwriter is the source of meaning, the director is the authoritative interpreter, the actor is the faithful executor, and the audience is the passive and safe receiver. In terms of physical space, this power topology is strengthened through the binary opposition of "stage-auditorium" and the insurmountable boundary of the "fourth wall".
However, analysis of P4 Theater must be wary of the oversimplified assertion that it completely "eliminates" position. In fact, before entering the p4 field, participants have already been engraved with various stubborn social "positions" - their class identity, educational background, gender temperament, cultural capital, etc. These pre-existing "positions" are like "ghosts" and will not disappear completely due to an artistic experience. They profoundly influence how individuals engage, their preferences for building relationships, and their sense of safety in the field. Therefore, the core argument of this study is not that p4 has created a "positionless" utopia, but rather points out more precisely: p4's practice consciously suspends, disturbs, and problematizes these pre-positioned and solidified social "positions" through a set of exquisite mechanisms. It creates an "exceptional state" in which "relationship" can temporarily gain priority over "position", thereby providing the possibility for the generation of new subjectivity and sociality.
2.2 Relational ontology: introducing actor network theory (ANT)
To understand how "relationships" gain priority, Bruno Latour's actor-network theory (ANT) provides us with the most fundamental "meta-theoretical" support. The revolutionary nature of ANT lies in its "generalized symmetry principle". It refuses to pre-divide the world into two realms: "human/society" and "nature/matter". Instead, it advocates treating all beings that can "make a difference" - whether human or non-human - as equal "actants". The so-called "society" or any order is not a pre-existing background, but a fragile and dynamic "Network" that is "assembled" by these heterogeneous actors through constant alliances, negotiations, and struggles through a process called "Translation."
Applying ANT to the analysis of P4 Theater means that we will no longer regard space, objects, and rules as passive "environments" or "props", but as actors as important as human participants.
The space itself (such as the smallness of the 510 office) enforces interpersonal distance by its physical properties.
A rule (such as "You can pause at any time") authorizes or prohibits specific behavior.
An object (such as a chair) "invites" or "rejects" certain postures by its form.
The perspective of ANT provides the ontological cornerstone for our transformation "from position to relationship". It allows us to see that the field of p4 is not a container in which "people" move, but a constantly generated network of relationships woven by humans and non-humans. Analyzing p4 is to track the assembly process of this network.
2.3 The Quaternary Model as a Microscope: Architect, NPC, Player and Peeper
If ANT provides a world view, then we need a specific "microscope" to observe the microscopic world of p4. To this end, this study constructed an original analysis tool: the "architect-NPC-player-peeper" four-element dynamic model. The four roles in this model are not fixed identities but functional positions that any human actor in the network may temporarily occupy
Architect: The designer and founder of the network. Its function is to complete the "Problematisation" of the network by setting rules, transforming space, and issuing recruitment before the event begins, and injects unstable "potential energy" into the entire field.
NPC (Non-Player Character): The catalyst and stabilizer of the network. Usually played by a core group of members who perform simple, repetitive tasks. Its function is to initiate events, break deadlocks, and serve as a predictable variable to "interessement" other actors into the network.
Player: The core builder of the network. They are those participants who have accepted the network "contract" and actively interact, game, and create. They are actors who have been "enrolled" and successfully "mobilized" (Mobilisation), and the formation of the community mainly occurs among them.
Peeper: The boundaries and tensions of the Internet. They are those players who try to maintain their traditional audience position but find themselves in an awkward position due to topological changes. Their "non-participation" is an action in itself, and their "gaze" constitutes pressure on players and maintains the dynamic tension of the network.
The key to this model is its dynamic nature. Individuals can continuously "jump" between these four functional positions, and it is this fluidity that constitutes the internal driving force for the continuous self-generation of P4 Theater network topology.
2.4 Interpretive Lens: The Intervention of Lacan, Turner and Bishop
Based on the analytical tools of ANT's meta-theory and four-element model, we introduce three "interpretive lenses" to provide in-depth explanations of specific observed phenomena, thereby building a multi-level theoretical collaboration system.
Jacques Lacan's psychoanalysis: When we observe the intense anxiety in the p4 field, the obsessive pursuit of the "real" and the pressure caused by the "gaze", Lacan's theory will provide key explanatory power. Its concepts of the Real (the Real), Gaze and the Big Other will help us understand the deep psychodynamic and ethical dimensions of p4 practice.
Victor Turner's Ritual Theory: Turner's theory is indispensable when we try to define the nature of the "community" generated by p4. The concepts of liminality and communitas can accurately describe the temporary, equal, strong emotional connection state that breaks the daily social structure.
Claire Bishop's Participatory Art Criticism: Bishop's critical framework provides a powerful weapon when we need to distinguish p4's practice from other contemporary participatory arts. Her theory helps us discern the essential difference between p4's practice and those "artificial hells" that she criticizes as "experience consumption", thus highlighting p4's ethical seriousness and social criticism.
To sum up, the theoretical toolbox assembled in this chapter aims to establish a comprehensive research framework that has both a grand ontological vision and fine micro analysis tools, as well as a profound interpretive lens. It will guide us in the following chapters to launch a systematic and in-depth topological exploration of the complex practice of P4 Theater.
Chapter 2 The "Architect's" Blueprint: Rules, Space and the Politics of Recruitment
From the perspective of actor-network theory, the formation of any network begins with a "translation" process initiated by one or more core actors. In the practice of P4 Theater, we summarize the function of this initial stage as the function of "Architect". This chapter will focus on this function and explore how p4 lays the foundation for its network topology through careful rule design, strategic use of space, and unique recruitment politics, and completes the initial "Problematisation" of participants. This is not a simple technical preparation process, but a foundational action full of power, desire and political implications. It prescribes the "laws of the game" and the boundaries of possibility for the entire field.
3.1 Groundbreaking: Recruitment as "problematization"
The network assembly of P4 Theater does not begin the moment participants step into the physical space, but begins when its recruitment copy is released in the public domain. These texts, whether posted on social media or spread through specific communities, constitute the first step in the formation of the network - "problematization" in the ANT sense. The core of "problemization" is to raise a "problem that must be solved through me" (Obligatory Passage Point, OPP). p4's recruitment text attracts and screens its initial actors by constructing such an OPP.
By analyzing p4's recruitment texts over the years, we can discover several typical strategies of "problemization"
Constructing a "puzzle": A title such as "ComeP4 TheaterPlant Your Seed | A Journey from Mystery to History" does not provide clear performance information, but proposes a "puzzle" full of mystery and unknowns, packaging the art event into a "mysterious journey" that requires the participants' personal investment to solve.
Appealing to "trauma" and "desire": Recruitment such as "A centrist self-help guide for accusing love after failure" or "Drama and Fear | "Personal Chronicles - Dedicating Our Future"" directly touches on the common emotional dilemmas and existential anxieties of contemporary urban youth. It defines the p4 field as a "safe" space where personal trauma can be processed and desires that have no place to release, thereby attracting those with such emotional needs.
Issue "challenges" and "commitments": "p4X Challenge Recruitment", "Come and be the torch that ignites the fireworks of occasional sequence combinations!", etc., with a radical and challenging attitude, summoning participants who are eager to take risks and seek breakthroughs. What it promises is not a comfortable "watching" but a transformative experience of "becoming".
It is worth noting that this process of "problematization" is inherently political. It does not treat everyone equally. Its discourse system (such as the frequent use of terms such as "generation," "disenchantment," and "community") and emotional appeals have invisibly constructed an invisible "entry threshold." It is more likely to attract young intellectuals or literary lovers who have certain cultural capital, some understanding of experimental art, and a specific emotional structure. Therefore, when the "architect" laid the foundation, he had already unconsciously delineated an initial, homogeneous boundary for this seemingly open community.
3.2 "Rules" and "space" as core actors
When participants are "problematized" by recruitment copywriters and enter the field, they immediately encounter the two most powerful inhuman actors: rules and space. In the practice of p4, these two are endowed with strong initiative by the "architect". They are no longer passive backgrounds, but the core force that actively shapes the relationship network.
Rules as actors: The rules of p4 are usually announced at the beginning in the form of a verbal contract, which is characterized by simplicity and fundamentality. For example, "There are no fixed seats here", "You can remain silent, but your silence will be seen", "This is a place without a 'fourth wall'". The function of these rules is to
Authorize: The rule "You can pause the event at any time" gives each participant unprecedented power and breaks the director's absolute authority.
Prohibit: The "please put away your cell phone" rule is intended to cut off participants from external social networks and force them to focus on the network of relationships being formed within the venue.
Guide: Rules guide the relationship network by setting the basic interaction grammar, making it develop in a more unpredictable and risky direction.
Space as Actor: p4's use of non-traditional spaces is a major feature. Space is no longer a neutral container, but an active accomplice.
Case Study: From "Sculpture Table" to "510" - Network Topology Reconstruction under Space Compression. In 2021, p4 moved from a large factory building with "two hundred square meters and eight meters high" to an office with only "16 square meters". This drastic spatial change provides us with an excellent case to observe the dynamics of space.
In large factories, wide spaces allow for great physical distance between participants. This makes the position of the "peeper" very safe, and connections between individuals require greater initiative to establish. The network is sparse and polycentric in the initial stage.
In the "510" office, the extremely small space (non-human actors) forcibly compresses the interpersonal distance. The founder of p4 described: "Everyone who came had to squeeze together, so that connection had to happen." Here, unintentional physical contact and unavoidable eye contact have become the norm. The space itself minimizes the threshold for building relationships, whether awkward, conflictual or intimate. It rudely deprives "peepers" of their safe distance and forces everyone to immediately become a closely connected node in the network. It can be said that the space "510", with its own physical properties, has powerfully promoted the densification of the network and the rapid formation of communities.
3.3 The invisibility of the "architect" and the dispersion of power
After completing the initial setting of the network through recruitment, rules and space, the "architect" (usually the founder or core organizer) often chooses to be "invisible" or retreat to the margins during the event. This seems to be a transfer of power, aiming to achieve a "decentralized" and self-generated field.
However, from the perspective of Foucault's power analysis, this is not the disappearance of power, but the dispersion and transformation of power. The architect's power has been deeply inscribed in the "physical laws" of the entire network through the rules he/she designs and the spaces he/she chooses. He/she no longer needs to control the field by giving direct orders, as the field itself regulates itself according to his/her blueprint. The "freedom" that participants gain in the venue is actually a kind of "controlled freedom" within carefully designed boundaries.
The analysis in this chapter thus reveals the complexity of P4 Theater "creation" phase. It is a "groundbreaking" process full of strategy and politics. Through a series of exquisite designs, the "architect" "translated" his intentions into the basic operating logic of the entire network, and successfully involved a group of heterogeneous and unrelated actors into a "problem" he set, paving the way for the next stage - the comprehensive generation and game of the network.
Chapter 3 The Generation of Network: NPC Catalysis and Player Game
If the function of the "architect" is to draw a blueprint for the network and inject initial "potential energy", then the real vitality of the network is reflected in its internal dynamic generation process. This chapter will focus on the evolution of the p4 field as the event progresses, using the "architect-NPC-player-voyeur" four-dimensional model to trace in detail how a sparse collection of unfamiliar individuals is gradually "translated" into a tight and dynamic network of actors. This process begins with the "benefit conferment" of NPC as a catalyst, passes through the critical "recruitment" of "players" by "peepers", and finally leads to the emergence of the community as a result of "mobilization" in the complex game of "players".
4.1 "Benefit Granting" of NPC: Catalyst to Start Network Transformation
In the initial stage of the p4 field, although the participants have been "problematized" and placed in an environment full of rules and spatial power, the network is usually still in a wait-and-see, high-tension state of silence. It is often the "NPCs" (non-player characters) in our models that break this deadlock and initiate network transformation. In p4's practice, NPCs are not "minor characters" in the traditional dramatic sense, but core actors programmed to perform specific tasks and serve as network catalysts. Their functions perfectly correspond to the second moment of "translation" in ANT - "Interessement".
"Benefit conferring" refers to an actor using a series of devices and strategies to "seduce" and "lock" other actors, making them "interested" in joining their own network, and at the same time cutting off their connections with other networks. The NPC in p4 achieves this function in the following ways
Creating "events" to attract attention: NPCs create the first "event" in an otherwise homogeneous field by performing simple, repetitive or even bizarre actions (such as endlessly drawing lines on the ground and asking everyone the same question). This event is like a magnet, forcibly attracting the wandering eyes (attention network) of the "peepers", forcing them to shift their attention from their inner monologue or observation of the environment to the action that is taking place and needs to be interpreted.
Provide a "low-risk" interaction entrance: Since the behavior of NPCs is predictable, non-emotional, and programmed, the social risk of interacting with them is much lower than interacting with a completely unknown and unpredictable "peeper". When an NPC hands you an item, it is a clear, scripted "proposal" that provides hesitant participants with a relatively safe transition into the "player" role.
Interpreting the field as "living rules": The actions of NPCs are the embodiment of the abstract rules set by the "architect". Their presence allows other participants to learn the "grammar" of this strange world through observation, thereby lowering the cognitive threshold for participation.
Through these methods, the NPC successfully "seduce" the participants, pulling them out of their isolation and inward contraction, and creating the necessary conditions for the next stage - "recruitment" to occur.
4.2 From "voyeur" to "player": a phenomenology of topological transition
Enrollment is the most critical and fragile step in the network formation process. It refers to actors successfully assigning and locking roles to other members, making them accept and start playing them. In the field of p4, this is embodied in the functional position of the participant from "peeper" to "player" topological transition. This transition was not a simple decision, but a phenomenological event full of internal struggles and external pressures.
Transition critical point: This critical point is usually triggered by a direct "call". This call may come from an NPC (such as asking you a question directly), or from a participant who has become a "player" (such as inviting you to join their game), or even from the silent pressure of the atmosphere of the field. At this moment, the "peeper's" safe distance is broken, and he/she is pushed to a crossroads where a choice must be made.
"Shooting" as a special way of transition: As the founder of p4 emphasized, the act of picking up a camera or mobile phone and "shooting" constitutes a unique way of transition in the p4 field. It is neither a fully engaged "player" nor a completely alienated "voyeur", but a "suspended" participation. Through the action of "shooting", the actor not only maintains a certain aesthetic distance from the event, but also actively intervenes and constructs the meaning of the event through the selection of shooting objects, composition, etc. This behavior enables participants to occupy a reflexive (self-reflexive) position and find a unique and subjective foothold of their own between "seeing" and "doing". It is p4's original development of the traditional participation model.
Consequences of the jump: Once an individual completes this jump, whether as a "player" or a "photographer", his/her position in the network topology has fundamentally changed. He/she changes from a passive observer of the network to an active constructor. Every action he/she takes will create ripples that affect other nodes in the network, and must also bear the risks and responsibilities that come with the action.
4.3 The game of "players" and the emergence of "community"
When enough participants are "recruited" as "players," the entire p4 field enters its core stage: a complex interactive gaming network dominated by "players." This corresponds to the last moment of "translation" in ANT - "mobilization". At this stage, the recruited members no longer play passive roles, but actively and spontaneously act on behalf of the interests of the entire network, allowing the network as a whole to operate stably and reproduce itself.
Complex relationships between players: The interactions between players generate a variety of relationship types, including collaboration, confrontation, negotiation, imitation, betrayal, etc. These relationships are fluid and unstable, and together they weave a complex and ever-changing "event script." Meaning is no longer preset by "architects" but "emerges" from these unpredictable games.
The emergence of community: The "state of blending" appears during the game process of players. At a specific moment, "community" will emerge as a peak experience. Using Victor Turner's theory, we can accurately define this community as "Communitas". It usually occurs in the following situations
Complete tasks together: When a group of players successfully collaborate toward a common goal (no matter how absurd), a sense of collective accomplishment transcends individual boundaries.
Shared failure: When a collective attempt fails and all participants face the ensuing embarrassment, silence, or frustration, a deeper connection based on "shared vulnerability" is established.
Sharing a taboo or secret: The "meme" or secret generated in the field and understood only by those present constitutes a strong link that separates this temporary group from the outside world.
The emergence of this "fusion state" marks the peak of p4's network assembly. At this moment, isolated individuals were successfully "mobilized" to form a temporary, efficient network of actors full of emotional energy. At this point, P4 Theater's core goal of "generating a community" has been realized through specific and non-replicable events.
Chapter 4 Critical Reflection: The Ethics of Failure, Regenerative Power and the Price of the Real
If the analysis of P4 Theater only stops at praising its generating mechanism and affirming its community experience, it will inevitably fall into a naive romanticism. A rigorous academic study must conduct a critical reflection on its claimed concepts and actual operations. P4 TheaterAs a radical social laboratory, while breaking the old framework, does it give birth to new and more hidden power structures? Does its persistent pursuit of "truth" come with ethical risks that cannot be ignored? What critical value does its unique "ethic of failure" have in the contemporary art ecology? This chapter will focus on these issues and carry out critical reflection from three levels, aiming to reveal the complex contradictions and profound tensions behind p4 practice.
5.1 The Ethics of Failure: "Embracing Failure" as a Method
In P4 Theater's self-narration and practice, "failure" is a core concept that is repeatedly emphasized - from the naming of "Loser Salon and Loser Alliance" to the calmness of "mistakes can only be concluded after being proven." This constitutes p4's most distinctive ethical stance. Rather than viewing failure as an accident to be avoided, it elevates it to a necessary methodological and ethical principle.
Resistance to consumerist "experience": We can refer to Claire Bishop's critique of mainstream participatory art in Artificial Hell as a reference. Bishop pointed out that the essence of many so-called "immersive" or "participatory" projects is to provide middle-class consumers with a well-designed, safe and controllable "experience product" that ultimately leads to pleasure. Under this logic, negative experiences such as "failure", "embarrassment" and "conflict" are strictly excluded. p4's "ethics of failure" constitutes a direct resistance to this logic of consumerism. It refuses to promise a smooth, enjoyable experience and instead throws participants into a situation filled with uncertainty that can lead to frustration and discomfort. What it provides is not a "work" for consumption, but an "event" that requires participants to bear together with their own vulnerability.
The social meaning of "failed community": The community generated by p4 can therefore be defined as a "failed community". The bonds of community are not based on shared success or identity, but on shared risks of failure and shared witnessing of each other's vulnerability. In a highly competitive social environment where "success studies" are highly valued, such a space that can legitimize "failure" and find connection and strength has a profound social and psychological comfort function. It provides a temporary asylum (asylum) for individuals who feel marginalized or "failed" in the mainstream value system.
However, this embrace of failure is not without its problems. Is it possible that it has evolved into a romanticization of "incompetence" that eliminates actors' political agency to change reality? Will the emphasis on "failure" screen out those participants who are unwilling or unable to withstand such psychological pressure, thus creating another form of exclusion in fact? These are the tensions that must be faced within an "ethics of failure."
5.2 New Power Generation: An Examination of the Myth of "Decentralization"
P4 Theater prides itself on its "decentralized", "co-created" and "anti-authority" stance. However, any field that claims to be "without power" is most worthy of us using Foucault's power analysis to examine the regeneration of new power relations. To what extent is p4's "decentralization" a reality, and to what extent is it a carefully constructed "myth"?
The unshakable meta-power of the "architect": Although the founder or core organizer (architect) chose to be "invisible" during the event, as analyzed in Chapter 2, they have already mastered the most fundamental "meta-power" by designing the initial rules, space, and recruitment. They define the boundaries and basic syntax of the entire "game". The "freedom" of participants is freedom within this preset framework. This kind of power is structural, more diffuse, less visible, and therefore potentially more stable.
The "Charisma" authority of the founder's charisma: In p4's texts and practices, the founder He Fa's personal will and artistic ideas are everywhere. From the introduction of psychoanalysis theory to the philosophical thinking on "failure", his personal imprint is deeply imprinted. Although this kind of "Charismatic" authority based on personal talent, vision and charisma is different from the institutional power of traditional directors, its influence may be more powerful and covert. To what extent is the participants' recognition of the p4 concept a result of following this personal charm? When "anti-authority" itself becomes a kind of authority, is it possible for participants to challenge it?
Invisible levels of "old players" and "new players": In any continuously operating community, a circle structure consisting of "core members" and "marginal members" will naturally form. For p4, there is inevitably an asymmetry in information and experience between those "old players" who have participated many times and deeply understand its "jargon" (terms such as "generation", "disenchantment", "field" and other terms) and unspoken rules, and the "new players" who are entering for the first time. This asymmetry translates into an invisible power relationship. The behavior of veteran players is more likely to be regarded as "examples", and their interpretation of the rules is more authoritative. This may invisibly suppress the spontaneity and creativity of new players, making the so-called "free generation" actually imitating an existing "p4 style".
Therefore, the power analysis of p4 reveals a paradox
In order to realize a decentralized and equal field, p4 must rely on a highly centralized initial design controlled by an "architect"; in order to resist external authority, it may internally generate a new authority based on personal charm and community qualifications. Acknowledging and examining this paradox is key to understanding the complexity of p4.
5.3 The Price of the Real: Ethical Risks from a Lacanian Perspective
P4 TheaterThe most radical pursuit is to capture the "reality" - the "reality that cannot be erased and suppressed". This pursuit can accurately correspond to "the Real" (the Real) in Jacques Lacan's psychoanalysis theory. the Real is the pre-symbolic, traumatic core of reality that transcends language (the symbolic realm) and imagination (the imaginary realm). p4's practice can be seen as a carefully designed "machine", whose purpose is to break the daily symbolic order and imaginative identification, so that the moment of the Real can "pierce" the surface of reality, so that participants can have a shocking experience.
Theater as a "trauma machine": When a participant is asked to perform an embarrassing task in front of everyone, when a heated argument touches the deep personal pain, when the sudden silence makes all disguises invisible... At these moments, the "script" of daily life fails, and the traumatic core of the Real is exposed. This experience is undoubtedly profound and can "liberate" suppressed emotions, but it also comes with huge ethical risks. Does p4 provide participants with adequate psychological preparation and "safety net" to face this possible trauma? When a participant suffers psychological harm during an experience, who in this "decentralized" collective will bear responsibility?
The Gaze of the "Big Other" and Subject Anxiety: The p4 field eliminates the "fourth wall", making every participant completely exposed to the gaze of others (the big Other). This gaze with nowhere to escape will greatly arouse the subject's existential anxiety. As p4's article says: "When you meet naked, you will always feel helpless again under the gaze of the 'big other'." This kind of anxiety is certainly the driving force for "real" reactions, but it may also lead to defensive withdrawal or destructive behavior. To what extent is p4 exploiting this anxiety to achieve its artistic goals? Where are the boundaries of this kind of utilization?
To sum up, p4's pursuit of "truth" is a double-edged sword. It gives his artistic practice unparalleled depth and power, allowing it to access fundamental levels of existence. But at the same time, it also places it in a dangerous ethical terrain. A complete evaluation of p4 must include a sober assessment of the "cost" it may cause. It is not only an artistic community, but also a social and psychological laboratory that needs to take its ethical responsibilities seriously.
Conclusion
6.1 Research summary: P4 Theater as a relational topology laboratory
Through a systematic theoretical construction and case analysis, this study draws a dynamic topological map for the complex practice of P4 Theater in the past ten years. We traverse its seemingly chaotic appearance, delve deeply into its inner generative mechanism, and finally reveal its core logic as a radical sample of contemporary experimental art. The core argument of the study is that the fundamental innovation of p.4 theater stems from its successful ontological transformation from "position" to "relationship". It no longer sees actors as identity entities occupying fixed social "positions"-whether as "actors" or "audiences"-but rather as action nodes that continuously generate their own functions in a fluid network of relationships. Here, action precedes identity and connection defines presence.
To dissect this process, we first critically reviewed the "position"-based topology of traditional drama, and introduced Actor Network Theory (ANT) as a "meta-theory" throughout the text, viewing the field of p.4 as a heterogeneous network "assembled" by human and non-human actors (space, objects, rules, emotions). On this basis, this study originally proposed a four-element dynamic model of "Architect-NPC-Player-Peeper" as a sophisticated analysis tool to track the "translation" process and the flow of functional roles within the network.
Through this theoretical framework, we clearly show that p4's network generation follows a path that can be analyzed: it begins with the "architect"'s foundational "problematization" through rules, space, and recruitment; then, the "NPC" serves as a catalyst to complete the "benefit assignment" to the participants by creating events. "give"; in the most critical link, the individual is "recruited" as an active "player" or a reflexive "photographer" through a phenomenological "leap" full of inner struggle; in the end, in the complex game of "players", the entire network is successfully "mobilized", a Victor Turner (Victor Turner) Turner, "Communitas" based on shared risk can emerge in an unrepeatable moment.
At the same time, this study does not stop at description and praise. In the critical reflection in Chapter 4, we deeply explore the inherent contradictions and tensions of p4 practice. We demonstrate how its "ethics of failure" constitutes a powerful resistance to consumerist art; we examine the regeneration of a new power relationship based on the meta-power of the "architect" and the seniority of the community behind its myth of "decentralization"; and with the help of Jacques Lacan's theory, we reveal the ethical risks and psychological costs that accompany its persistent pursuit of "truth" that cannot be ignored.
6.2 Theoretical contributions and research limitations
The theoretical contribution of this study is mainly reflected in three aspects
Methodological innovation: This article provides a comprehensive analytical framework with sociological and philosophical depth for participatory art and experimental theater research that goes beyond traditional aesthetic judgment and phenomenon description. This framework combines the grand vision of ANT with the micro insights of our original four-component model, demonstrating a possible path for how to systematically study complex, fluid art practices.
Cross-field application and development of theory: By applying ANT to the specific art case of p4, this study not only verified the explanatory power of ANT in the art field, but also enriched and developed the application strategy of ANT through concrete tools such as the "quaternary model".
Promote interdisciplinary dialogue: This study consciously integrates theoretical resources from theater theory, sociology (ANT), psychoanalysis (Lacan), anthropology (Turner) and art criticism (Bishop), aiming to break down disciplinary barriers and explore new possibilities for art research in contemporary theoretical trends.
At the same time, we must be honest about the limitations of this study. First, due to constraints, this study mainly relied on the analysis of public text materials and the interpretation of second-hand experiences, lacking long-term, in-depth fieldwork and participant observation. This makes the analysis of the specific experiences of individual participants potentially insufficient and more of a theoretical deduction. Secondly, this study failed to track the long-term impact of the p4 community after the event-that is, whether and how the experience of this "instantaneous community" was transformed into the participants' daily lives.
These limitations also point out the direction for future research. For example, future research can use more in-depth ethnographic methods to examine how the experience of p4 affects their social relationships and self-perception by following a group of participants over a long period of time. Alternatively, a broader comparative study can be conducted to compare p4 with other domestic and foreign community art projects and alternative organizational forms, so as to locate its uniqueness and universality in a broader perspective.
6.3 Epilogue: Unfinished topology and the social mission of art
The practice of P4 Theater is, by its nature, "generative" and "unfinished". Its topological exploration is always in dynamic change, rejecting any final definition. This may be its most valuable quality today. In a world that is increasingly solidified and "disenchanted" by algorithmic recommendations, virtual social interaction and consumer logic, p4 uses its rough, direct and even risky approach to tenaciously open up a "state of exception", a field where the "iron cage" of modernity is temporarily ineffective.
Here, "playing" is disenchanted, just to allow real encounters to be enchanted; "failure" is embraced, just to allow fragile individuals to connect; "authority" is questioned, just to allow the possibility of co-creation to occur. P4 Theater ultimately reveals to us that community is not a distant utopia, nor is it a ready-made product that can be purchased. It is only when we bravely give up the sense of security conferred by our "position" and devote ourselves wholeheartedly to the unpredictable web of "relationships" that we can experience the fragile and precious reality that we have woven together with our own hands.
This may be the social mission that P4 Theater undertakes at the moment. It reminds us that art can serve far more than just aesthetics or entertainment. It can be a social experiment, an ethical practice, a tool for liberation. It is not only exploring new forms of drama, but also exploring new ways of connection between "people" and "people". It is a painful but necessary exercise that teaches us how to relearn "togetherness" in this age of fragmentation.

P4 Theater and You
2025-07-17
Project and brand narrative
"Devil's Saliva"
The photographer's operation is always a kind of displacement: to replace his personal way of seeing the world with the insidious way of seeing forced on...
Devil's saliva (Las babas del diablo)
Julio Cortázar
No one will ever know how this was revealed. In the first person, or in the second person? Or are you borrowing the shell of the third person plural, or are you constantly forging words that will eventually disappear like smoke? If it can be said like this: I, with the eyes of all living beings, witnessed the moonrise; or: We, it hurts my eyes; especially this sentence: You, the blond woman, were once a flowing cloud, passing over the intertwined faces of mine, you, him, us, and them. --Oh, what a devil.
If I have to talk about it, the most perfect situation is to retreat to the street corner, sip a glass of white wine, and let the machine continue writing alone (I am tapping a machine). This statement is true. Yes, perfect. Because the "hole" that needs to be told is also a machine (another kind, a Contax 1.1.2), and the machine may know the soul of the other machine far better than me, you, and her - the blond woman and Liu Yun -. But my stupidity is only a result of luck. I know very well that if I leave the table, this Remington will turn to stone on the table, with a double deathly silence - the kind of ghostliness that is unique to moving things when they are stagnant. Therefore I must write. One of us must write if all this is to be told. Then, it is better for me to do it. I, a dead person, have less worries than the rest of you. I have nothing but flowing clouds. I can think quietly without any distractions. I can write quietly without distractions (here, another piece of silver passes by, edged with dead gray). I can calmly remember without distractions. I, the dead person (but I am also alive, I have no intention of deceiving, when that moment comes, everything will become clear, because I have to find a broken wall in the end, and I have chosen this end, the end of this story, the source of time, when people want to tell it, this is the sharpest end of all beginnings after all).
Suddenly, I asked myself why I had to tell all this. But if people always ask why they do everything they do, if people just ask why they agree to a dinner party (at this moment, a dove flies by, like a sparrow), or why when someone tells us a wonderful story, After reading a wonderful story, there will be an itch and restlessness in the stomach immediately, and the person will not stop until he rushes into the office next door and tells the story again. Only then will the person feel comfortable and satisfied, and can return to his work. As far as I know, no one has ever explained this. Therefore, the best way is to put aside all shyness and tell the story. Because at the end of the day, no one should be ashamed of breathing or putting on shoes; if we do these things, we do them. And when the weird comes, when we find a spider in our shoes, or feel a piece of broken glass while breathing, then we must tell what happened, tell it to colleagues in the office, or to the doctor.
Oh, doctor, every breath... has to be spoken, has to quiet that annoying turmoil in the stomach.
Since we have to talk, let's establish some order. Let's go down the steps of this mansion and go back to Sunday, November 7th, exactly one month ago. After descending five steps, we have entered that Sunday, bathed in an unexpected sun that hardly belongs to Paris in November, and my heart is filled with the desire to wander around, watch, and hunt for images (because we were, and I was, a person who captures light and shadows). I know that the most difficult thing will be to find the way to tell the story, and I am not afraid of repetition. The reason why it is difficult is that no one knows for sure whether what I am really telling is me, or what has already happened, or what I see at the moment (flowing clouds, occasionally, a dove), or whether I am just telling a truth that only belongs to me, and that truth will no longer be true if it is not for my stomach, for my desire to run away and to end it all in some way, no matter what it will be in the end.
Let us tell the story slowly. As we write, we will see what will happen. If someone replaces me, if I have nothing to say, if the clouds dissipate and something else emerges (because this cannot always be watching the clouds drift by, and occasionally, a dove), if all this... After the word "ruo", what should I continue, and how should I draw an impeccable end to this sentence? But once I start asking questions, there is nothing I can do; it is better to tell, and the telling itself may be an answer, at least, to someone who will read it.
Roberto Michel, a French-Chilean, translator, and photographer in his spare time, walked out of No. 11, Rue de Princes, on Sunday, November 7th of that year. (At this moment, two smaller flowers, trimmed with silver, floated by). He has spent three weeks on the French translation of Professor José Norberto Allende's monograph on legal avoidance and appeals at the University of Santiago in Chile. It is rare for Paris to have wind, let alone the kind of wind that whirls around the street corners and whips against the old wooden shutters. Behind the windows, frightened ladies are talking in various words about the increasingly unpredictable weather in recent years. But the sun is also there. It controls the strong wind and makes friends with cats. Therefore, nothing can stop me from going to the docks of the Seine to roam and capture a few frames of light and shadow for the ancient prison and Sainte-Chapelle. It was only ten o'clock, and I calculated that by eleven o'clock, the light should be just right, the best that can be achieved in autumn. In order to kill the light, I drifted to the Ile Saint-Louis, walked along the Anjou river promenade, stopped for a moment, and stared. At the Rozan Residence, I recited a few verses of Apollinaire to myself. Whenever I passed by the Rozan Residence, these verses would come to my mind on their own (although I should have remembered another poet, but Michel has always been stubborn). Then, when the storm suddenly died down and the sun suddenly swelled at least twice as much (warmer, I mean, but essentially the same), I perched on the parapet and felt a terrible, unparalleled bliss on that Sunday morning.
Among the countless methods of combating the void, photography is one of the supreme. This skill should be taught early in childhood as it requires discipline, aesthetic education, a keen eye and a steady hand.
This is not like an ordinary reporter, spying on lies and capturing the foolish profile of a big shot as he walks out of No. 10 Downing Street. However, no matter what, once you carry a camera, you feel like you have a responsibility, a responsibility to be alert at all times, not to miss the rapid and sweet rebound of the sunlight on an ancient stone, or the running arc of a girl with flying braids carrying a loaf of bread or a bottle of milk. Michel knows very well that the photographer's operation is always a kind of displacement: replacing his personal way of viewing the world with the insidious way of viewing forced on him by the camera (at this moment, a giant cloud of almost pure black drifts by). But he had no doubts. He knew that just taking a Contax camera out with him would be enough to regain that careless tone, that frameless vision, that light without aperture or 1/250 second shutter speed. At this very moment ("this moment", what a foolish lie), I could have sat on the wall of the riverside, watching the black and red barges flowing past, without any thought of photographic composition in my mind, and just surrendering myself to the flow of all things, running still along with time. And the wind has stopped.
I then walked along the Bourbon Strand to the tip of the island, that small, secret square (it is said to be secret because of its small size, not its secludedness, because it exposes the whole chest to the river and the sky). I love it, I love it deeply. There was only a man and a woman there, and of course, there were also a flock of pigeons; perhaps a few of them were flying over the scene I saw at this moment. I jumped onto the parapet and let the sun wrap and bind me, entrusting my face, ears, and hands to it (I had put my gloves in my pocket). I had no desire to take pictures, so I lit a cigarette for comfort; I think the moment I put the match close to the tobacco, I saw the boy for the first time.
At first I thought it was a couple, it looked more like a boy and his mother, but at the same time I understood that he was not walking with his mother, they were a couple, the meaning we give to "a couple" in those partners leaning against the parapet or hugging each other on the benches in the square. Since I had nothing to do, I had a lot of time to think about why the boy was so nervous. Like a pony or a hare, he put his hands into his pockets, then pulled out one, and then the other, combing his fingertips through his hair, constantly changing his posture, and especially why he was so scared. Yes, fear was evident in every gesture of his, a fear suffocated by shame, an impulse to retreat, that impulse appeared in his body, as if he was on the verge of escape, but was forcibly maintained by the last pitiful bit of dignity.
It was so clear - just five meters away, on the tip of the island, we were the only ones alone - that at first the boy's fear prevented me from seeing the blonde woman clearly. Now, looking back, I feel that in that first moment, I saw her face more clearly (she turned around suddenly, like a copper weather vane), her eyes, her...
The eyes are there), when I vaguely understood what might be happening to the boy, I told myself that it was worth staying and staring (the wind swept away the words, leaving only an inaudible whisper). I believe I know how to gaze, if I know anything at all. And all gaze is permeated with falsehood, because it throws us to the farthest place outside ourselves, without any guarantee. Instead, it's sniffing, or (but Michel is easily distracted, so don't let him chant as he pleases). In any case, if you understand the possible falseness in advance, gazing becomes possible; perhaps, you only need to make the right choice between "gazing" and "the thing being gazed at", and peel off the layers of foreign clothes for everything. However, all this is difficult after all.
Regarding the boy, I remembered his image before his actual body (this will become clear later); and about the woman, I am now convinced that I remembered her body far better than her image. She is slender and graceful. These two words are not enough to describe her, and it is unfair. She was wearing an almost black fur coat, almost floor-length, almost gorgeous. The entire morning wind (there was only a breeze at the moment, and it was not cold) had penetrated her blond hair that cut into her pale and gloomy face - two more unfair words - leaving the whole world alone and horribly abandoned in front of her black eyes. Those eyes were like two falcons, falling above all things, like two leaps into the void, like two streams of green mud. I'm not describing, I'd rather understand. And I said, two streams of green mud.
To be fair, the boy was well-dressed, wearing a pair of yellow gloves that I was sure belonged to his brother, perhaps a law or sociology student; it was laughable to see the fingertips of the gloves poking out of his jacket pocket. For a long time, I didn't see his face, only a profile that was not stupid-a frightened bird, the angel in Brother Filippo's painting, a bowl of milk and rice cloth, and the back of a young boy who was eager to practice judo. He had fought once or twice for a certain idea or a certain sister. From his age of fourteen or fifteen years, it can be inferred that he was fed and groomed by his parents, but had no money in his pocket. He had to discuss with his companions for a long time before he dared to decide whether he wanted a cup of coffee, a cup of cognac, or a pack of cigarettes. He should be the kind of person who would wander in the streets, thinking about his female classmates, thinking about how wonderful it would be to go to a movie, watch the latest movie, or buy a few novels, a few ties, or a few bottles of liquor with green and white labels. In his home (that home should be decent, with lunch served on time at twelve o'clock, romantic landscape paintings on the walls, a dark foyer and a rattan umbrella stand next to the door), time will fall slowly, like rain, the time to study, the time to become what his mother expected, the time to become like his father, the time to write letters to his aunt in Avignon. That's why there are so many streets, the whole river flows for him (but not a penny), and the fifteen-year-old mysterious city, with the code on its door, its shuddering cat, the thirty-franc bag of French fries, the pornographic magazines folded four times, the empty loneliness in the pocket, the happy encounters, and the enthusiasm for many incomprehensible things, but they are illuminated by a kind of complete love, a kind of complete openness like the wind and the streets.
This biography is for boys, and for any boy. However, the one in front of me became isolated and unique because of the presence of the blonde woman. She was chattering to him. (I am tired of repeating it, but two more long, broken clouds floated by. I think that that morning, I never looked at the sky once, because as soon as I realized what happened between the boy and the woman, I could only stare at them, wait, stare at them, and then...)
All in all, the boy was so disturbed that it didn't take much effort to guess what had happened just a few minutes ago, or at most half an hour ago. The boy reached the tip of the island, saw the woman, and was smitten with her. And what the woman is waiting for is exactly this, because she is right there, waiting for this. Or maybe the boy arrived first, and she saw him from a balcony or a car, so she walked up to him and struck up a conversation casually. She was sure from the beginning that he would be scared and want to run away, but she would naturally stay, puffing out her chest and looking sullen, pretending to be experienced and adventurous. The rest is easy, because everything happened five meters away from me, and anyone can measure every stage of this game, this absurd fencing; its greatest charm lies not in its present, but in the foreshadowing of its outcome. The boy would eventually excuse himself to a date, an obligation no matter what, and then stumble away confused, longing for a leisurely pace, yet naked and exposed to the mocking gaze that would follow him all the way. Or he would stay, charmed, or simply unable to take the initiative, and then the woman would start caressing his face, ruffling his hair, words lost to words, and then suddenly take him by the arm and lead him away. Unless, with an irritability that might have begun to be colored by desire and the risk of taking risks, he mustered up the courage to put his arms around her waist and kiss her. All this could happen, but it hasn't happened yet. And Michelle, with a kind of evil pleasure, sat on the parapet, almost unconsciously raising the camera, preparing to take a picturesque photo: in the corner of the island, an unusual pair of men and women were talking and staring.
Strangely, this scene (this nothingness, almost nothingness: two people there, very different in age) has an unsettling aura about it. I once thought that I gave it to myself, and that my photos, if I took them, would restore everything to its dull truth. I wanted to know what the man in the gray hat sitting behind the wheel of the parked car on the pier leading to the pier was thinking about, whether he was reading a newspaper or taking a nap. I had just discovered him because the people in the parked car had almost disappeared, lost in that poor, private cage that had lost its beauty by depriving it of movement and danger. The car, however, was always there, forming (or distorting) part of the island. A car: like a street light, a park bench. But never as good as the wind, not as good as the sun, not as good as those ever-living substances made for skin and eyes, not as good as that boy and that woman, those unique two people who were put here to change this island, to show me this island in another way. Well, maybe the man reading the newspaper was also paying attention to what was happening, and feeling the malicious pleasure that came from total anticipation just like me. At this moment, the woman turned around gently and placed the boy between her and...
I could almost see their silhouettes between the parapets. He was taller than her, but not by much, yet she enveloped him, hovering over him like a dark cloud (her laughter, suddenly, like a whip of feathers), crushing him with just her presence, her smile, her hand across the air. Why wait? Use an aperture of sixteen, and use a frame that does not let the ugly black car enter the lens, but can accommodate the tree. The tree is necessary to break up an overly gray space...
I raised the camera, pretending to examine a focal length that did not include them, and then I lurked, convinced that I would eventually capture that finishing touch, that condensed expression, that synchronized rhythm with life that was destroyed by the rigid image when it split time-unless we could select that imperceptible, essential moment. I don't have to wait long. The woman was advancing her project of tenderly binding the boy, stripping away the last remaining freedom from him piece by piece in a slow and sweet torture.
I imagined the possible outcome (a small, frothy cloud now appeared, hanging almost alone in the sky), I foresaw their arrival in the room (probably the ground floor, which she would fill with countless cushions and cats), I imagined the boy's panic, his desperate determination to pretend, to let it be, to pretend that nothing was new to him. I closed my eyes. If I had closed my eyes, I would have rehearsed the whole scene in my mind: the mocking kiss, the woman gently pushing away the hands that tried to untie her clothes like in the novel, and placing him on a bed covered with lilac quilts. Then she forced him to take off his clothes, like a real mother and son, under the dim light of a milky white glass. Then, everything will end as normal, maybe. But maybe, everything will be different, the boy's enlightenment will not be able to pass, will be blocked, after that long foreplay, those clumsiness, those anxious caresses, those busy hands, will eventually dissipate into who knows what, a kind of independent, lonely and self-sufficient joy, or an arrogant rejection mixed with the art of killing and disturbing that wounded innocence. It may be so, it may well be so; the woman who does not seek a lover in a boy, but who at the same time possesses him for a purpose that is incomprehensible except by imagining it as a cruel game, as an insatiable lust, as an excitement for another other who can never be the boy.
Michel is a sinner of literature, a weaver of illusions. He loved nothing more than imagining exceptions, individuals outside of their species, monsters that weren't always disgusting. But this woman herself invites fiction, and perhaps gives enough clues to touch upon the truth.
Before she left, before my contemplative memory filled many days and nights to come, I decided not to waste any more time. I put everything into the frame (including the tree, the parapet, the eleven o'clock sunshine), and then I pressed the shutter. Just in time to understand, the two of them were aware of it and were looking at me. The boy was surprised and inquiring; while she was full of anger and decisive hostility. Her...
Both the body and the face know that they have been stolen and shamefully imprisoned in a small chemical image.
I could describe it in detail, but it would be of no value. The woman said no one had the right to take pictures without permission and asked me to hand over the film. All this was said in a dry and clear voice with a pure Parisian accent, which continued to rise in timbre and pitch with every word. It doesn't matter to me whether I hand over the roll of film or not, but anyone who knows me knows that asking for things from me must be done in a gentle way. As a result, I am limited to stating my point of view: not only is photography not banned in public places, but it enjoys the strongest official and private support. And as I spoke, I was enjoying with a mocking pleasure how the boy flinched, fell behind - simply by not moving - and then suddenly (almost unbelievably) turned around and ran away, the poor man thinking he was just walking, but really running, speeding past the car like a wisp of a virgin's hair, dissipating in the morning air.
However, the Virgin's hairspring was also called the devil's saliva, and Michel had to endure those trivial accusations, hearing himself called nosy and an idiot, while he deliberately tried hard to smile and declined them all with a few simple shaking of his head. What a cheap rejection. Just when all this was starting to bore me, I heard a knock on the door of a car. The man in the gray hat was there, staring at us. Only at that moment did I realize that he was also a character in this comedy.
He started walking toward us, holding the newspaper he pretended to read. What I remember most clearly is the grimace that twisted the corners of his mouth. The grimace made his face full of wrinkles. Something shifted and deformed on his face because his lips were trembling. The grimace was like an independent and living thing, moving around his lips without the control of his will. But everything else is frozen, a clown with a whitened face, or a man without blood, with dull and shriveled skin, sunken eyes, and the black holes in his nostrils are clearly visible, darker than his eyebrows, hair or that black tie.
He walked cautiously, as if the pavement stung his feet; I caught a glimpse of his patent leather shoes, with soles so thin that I could feel every bit of roughness in the street. I don't know why I came down from the parapet, and I don't know exactly why I decided not to hand over the photos, why I refused a request that I could detect as fear and cowardice. The clown and the woman exchanged glances in silence: we formed an unbearable perfect triangle, something that must break with a snap. I smiled in their faces, then turned and walked away, more slowly, I guess, than the boy. When I reached the first row of houses and approached the iron trestle, I looked back at them. They didn't move, but the man had already thrown away the newspaper; I felt that the woman, with her back to the parapet, was rubbing her hands on the stone, with the classic and absurd gesture of a besieged person seeking an exit.
What happened next was right here, almost at this moment, in a room on the fifth floor. It took Michel several days to develop the photos of that Sunday; he photographed the Convent and Sainte-Chapelle exactly as they should be. He found two or three forgotten test shots, a botched attempt to capture a cat perched startlingly on top of a street urinal, and the photo of a blonde woman and a boy. The negative was so good that he developed an enlargement. The enlargement was so good that he made a larger one, almost a poster. It had not occurred to him (he asked himself now, he kept asking himself) why only the pictures of the ancient prison were worth the trouble. Among all the photos, only the snapshot at the tip of the island interested him; he pinned the enlarged sample to the wall of the room, and on the first day, he just stared at it, remembering, and performing the comparison between "memory" and "passed reality", a melancholy operation; it was a petrified memory, like all photos, lacking nothing, even, or especially, not even "nothingness" - the real coagulant of that scene. The woman is here, the boy is here, the trees above them stand frozen, the sky is as solid as the stone of the wall, and the clouds and stones are mixed into an indivisible substance (at this moment, a cloud with sharp edges floats by, like running in the head of the storm). In the first two days, I accepted everything I had done, from the photos themselves to the enlargements on the wall. I never even asked myself why I would interrupt the translation of José Norberto Allende's monograph just to see the woman's face and the dark stain on the wall again. The first surprise was silly; I never thought that when we look at a photo, our eyes repeat the position and angle of the lens; these are things we take for granted and no one thinks about. From my chair, across the typewriter, I stared at the photo three meters away, and then I realized that I had placed myself right in the crosshairs of the camera. That's fine; it's undoubtedly the most perfect way to view a photograph, although squinting may have its charms and even its discoveries. Every few minutes, for example, when I could not find the right words in French to express what José Alberto Allende expressed so beautifully in Spanish, I would raise my eyes and stare at the picture; sometimes it was the woman who attracted me, sometimes it was the boy, sometimes it was the pavement where a dry leaf happened to fall, adding value to a corner of the picture in a wonderful way. Then, I would take a break from my work and happily merge into that morning soaked in photos again, with a hint of sarcasm, recalling the angry face of the woman when she asked me to hand over the photos, the absurd and tragic escape of the boy, and the appearance of the white-faced man. Deep down, I was pleased with myself; my departure was not a glorious one, for if the French were endowed with the gift of swift response, I could not see why I should have chosen to leave without giving them a full demonstration of their privileges, immunities, and civil rights. What matters, what really matters, is that I helped the boy escape in time (if...
The validity of my theories has not yet been fully proven, but the escape itself seems to have proved everything). Out of pure nosy, I gave him a chance to finally use his fear to do something useful, and now he would regret it, feel small, and feel less than a man. But that was better than being in the company of a woman who could stare at him with that island gaze; Michel was occasionally a puritan who believed that people should not be corrupted by violence. After all, that photo was an act of kindness.
But I stare at it, between paragraphs of my work, not because it is an act of kindness. At that moment, I didn't know why I was staring at it and why I nailed the large sample to the wall; perhaps, this is the case for all destined things, and that is the condition for its completion. I believe that the almost imperceptible trembling of the leaves did not alert me. I believe that I just started a sentence and then ended it successfully. Customs, like giant herbariums. Ultimately, an eighty-by-sixty-by-sixty photo, like a screen on which a movie is projected, shows a woman and a boy talking at the far end of the island, a tree shaking its dry leaves above them.
But those hands were too much. I had just written: Donc, la seconde clé réside dans la nature intrinsèque des difficultés que les sociétés… (The second key therefore lies in the intrinsic nature of social dilemmas…) - and I saw the woman's hand, which was slowly beginning to close, one finger after another. There is nothing left in myself, only a French sentence that can never be completed, a typewriter falling to the ground, a creaking and shaking chair, and a fog. The boy lowered his head, like a boxer unable to fight anymore, waiting for the fatal blow; he raised the collar of his coat, looking more than ever like a prisoner, a perfect victim who had contributed to the disaster. Now the woman was whispering in his ear, and the hand opened again and touched his cheek, caressing, caressing, burning him without a trace of eagerness. The boy was more wary than panic. He glanced over the woman's shoulder in that direction once or twice, while she continued to speak and explain something. The explanation always forced him to look in the direction where Michelle knew that a car was parked, the direction where the man in the gray hat was. That person was carefully excluded from the photo, but reflected in the boy's pupils, (how could he still doubt it now?) echoing in the woman's words, in the woman's hands, in the woman's agent-like presence. When I saw the man coming, stopping near them, staring at them, with his hands in his pockets, with an air that was both bored and stern, like a master who is waiting for his dog to finish playing in the square and is ready to blow the whistle, I understood, if that can be called understanding, what was about to happen, what should have happened, what should have happened in that moment, among those people, after I had intruded and naively disturbed an order, an order that had not yet happened but was about to happen, about to be fulfilled. But what I imagined at the time was far less terrifying than reality. That woman, she did not come for herself, she did not come for her own pleasure to caress, to encourage, to seduce, to take away that fledgling angel, to play with his fears and his yearning grace. The real master is waiting...
With a smug smile, convinced that his plan had succeeded; he was not the first to send a woman as a vanguard to bring him prisoners bound with flowers. The rest will be as simple as that car, any house, those drinks, those exciting pictures, too late tears, and waking up in hell. And I am powerless. This time, I am absolutely powerless. My power was once a picture, right there. In that picture, they were taking revenge on me, showing me without any cover what was about to happen. The photos have been taken, time has passed; we are so far apart from each other, the corruption must have been completed, the tears must have been shed, and the rest is just speculation and sorrow. Suddenly, the order was reversed, they were alive, moving, deciding and being decided, moving towards their future; and I, on this side, a prisoner in a different time, a prisoner in a room on the fifth floor, I don't know who the woman, the man and the child are, I can only be a lens of my camera, something rigid, unable to intervene. They threw the most terrible mockery in my face, that is, in the face of my powerlessness, they have the power to "decide"; that is, the boy looked at the clown with the whitened face again, and I knew that he was about to accept that the offer contained money or deception, and I could not shout to him to run away, or just use a new photo, a small and humble intervention to destroy the scaffolding constructed of saliva and perfume. Everything will be in this moment, in that...
Instantly, it was resolved; there was a tremendous silence that had nothing to do with physical silence. That thing is stretching and building. I believe I shouted, I shouted at the top of my lungs, and at that same second I felt myself getting closer, ten centimeters, step by step, the tree spinning its branches gracefully in the foreground, a stain on the parapet sliding out of the frame, the woman's face, turning towards me, with The shock grew bigger and bigger, and then I turned a little, I mean the camera turned a little, without losing the woman, and started to get closer to the man who looked at me with black eye sockets. He looked at me in shock and anger, wanting to wash me away in the air. At that moment, I glimpsed a large, out-of-focus bird that flapped its wings and flew across the frame. I leaned against my wall, I was happy because the boy had just escaped and I saw him running, again in sharp focus, with his hair flying in the wind, as he finally learned to fly around the island, reached the trestle, and returned to the city. The second time, he slipped away from them; the second time, I helped him escape, I returned him to his precarious paradise. Panting, I faced them; there was no further progress, the game was over. The woman, with only one shoulder and a strand of hair, was roughly cut off by the frame; and the man, facing me, with his mouth slightly open, could see a black tongue trembling, he slowly raised his hands and stretched out towards the foreground, still in perfect focus at that moment. Then he turned into a blur, obliterating the island and the tree. I closed my eyes and didn't want to see it anymore. I covered my face and cried like a fool.
